conceptual.question: What is the bias-variance tradeoff? How does it guide model selection?
conceptual.model_answer: Bias measures how far a model's average prediction is from the true value — high bias means the model underfits, failing to capture underlying patterns. Variance measures how sensitive the model is to fluctuations in the training set — high variance means the model overfits, memorising noise. The tradeoff arises because reducing bias (increasing model complexity) tends to increase variance, and vice versa. Total expected error = Bias² + Variance + Irreducible Noise. In practice: simple models (linear regression) have high bias/low variance; complex models (deep trees, large NNs) have low bias/high variance. Regularisation, ensembling, and cross-validation are the primary tools to navigate this tradeoff.
evaluation_criteria: Defines bias and variance precisely, not just intuitively
States the decomposition: Bias² + Variance + Irreducible Error
Connects to underfitting and overfitting correctly
Mentions at least one mitigation strategy per side
common_mistakes: Conflating bias with intercept/constant term in linear models
Saying 'more data always fixes variance' — true asymptotically but not always practical
Not mentioning irreducible noise as the floor on total error
conceptual.follow_up: How does regularisation (L1 vs L2) specifically shift this tradeoff?

conceptual.question: Explain the difference between generative and discriminative models. Give one example of each.
conceptual.model_answer: Discriminative models learn the conditional distribution P(Y|X) directly — they model the decision boundary between classes. Examples: logistic regression, SVMs, most neural classifiers. Generative models learn the joint distribution P(X, Y) = P(X|Y)P(Y), which implicitly models how the data was generated. At inference, Bayes' theorem gives P(Y|X). Examples: Naive Bayes, GMMs, VAEs, GANs. Key tradeoff: discriminative models are generally more accurate for classification when labelled data is sufficient; generative models can handle missing data, generate new samples, and work in semi-supervised settings.
evaluation_criteria: Correctly identifies discriminative = P(Y|X), generative = P(X,Y) or P(X|Y)
Gives valid examples of each
Articulates when each is preferable
common_mistakes: Saying GANs 'learn P(X)' without mentioning the conditional structure
Claiming discriminative models are always better
Confusing generative with unsupervised
conceptual.follow_up: Can a model be both? Where does a conditional VAE sit?

conceptual.question: What is cross-entropy loss? Why is it preferred over MSE for classification?
conceptual.model_answer: Cross-entropy loss for classification is H(p, q) = -Σ p(x) log q(x), where p is the true label distribution (one-hot for hard labels) and q is the model's predicted probability. For binary classification this reduces to -[y log(ŷ) + (1-y) log(1-ŷ)]. It is preferred over MSE for classification because: (1) MSE applied to sigmoid/softmax outputs produces vanishing gradients when the model is confidently wrong, since the gradient is proportional to (ŷ - y)·σ'(z) which saturates. Cross-entropy gradients are proportional to (ŷ - y) directly, keeping gradients healthy. (2) Cross-entropy has a probabilistic interpretation — minimising it is equivalent to maximum likelihood estimation under the model's output distribution.
evaluation_criteria: States the formula or at minimum the form -Σ y log(ŷ)
Identifies the vanishing gradient problem with MSE + sigmoid
Mentions MLE equivalence
common_mistakes: Saying MSE 'doesn't work at all' — it works, it just trains slowly
Confusing cross-entropy with KL divergence (they differ by the entropy of p)
conceptual.follow_up: How does label smoothing modify cross-entropy and why does it help?

conceptual.question: Explain how gradient descent works. What are the key differences between SGD, mini-batch GD, and full-batch GD?
conceptual.model_answer: Gradient descent minimises a loss function L(θ) by iteratively updating parameters in the direction of the negative gradient: θ ← θ - η·∇L(θ). Full-batch GD computes the gradient over the entire dataset — accurate but computationally prohibitive for large datasets and can get stuck in sharp minima. SGD uses a single sample per update — very noisy but fast and the noise can help escape local minima and sharp basins; generalises better empirically. Mini-batch GD is the practical standard — batches of 32–512 samples balance variance reduction, hardware efficiency (GPU vectorisation), and regularisation effect from noise.
evaluation_criteria: Correctly states the update rule
Explains the noise tradeoff across the three variants
Mentions hardware/vectorisation efficiency for mini-batch
Bonus: mentions that flatter minima correlate with better generalisation
common_mistakes: Saying SGD is 'less accurate' — it often generalises better
Ignoring learning rate scheduling as part of the full picture
conceptual.follow_up: How does Adam differ from SGD with momentum? What pathologies can Adam exhibit?

conceptual.question: What is the difference between L1 and L2 regularisation? When would you choose one over the other?
conceptual.model_answer: L2 (Ridge) adds λ·Σwᵢ² to the loss, penalising large weights quadratically. It shrinks all weights toward zero but rarely to exactly zero — produces dense, small-valued solutions. L1 (Lasso) adds λ·Σ|wᵢ|, which has a kink at zero that makes the penalty non-differentiable there. This property causes L1 to drive many weights to exactly zero, producing sparse solutions. Choose L1 when you believe the true model has few relevant features and you want built-in feature selection. Choose L2 when most features contribute and you want smooth, stable weight decay. Elastic Net combines both for high-dimensional correlated features.
evaluation_criteria: Correctly states the penalty terms
Identifies sparsity as the key L1 property and explains why (geometry of the L1 ball)
Gives a concrete use-case for each
common_mistakes: Saying L1 is 'just slower to compute' without noting the sparsity implications
Forgetting that L1 is non-differentiable at zero (matters for optimiser choice)
conceptual.follow_up: Explain the geometric intuition for why L1 produces sparsity using the constraint region picture.

conceptual.question: What is the curse of dimensionality and how does it affect distance-based algorithms?
conceptual.model_answer: As dimensionality increases, the volume of the space grows exponentially, causing data to become increasingly sparse. Three key manifestations: (1) Distance concentration — in high dimensions, the ratio of max to min pairwise distance converges to 1, making nearest-neighbour queries meaningless. (2) Data requirements — the number of samples needed to maintain the same density grows exponentially with dimensions. (3) Boundary dominance — most of the volume of a high-dimensional hypersphere is concentrated near its surface. This directly hurts kNN, kernel density estimation, and any algorithm relying on geometric proximity. Mitigations: dimensionality reduction (PCA, UMAP), feature selection, learned embeddings.
evaluation_criteria: Quantifies the exponential volume growth
Explains distance concentration specifically
Names at least two affected algorithms
Mentions at least one mitigation
common_mistakes: Describing it vaguely as 'more dimensions = harder' without the geometric intuition
Forgetting that neural networks partially sidestep this via learned representations
conceptual.follow_up: Why do deep neural networks appear to be relatively immune to the curse of dimensionality compared to kNN?

applied.question: You train a model that achieves 98% training accuracy but 61% validation accuracy. Walk me through your diagnosis and remediation steps.
applied.model_answer: This is a classic high-variance / overfitting pattern. Diagnosis steps: (1) Plot learning curves — if training loss keeps dropping while validation loss diverges, confirmed overfitting. (2) Check dataset size — if training set is small, the model memorised it. (3) Check model complexity relative to data size. Remediation, roughly in order of try-first: (1) Regularisation — add L2/dropout to the model. (2) Data augmentation — synthetically expand training set. (3) Early stopping — stop training when validation loss stops improving. (4) Reduce model capacity — fewer layers/parameters. (5) Collect more data if possible. (6) Cross-validation to get a reliable estimate of true generalisation. If the gap is suspiciously large, also check for train/val distribution mismatch — a data pipeline bug.
evaluation_criteria: Correctly identifies overfitting
Mentions learning curve diagnosis
Lists at least 3 concrete remediation strategies in a sensible priority order
Raises the possibility of distribution mismatch as an alternative explanation
common_mistakes: Jumping straight to 'add more data' without considering cheaper fixes first
Not checking for data leakage as a cause of inflated training accuracy
applied.follow_up: How would your diagnosis change if training accuracy was 72% and validation was 71%?

applied.question: Your classification model achieves 95% accuracy on a dataset where 95% of samples are class 0. What's wrong and what metrics should you use instead?
applied.model_answer: A model predicting class 0 always achieves 95% accuracy trivially — this is the class imbalance problem. Accuracy is misleading here. Better metrics: (1) Precision and Recall per class — especially recall on the minority class (class 1). (2) F1 score — harmonic mean of precision and recall, giving equal weight to both. (3) AUC-ROC — measures discriminative ability across all thresholds, robust to imbalance. (4) AUC-PR (Precision-Recall curve) — even more informative than ROC when the positive class is rare, as it focuses on minority class performance. (5) Cohen's Kappa — adjusts for chance agreement. For the model itself: oversample the minority class (SMOTE), undersample the majority, or use class-weighted loss.
evaluation_criteria: Immediately identifies the dummy classifier baseline
Names Precision, Recall, F1 and explains them correctly
Mentions AUC-ROC and ideally AUC-PR
Distinguishes when AUC-PR is preferable to AUC-ROC
common_mistakes: Stopping at F1 without mentioning threshold-independent metrics
Confusing macro vs micro averaged metrics
applied.follow_up: When would you prefer a high-recall model over a high-precision model? Give a medical example.

applied.question: Compare Random Forests and Gradient Boosted Trees. When would you use each in a production ML system?
applied.model_answer: Random Forests: ensemble of deep, independent trees trained on bootstrapped subsets with random feature subsets. Trees are trained in parallel. High variance reduction via averaging. Robust to outliers, rarely overfits badly, easy to tune. Gradient Boosted Trees (GBT, e.g., XGBoost, LightGBM): ensemble of shallow trees trained sequentially, each correcting the residuals of the prior ensemble. Typically higher accuracy than RF on structured/tabular data. More sensitive to hyperparameters and outliers. Slower to train (sequential), but LightGBM is highly optimised. Use RF when: fast training is critical, interpretability through feature importance is needed, data has many outliers, or you need a robust baseline. Use GBT when: maximising predictive accuracy on tabular data is the priority, you have time to tune, and data is relatively clean. In production: GBT (XGBoost/LightGBM) is typically the default for tabular ML competitions and industrial systems; RF is often the safer out-of-the-box choice.
evaluation_criteria: Correctly contrasts parallel vs sequential training
Identifies the bias-variance tradeoff positioning of each
Gives concrete production guidance, not just textbook differences
Mentions specific implementations (XGBoost, LightGBM)
common_mistakes: Saying RF is always 'worse' — it's often competitive and more robust
Not mentioning the sequential vs parallel training distinction
applied.follow_up: How does LightGBM's leaf-wise growth strategy differ from XGBoost's level-wise growth, and what are the tradeoffs?

applied.question: Walk me through how you would approach a new tabular ML problem from raw data to a deployed model.
applied.model_answer: 1. Understand the problem: Define the target, success metric, and constraints (latency, interpretability, data freshness). 2. EDA: Distributions, missing values, class balance, correlations, target leakage checks. 3. Data cleaning and preprocessing: Handle missing values (imputation or indicator flags), encode categoricals (target encoding, OHE), scale numerics. 4. Baseline model: Logistic regression or decision tree — establishes a floor. 5. Feature engineering: Domain-informed features, interaction terms, time-based features if applicable. 6. Model selection and tuning: Try RF and GBT. Tune hyperparameters via Bayesian optimisation or grid search with cross-validation. 7. Evaluation: Use the metric defined in step 1. Check calibration if probabilities matter. 8. Error analysis: Inspect misclassified samples — often reveals data issues or missing features. 9. Deployment: Wrap in a serving API, set up monitoring (data drift, prediction drift, model performance on live labels). 10. Retraining strategy: Define staleness criteria and retrain triggers.
evaluation_criteria: Starts with problem definition and metric, not modelling
Includes baseline before complex models
Mentions data leakage check
Addresses deployment and monitoring, not just training
common_mistakes: Jumping straight to deep learning for a tabular problem
Skipping error analysis
Treating deployment as an afterthought
applied.follow_up: How would your approach change if labels arrive with a 2-week delay after prediction?

applied.question: You need to choose between a neural network and a gradient boosted tree for a fraud detection system processing 10,000 transactions/second. What factors drive your decision?
applied.model_answer: Key decision factors: (1) Latency: GBT (XGBoost/LightGBM) inference is extremely fast — sub-millisecond for a single prediction. NN inference at 10k RPS requires careful batching or GPU serving, which adds latency and infrastructure cost. (2) Feature type: If features are purely tabular and engineered, GBT will likely match or beat NN accuracy with far less complexity. If raw inputs include sequences, graphs, or embeddings, NN may be necessary. (3) Interpretability: Fraud systems often require explainability for regulatory compliance. GBT + SHAP provides solid local explanations. NNs require LIME/Integrated Gradients which are approximations. (4) Data volume: NNs benefit significantly from very large datasets; GBTs plateau earlier. (5) Operational complexity: GBTs are simpler to deploy, monitor, and retrain. Default recommendation: Start with LightGBM. It handles imbalanced data well with class weights, is fast to deploy and explain, and achieves state-of-art on tabular fraud data. Add a NN layer only if you have unstructured inputs or have exhausted tabular approaches.
evaluation_criteria: Addresses latency quantitatively
Raises interpretability/regulatory constraint
Doesn't default to NN without justification
Gives a concrete recommendation with reasoning
common_mistakes: Choosing NN because 'it's more powerful' without addressing operational constraints
Ignoring the class imbalance inherent in fraud detection
applied.follow_up: How would you set up an online learning pipeline to adapt the model to new fraud patterns without full retraining?

deep_dive.question: Derive the gradient update rule for a two-layer neural network with sigmoid activations from first principles using the chain rule.
deep_dive.model_answer: For a network: input x → layer 1: z¹ = W¹x + b¹, a¹ = σ(z¹) → layer 2: z² = W²a¹ + b², ŷ = σ(z²) → loss L = -[y log ŷ + (1-y) log(1-ŷ)]. Output layer gradient: ∂L/∂z² = ŷ - y (clean result from cross-entropy + sigmoid). Weight gradient for W²: ∂L/∂W² = (ŷ - y)·(a¹)ᵀ. Backprop to layer 1: ∂L/∂a¹ = (W²)ᵀ·(ŷ - y). Through activation: ∂L/∂z¹ = ∂L/∂a¹ ⊙ σ'(z¹) = ∂L/∂a¹ ⊙ σ(z¹)·(1-σ(z¹)). Weight gradient for W¹: ∂L/∂W¹ = ∂L/∂z¹·xᵀ. The σ'(z¹) term is what causes vanishing gradients — sigmoid saturates near 0 and 1, driving σ' → 0 and killing the gradient signal for earlier layers.
evaluation_criteria: Sets up the forward pass notation explicitly
Correctly applies chain rule at each layer
Identifies the ∂L/∂z = ŷ - y simplification from cross-entropy + sigmoid
Explicitly names the vanishing gradient problem from the sigmoid derivative
common_mistakes: Confusing the order of matrix multiplications in the weight gradient
Not using the clean cross-entropy + sigmoid result and carrying through a messier derivation
deep_dive.follow_up: How does batch normalisation alleviate the vanishing gradient problem beyond just activation function choice?

deep_dive.question: Explain the VC dimension. What does it tell you about generalisation, and what are its practical limitations?
deep_dive.model_answer: The VC (Vapnik-Chervonenkis) dimension of a hypothesis class H is the largest number of points that H can shatter — i.e., correctly classify in all 2ⁿ possible binary labellings. It measures the expressive capacity of H. The fundamental theorem of statistical learning: if VC(H) = d, then with n training examples, the generalisation gap is bounded by O(√(d/n)) with high probability. Practical implications: higher VC dimension requires more data to generalise. For linear classifiers in ℝᵈ, VC dim = d+1. For a single neuron (perceptron) in ℝᵈ, VC dim = d+1. Limitations: (1) VC dimension is a worst-case measure — it can be very loose for real models (deep NNs have enormous VC dim yet generalise with far less data than the bound requires). (2) The bound is vacuous for deep learning — a ResNet's VC dim far exceeds typical dataset sizes. (3) Better modern theory: PAC-Bayes bounds, compression-based bounds, and the double-descent phenomenon show that overparameterised models can still generalise, contradicting classical VC wisdom.
evaluation_criteria: Defines shattering precisely
States the √(d/n) generalisation bound
Explains why VC bounds are vacuous for deep learning
Mentions at least one modern alternative framework
common_mistakes: Confusing VC dimension with model complexity in a loose sense
Not addressing the double-descent phenomenon
deep_dive.follow_up: What is the double-descent phenomenon and how does it challenge classical bias-variance theory?

deep_dive.question: Compare maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) and maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimation. Show that L2 regularisation corresponds to a Gaussian prior under MAP.
deep_dive.model_answer: MLE: θ_MLE = argmax P(D|θ). We maximise the likelihood of the data given parameters — no prior beliefs. MAP: θ_MAP = argmax P(θ|D) = argmax P(D|θ)·P(θ) (by Bayes, the evidence P(D) is constant w.r.t. θ). MAP incorporates a prior P(θ). Taking log: log P(D|θ) + log P(θ). For a Gaussian prior P(θ) = N(0, σ²I), log P(θ) = -||θ||²/(2σ²) + const. So: θ_MAP = argmax [log P(D|θ) - λ||θ||²] where λ = 1/(2σ²). The second term is exactly the L2 regularisation penalty. Thus L2 regularisation is MAP estimation with a zero-mean Gaussian prior on weights. Similarly, L1 regularisation corresponds to a Laplace prior (which has heavier tails and a spike at zero, encouraging sparsity).
evaluation_criteria: States both estimators correctly
Shows the log-posterior decomposition explicitly
Derives λ = 1/(2σ²) connecting regularisation strength to prior variance
Mentions the Laplace prior ↔ L1 connection as well
common_mistakes: Skipping the algebraic derivation and just asserting the connection
Not noting that a tighter prior (smaller σ²) corresponds to stronger regularisation
deep_dive.follow_up: What does full Bayesian inference give you that MAP does not? Why is it computationally expensive?

deep_dive.question: Explain the kernel trick. Derive the dual form of the SVM and show how the kernel replaces explicit feature mapping.
deep_dive.model_answer: The SVM primal: minimise ½||w||² subject to yᵢ(wᵀxᵢ + b) ≥ 1. The Lagrangian dual replaces this with: maximise Σαᵢ - ½ΣᵢΣⱼ αᵢαⱼyᵢyⱼ(xᵢᵀxⱼ), subject to Σαᵢyᵢ = 0, αᵢ ≥ 0. The decision boundary becomes: ŷ = sign(Σ αᵢyᵢ(xᵢᵀx) + b). Notice the data appears only as dot products xᵢᵀxⱼ. The kernel trick replaces xᵢᵀxⱼ with K(xᵢ, xⱼ) = φ(xᵢ)ᵀφ(xⱼ) — the inner product in a (possibly infinite-dimensional) feature space — without ever computing φ explicitly. The RBF kernel K(x,z) = exp(-||x-z||²/2σ²) implicitly maps into an infinite-dimensional space. This allows non-linear decision boundaries in input space at the cost of only O(n²) kernel evaluations, not O(d²) where d could be infinite.
evaluation_criteria: Writes the dual objective and identifies where dot products appear
Explains that kernel = inner product in transformed space
Shows that φ is never computed explicitly
Gives an example (RBF) with the correct formula
common_mistakes: Confusing the primal and dual objectives
Saying the kernel trick only applies to SVMs — it applies to any algorithm expressible through inner products
deep_dive.follow_up: What is Mercer's theorem and why is it necessary for a valid kernel function?

conceptual.question: Explain the vanishing gradient problem in deep neural networks. What causes it, and what are the primary solutions?
conceptual.model_answer: During backpropagation, gradients are propagated backward via the chain rule. For a depth-L network, the gradient at layer k involves a product of L-k Jacobian matrices. If these matrices have spectral radius < 1 (which sigmoid/tanh activations encourage — their derivatives max out at 0.25 for sigmoid), the gradient shrinks exponentially with depth. By layer 1, it may be effectively zero, leaving early layers untrained. Solutions: (1) ReLU activations — gradient is 1 for positive inputs, no saturation. (2) Residual connections (skip connections) — provide a gradient highway bypassing nonlinear blocks. (3) Batch normalisation — keeps activations in a well-scaled regime. (4) Careful weight initialisation (He, Xavier/Glorot) — controls the variance of activations and gradients at initialisation. (5) Gradient clipping — addresses the related exploding gradient problem.
evaluation_criteria: Identifies the product of Jacobians as the mechanism
Explains why sigmoid is particularly problematic (derivative ≤ 0.25)
Lists at least 3 solutions
Distinguishes vanishing from exploding gradients
common_mistakes: Saying 'deep networks are harder to train' without the Jacobian product explanation
Confusing vanishing gradients with the dying ReLU problem (different issue)
conceptual.follow_up: How do residual connections specifically solve vanishing gradients? Walk through the math.

conceptual.question: Compare LSTMs and GRUs. What problem do they both solve compared to vanilla RNNs, and what are the tradeoffs between them?
conceptual.model_answer: Vanilla RNNs: hidden state hₜ = tanh(Wxhₜ₋₁ + Wxₜ). The same weight matrix is applied recurrently, causing the gradient to vanish or explode over long sequences. LSTMs (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997): introduce a cell state cₜ — a 'memory conveyor belt' — controlled by three gates: forget gate (what to erase from memory), input gate (what new information to write), output gate (what to read). The cell state gradient highway allows gradients to flow across many timesteps without decay. GRUs (Cho et al., 2014): simplified variant with two gates (reset gate, update gate). No separate cell state — hidden state serves both roles. Tradeoffs: LSTMs have more parameters (4 gate matrices vs 3 for GRU) and are generally better on tasks requiring fine-grained memory control. GRUs train faster, are more parameter-efficient, and perform comparably on most sequence tasks. In practice, transformers have supplanted both for most NLP tasks, but LSTMs/GRUs remain relevant for streaming, low-latency, and resource-constrained settings.
evaluation_criteria: Explains what gating solves (long-range dependencies, gradient flow)
Correctly names and describes LSTM's three gates
Identifies GRU's simplification
Gives practical guidance on when to use each
common_mistakes: Saying LSTMs 'always outperform' GRUs
Not mentioning that transformers have largely replaced both in NLP
conceptual.follow_up: How does the LSTM cell state differ from the hidden state, and what does each represent semantically?

conceptual.question: What are residual connections (skip connections) and why were they transformative for deep learning?
conceptual.model_answer: A residual block computes F(x) + x instead of F(x) — the identity mapping is added to the learned transformation. Introduced in ResNet (He et al., 2015), which trained networks 152 layers deep when 20+ layers were previously impractical. Why they work: (1) Gradient highway — gradients can flow directly through the identity path without passing through nonlinear layers, addressing vanishing gradients. (2) Identity initialisation — at the start of training, if the residual mapping F(x) ≈ 0, the block approximates identity; it's easier to learn a small residual correction than to learn the full mapping from scratch. (3) Ensemble interpretation — a residual network can be viewed as an implicit ensemble of exponentially many shorter paths. Transformers adopt the same principle: each attention and FFN sublayer is wrapped in a residual connection.
evaluation_criteria: States the formula F(x) + x explicitly
Explains both gradient flow and identity initialisation benefits
Notes adoption in Transformers
common_mistakes: Saying residual connections 'prevent overfitting' — they don't primarily; they enable training depth
conceptual.follow_up: What happens when input and output dimensions differ in a residual block? How does ResNet handle this?

conceptual.question: Explain batch normalisation. What problem does it solve, and what are the learnable parameters?
conceptual.model_answer: Batch normalisation (Ioffe & Szegedy, 2015) normalises each feature across the mini-batch to zero mean and unit variance, then applies learnable scale and shift parameters: BN(x) = γ·(x - μ_B)/√(σ²_B + ε) + β. μ_B and σ²_B are the batch mean and variance. γ and β are the learnable parameters per feature. Problems it solves: (1) Internal covariate shift — as earlier layers update, the distribution of inputs to later layers shifts, destabilising training. BN reduces this shift. (2) Gradient flow — normalisation keeps activations in a healthy range, improving gradient magnitudes. (3) Regularisation — the noise introduced by using batch statistics acts as implicit regularisation, reducing the need for dropout. At inference, batch statistics are replaced by running averages computed during training. Key limitation: BN performance degrades with very small batch sizes (noise in batch statistics) and doesn't work well for recurrent architectures or online/streaming inference.
evaluation_criteria: States the normalise-then-scale-shift formula
Identifies γ and β as learnable
Explains at least two benefits
Notes the small batch limitation
common_mistakes: Confusing BN with Layer Norm (different normalisation dimension)
Forgetting that γ and β allow the network to undo normalisation if needed
conceptual.follow_up: Why is Layer Normalisation preferred over Batch Normalisation in Transformers?

conceptual.question: What is a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN)? Describe the training objective and the core training challenges.
conceptual.model_answer: A GAN consists of two networks trained adversarially: Generator G(z) maps noise z ~ p(z) to data space, trying to produce samples indistinguishable from real data. Discriminator D(x) estimates the probability that x is real. Minimax objective: min_G max_D E[log D(x)] + E[log(1 - D(G(z)))]. At equilibrium, G produces samples matching the real data distribution and D outputs 0.5 everywhere. Training challenges: (1) Mode collapse — G learns to produce a small set of highly discriminative samples rather than the full data distribution. (2) Training instability — the minimax game can oscillate rather than converge; gradients for G vanish when D is too strong. (3) Evaluation — no obvious scalar metric; FID (Fréchet Inception Distance) is the standard. Solutions: Wasserstein GAN (WGAN) replaces the Jensen-Shannon divergence objective with Wasserstein distance, providing a smoother, more stable gradient signal.
evaluation_criteria: States the minimax objective correctly
Describes mode collapse and training instability specifically
Mentions WGAN or another stabilisation approach
Names FID as an evaluation metric
common_mistakes: Confusing the objectives of G and D
Saying mode collapse means the model fails to train — it trains, but collapses to few modes
conceptual.follow_up: How does WGAN address training instability compared to the original GAN objective?

conceptual.question: Explain the encoder-decoder architecture. Where is it used, and what does each component learn?
conceptual.model_answer: An encoder maps input data to a compressed latent representation (bottleneck). A decoder maps the latent representation back to an output space (which may differ from the input space). The encoder learns to extract the information most relevant to the task; the decoder learns to reconstruct or generate from that compressed signal. Applications: (1) Autoencoders — input and output are the same; the bottleneck forces compression and denoising. (2) Sequence-to-sequence models (e.g., translation) — encoder reads the source sequence, decoder generates the target. (3) U-Net (image segmentation) — encoder downsamples via convolutions, decoder upsamples via transposed convolutions with skip connections preserving spatial detail. (4) Transformer encoder-decoder (T5, BART) — encoder processes input tokens bidirectionally, decoder generates output tokens autoregressively with cross-attention to encoder outputs.
evaluation_criteria: Explains the bottleneck concept
Gives at least 3 different application contexts
Distinguishes encoder-only, decoder-only, and full encoder-decoder architectures
common_mistakes: Treating encoder-decoder as synonymous with autoencoders
Forgetting cross-attention as the link between encoder and decoder in transformers
conceptual.follow_up: What specific architectural element in the Transformer allows the decoder to 'read' the encoder's output?

applied.question: You need to classify 10 million medical images into 5 categories. You have 50,000 labelled images and unlimited unlabelled images. How do you approach this?
applied.model_answer: With 50k labelled samples for 5 classes (10k per class), this is a regime where transfer learning is essential. Approach: (1) Start with a pretrained CNN (ResNet-50 or EfficientNet-B4) pretrained on ImageNet. Medical image domains have been shown to benefit from ImageNet pretraining even though the domains differ — low-level features (edges, textures) transfer well. (2) Fine-tune: first train only the classification head with the backbone frozen, then unfreeze and fine-tune the entire network with a low learning rate. (3) Use the unlabelled data via self-supervised pretraining (SimCLR, MoCo, or DINO) to pretrain on the unlabelled medical images specifically, then fine-tune on the 50k labelled. This is often better than ImageNet pretraining for domain-specific images. (4) Data augmentation: rotation, flips, colour jitter, MixUp — critical with limited labels. (5) Evaluation: stratified cross-validation, per-class recall (critical in medical contexts where false negatives matter differently per class).
evaluation_criteria: Identifies transfer learning as the primary strategy
Proposes self-supervised pretraining on unlabelled data
Addresses the medical domain specificity
Mentions evaluation considerations specific to medical settings
common_mistakes: Training from scratch with 50k images
Ignoring the unlabelled data entirely
Using accuracy as the primary metric for medical classification
applied.follow_up: How would you decide between MoCo and SimCLR for the self-supervised stage? What are the practical differences?

applied.question: Design a CNN architecture for real-time object detection on a mobile device (≤ 100ms latency, ≤ 5MB model size).
applied.model_answer: Constraints: 100ms on mobile CPU/NPU, 5MB model. Architecture choices: (1) Backbone: MobileNetV3 or EfficientNet-Lite. Both use depthwise separable convolutions — depthwise convolution (spatial filtering per channel) + pointwise convolution (channel mixing) — which reduce FLOPs by ~8-9x vs standard convolutions at similar accuracy. (2) Detection head: SSDLite (from MobileNetV3 paper) uses depthwise separable convolutions in the detection head rather than standard convolutions. For even tighter constraints, YOLO-NAS-S or NanoDet. (3) Quantisation: Post-training int8 quantisation reduces size 4x and speeds up inference 2-3x on most mobile hardware with < 1% accuracy drop. (4) Pruning: Structured pruning of channels with least L1 norm, followed by fine-tuning. (5) Input resolution: 320×320 instead of 640×640 — roughly 4x fewer FLOPs. (6) Deployment: CoreML (iOS) or TFLite + NNAPI (Android) for hardware-accelerated inference.
evaluation_criteria: Correctly identifies depthwise separable convolutions and their FLOP savings
Proposes quantisation as a size/speed optimisation
Mentions deployment framework
Balances accuracy vs efficiency tradeoffs explicitly
common_mistakes: Proposing a full ResNet or YOLO-v8 base without addressing the constraints
Ignoring the deployment platform's specific accelerator capabilities
applied.follow_up: What is the difference between post-training quantisation and quantisation-aware training? When does it matter?

applied.question: Your LSTM model for time-series forecasting performs well on the test set but degrades significantly in production after 3 months. Diagnose and fix this.
applied.model_answer: This is a data drift / distribution shift problem. Diagnosis: (1) Monitor feature distributions over time using statistical tests (KS test, Population Stability Index) — identify which input features have drifted. (2) Monitor prediction distribution — if model outputs are shifting systematically, the input distribution has changed. (3) Check for concept drift — the relationship between features and target may have changed (e.g., seasonal pattern, structural break in the time series). (4) Compare recent errors to test set errors — if MAE/RMSE is increasing monotonically, drift is likely; if it's episodic, check for data pipeline issues. Fixes: (1) Sliding window retraining — retrain periodically on recent data. (2) Online learning — update model weights incrementally as new labels arrive. (3) Ensemble with a trend model — combine the LSTM with a simple linear trend extrapolator for robustness to concept drift. (4) Improve monitoring — set automated alerts on prediction distribution drift so degradation is caught early.
evaluation_criteria: Distinguishes feature drift from concept drift
Names a specific statistical test for drift detection
Proposes a retraining strategy
Mentions monitoring as a systematic fix, not just one-off diagnosis
common_mistakes: Treating this as a model architecture problem rather than a data distribution problem
Not distinguishing between data pipeline errors and genuine drift
applied.follow_up: How would you design the retraining pipeline to handle the 2-week label delay mentioned earlier?

applied.question: Compare CNNs, RNNs, and Transformers for a document classification task with sequences up to 10,000 tokens. Which would you choose and why?
applied.model_answer: RNNs/LSTMs: O(n) computation, O(n) memory for sequence length n. Long-range dependencies are learned through the hidden state, but in practice the hidden state is a fixed-size bottleneck — at 10k tokens, critical early information is likely forgotten. Gradient flow over 10k steps remains problematic even with LSTMs. CNNs (1D text CNNs, TextCNN): O(n·k) complexity where k is kernel size. Excellent at capturing local n-gram features. Multiple dilated convolution layers can extend receptive field, but a 10k token sequence still requires many layers to capture global structure. Fast and memory-efficient. Standard Transformers: O(n²) attention — at 10k tokens, this is 100M attention entries per layer. Memory and compute prohibitive with standard attention. Better approaches for 10k tokens: (1) Longformer — sparse attention (local window + global tokens) O(n). (2) BigBird — combination of random, window, and global attention. (3) Hierarchical approach — chunk into 512-token segments, encode each with a pretrained BERT, then pool/attend over chunk representations. Recommendation: Hierarchical BERT or Longformer, depending on compute budget.
evaluation_criteria: States the quadratic complexity issue for standard Transformers at 10k tokens
Explains why LSTMs struggle with very long sequences
Names at least one efficient Transformer variant
Gives a concrete recommendation
common_mistakes: Recommending standard BERT without noting the 512-token limit
Dismissing CNNs entirely — they are very competitive for classification tasks
applied.follow_up: How does Longformer's sliding window attention work and what are the global tokens for?

applied.question: You are training a GAN for high-resolution image synthesis and observe mode collapse. How do you diagnose and resolve it?
applied.model_answer: Diagnosis: (1) Sample diversity — generate 1000 samples and check if they cluster into a few modes visually or via FID/IS scores. (2) Discriminator confidence — if D consistently outputs near-1 for all generated samples, the generator has found a 'fooling pattern' and collapsed. (3) Latent space interpolation — interpolate between z vectors; if outputs jump discontinuously rather than smoothly morphing, mode collapse is occurring. Resolution strategies: (1) Wasserstein GAN with gradient penalty (WGAN-GP) — provides more informative gradient signal even when D is much stronger than G. (2) Minibatch discrimination — D is given statistics about a whole batch, not just a single sample, making it harder for G to produce identical samples. (3) Spectral normalisation on D — controls the Lipschitz constant of D, stabilising training. (4) Progressive growing (ProGAN) — start at low resolution and progressively increase, making training more stable. (5) StyleGAN architecture — decouples style from structure, encourages diverse outputs.
evaluation_criteria: Describes a concrete diagnostic procedure, not just naming the symptom
Proposes WGAN or WGAN-GP
Mentions minibatch discrimination or another diversity-promoting technique
Names a production-grade architecture (StyleGAN, ProGAN)
common_mistakes: Suggesting only 'lower the learning rate' as the fix
Not distinguishing mode collapse from training instability

deep_dive.question: Derive the LSTM update equations from scratch and explain what each gate learns to do in practice.
deep_dive.model_answer: LSTM equations at timestep t, given input xₜ and previous state (hₜ₋₁, cₜ₋₁): Forget gate: fₜ = σ(Wf·[hₜ₋₁, xₜ] + bf) — sigmoid output ∈ (0,1). Learned to forget: determines what fraction of the previous cell state to retain. Input gate: iₜ = σ(Wi·[hₜ₋₁, xₜ] + bi) — what new information to write. Candidate cell: c̃ₜ = tanh(Wc·[hₜ₋₁, xₜ] + bc) — proposed new content. Cell state update: cₜ = fₜ ⊙ cₜ₋₁ + iₜ ⊙ c̃ₜ — the cell state is a linear combination of the old cell (gated) and new content (gated). This linear update is why gradients flow: ∂cₜ/∂cₜ₋₁ = fₜ, and if fₜ ≈ 1 the gradient flows unchanged. Output gate: oₜ = σ(Wo·[hₜ₋₁, xₜ] + bo). Hidden state: hₜ = oₜ ⊙ tanh(cₜ). In practice: forget gate learns to reset memory at sentence boundaries or topic changes; input gate learns to write named entities, numeric values, or task-relevant features; output gate learns to expose only task-relevant parts of memory to downstream layers.
evaluation_criteria: States all 5 equations correctly with the right notation
Explains why the linear cell update prevents vanishing gradients
Gives practical semantics for what each gate tends to learn
common_mistakes: Confusing hₜ and cₜ — they have different roles and different dimensionality semantics
Not explaining why the additive update (not multiplicative) is the key to gradient flow

deep_dive.question: What is the expressive power of deep vs wide neural networks? Discuss the Universal Approximation Theorem and its limitations.
deep_dive.model_answer: Universal Approximation Theorem (Cybenko, 1989; Hornik, 1991): A single hidden layer neural network with a finite number of neurons and a non-polynomial activation function can approximate any continuous function on a compact subset of ℝⁿ to arbitrary precision. Implications: a wide enough network is theoretically sufficient. Limitations: (1) The theorem says nothing about how wide — it may require exponentially many neurons. (2) It says nothing about whether gradient descent finds the approximating network. (3) It says nothing about generalisation — the approximating network may memorise rather than generalise. Depth advantage: Montufar et al. (2014) show that deep ReLU networks can represent exponentially more linear regions than shallow networks of the same parameter count. Lu et al. (2017) show that width O(n) with depth O(n log n) is sufficient to approximate Lipschitz functions that require exponential width for depth-1 networks. Empirically: depth appears to help via compositionality — deep networks learn hierarchical feature representations, which matches the structure of real-world data (pixels → edges → parts → objects).
evaluation_criteria: States UAT correctly including the compactness requirement
Identifies at least 3 limitations of UAT
Explains why depth is preferable to width
Mentions compositionality as the intuitive explanation
common_mistakes: Claiming UAT proves deep learning works — it only shows theoretical expressibility of shallow nets
Not addressing the generalisation gap between approximation and learning
deep_dive.follow_up: Does the Universal Approximation Theorem apply to deep networks with fixed width? What changes?

deep_dive.question: Explain the reparameterisation trick in Variational Autoencoders and why it's necessary for training.
deep_dive.model_answer: In a VAE, the encoder outputs parameters μ and σ of a Gaussian distribution q(z|x) = N(μ, σ²I), and we sample z ~ q(z|x) to pass to the decoder. The problem: sampling is a stochastic, non-differentiable operation. Gradients cannot flow through a sample node. The reparameterisation trick: instead of z ~ N(μ, σ²), write z = μ + σ ⊙ ε where ε ~ N(0, I). Now z is a deterministic function of μ, σ, and ε. The randomness is 'pushed into' ε, which is an auxiliary input with no parameters. Gradients can now flow through μ and σ to the encoder. Training objective (ELBO): L = E_q[log p(x|z)] - KL(q(z|x) || p(z)). First term: reconstruction loss. Second term: KL divergence regularises the posterior toward the prior N(0,I). The KL term has a closed form for Gaussian distributions: -½ Σ(1 + log σ² - μ² - σ²). The reparameterisation trick makes both terms differentiable.
evaluation_criteria: Explains why direct sampling blocks gradient flow
States the reparameterisation z = μ + σε explicitly
Writes the ELBO decomposition
Gives the closed-form KL for Gaussians
common_mistakes: Not explaining why the original sampling is non-differentiable
Confusing VAE with GAN — both are generative but with fundamentally different objectives

deep_dive.question: Explain how depthwise separable convolutions reduce computational cost compared to standard convolutions. Derive the FLOP ratio.
deep_dive.model_answer: Standard convolution: input H×W×Cᵢₙ, output H×W×Cₒᵤₜ, kernel K×K. FLOPs = H·W·Cᵢₙ·Cₒᵤₜ·K². Depthwise separable convolution: Step 1 — Depthwise convolution: apply one K×K filter per input channel. FLOPs = H·W·Cᵢₙ·K². Step 2 — Pointwise convolution: 1×1 convolution to mix channels. FLOPs = H·W·Cᵢₙ·Cₒᵤₜ. Total FLOPs = H·W·Cᵢₙ·(K² + Cₒᵤₜ). Ratio: FLOPs_dw / FLOPs_std = (K² + Cₒᵤₜ) / (K²·Cₒᵤₜ) = 1/Cₒᵤₜ + 1/K². For K=3 and Cₒᵤₜ=256: ratio ≈ 1/256 + 1/9 ≈ 0.115 — roughly 8-9x reduction. MobileNet uses this throughout to achieve 8-9x fewer FLOPs at comparable accuracy to standard CNNs. The intuition: standard convolutions mix spatial filtering and channel mixing simultaneously; depthwise separable convolutions factorize these into two sequential, cheaper operations.

Derives the FLOP formula for both stages of depthwise separable
Computes the ratio algebraically
Explains the factorisation intuition
common_mistakes: Getting the dimensions of the depthwise stage wrong

conceptual.question: Explain the scaled dot-product attention mechanism. Why is scaling by √d_k necessary?
conceptual.model_answer: Scaled dot-product attention: Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(QKᵀ / √d_k)·V. Q (queries), K (keys), V (values) are linear projections of the input. The dot products QKᵀ measure similarity between each query and all keys. Dividing by √d_k: without scaling, for large d_k, the dot products grow in magnitude as O(d_k). This pushes the softmax into regions with extremely small gradients (near-zero for all but the maximum entry). Intuitively, if d_k = 64, a typical dot product has standard deviation ~√64 = 8; dividing by √64 = 8 normalises this to ~1, keeping the softmax in a well-behaved gradient regime. The result is a weighted sum of value vectors, where weights reflect query-key similarity.
evaluation_criteria: States the formula correctly with the scaling factor
Explains why large d_k causes softmax saturation
Quantifies the std dev argument
Explains the output as a weighted sum of values
common_mistakes: Saying 'to prevent overflow' — it's about gradient flow, not numerical overflow
Confusing keys and queries conceptually

conceptual.question: What is positional encoding in Transformers? Why is it needed, and what are the tradeoffs between sinusoidal and learned positional embeddings?
conceptual.model_answer: Self-attention is permutation-equivariant — it treats the input as a set, not a sequence. Without positional information, 'the dog bit the man' and 'the man bit the dog' are identical inputs. Positional encoding injects sequence order information. Original Transformer (Vaswani et al.): sinusoidal encoding PE(pos, 2i) = sin(pos/10000^(2i/d_model)), PE(pos, 2i+1) = cos(...). Sinusoidal: (1) No parameters to learn. (2) Deterministic, can extrapolate to lengths unseen during training. (3) Relative positions can be expressed as linear functions of the encodings. Learned positional embeddings: (1) Tuned to the training distribution — generally slightly better on in-distribution lengths. (2) Cannot extrapolate beyond training length. (3) BERT, GPT-2 use learned; original Transformer used sinusoidal. Modern approaches: RoPE (Rotary Position Embedding) — multiplies Q and K by rotation matrices encoding relative position, enabling better length generalisation and used by LLaMA, Mistral. ALiBi — adds a linear bias to attention scores based on distance, simple and effective for length generalisation.
evaluation_criteria: Explains why attention is permutation-equivariant and needs positional info
Describes sinusoidal encoding
Contrasts learned vs sinusoidal with concrete tradeoffs
Mentions at least one modern approach (RoPE or ALiBi)
common_mistakes: Saying positional encoding 'tells the model the absolute position' without noting that relative positions are what matter for most tasks
Not knowing any modern positional encoding scheme

conceptual.question: Explain the difference between encoder-only, decoder-only, and encoder-decoder Transformer architectures. Give an example of each.
conceptual.model_answer: Encoder-only (BERT family): processes all tokens bidirectionally — each token attends to all other tokens via full self-attention. Trained with masked language modelling (predict masked tokens). Best for: text classification, NER, sentence similarity — tasks requiring understanding of the full input. Decoder-only (GPT family): uses causal (autoregressive) self-attention — each token attends only to previous tokens. Trained with next-token prediction. Best for: text generation, completion, reasoning via chain-of-thought. Has become dominant for general-purpose language models. Encoder-decoder (T5, BART, original Transformer): encoder processes the input bidirectionally; decoder generates output autoregressively with cross-attention to encoder outputs. Best for: seq2seq tasks — translation, summarisation, question answering with long contexts. T5 frames all NLP tasks as text-to-text. The field has largely consolidated on decoder-only for large-scale pretraining (GPT-4, Claude, Gemini) because it unifies generation and understanding.
evaluation_criteria: Correctly describes the attention masking pattern for each
Names a real model for each
Gives appropriate use cases
Notes the industry trend toward decoder-only
common_mistakes: Saying encoder-only can't do generation at all — it can with modifications like BERT for MLM fill-in
Confusing cross-attention and self-attention in encoder-decoder models
conceptual.follow_up: Why have decoder-only models superseded encoder-decoder models for most tasks despite enc-dec seeming better suited for seq2seq?

conceptual.question: What is multi-head attention? What does each head learn, and why is it beneficial over single-head attention?
conceptual.model_answer: Multi-head attention runs h attention operations in parallel, each with different learned projections: MultiHead(Q,K,V) = Concat(head₁,...,headₕ)Wᴼ where headᵢ = Attention(QWᵢQ, KWᵢK, VWᵢV). The projection matrices Wᵢ{Q,K,V} ∈ ℝ^(d_model × d_k) where d_k = d_model/h. Benefits: (1) Each head can attend to different aspects of the input simultaneously — syntactic relations, coreference, semantic similarity, positional patterns. Empirically, heads specialise in different relation types. (2) The dimension reduction per head (d_model/h) makes each head less prone to attending to a single dominant feature. (3) Total computation is similar to single-head attention with d_model because d_k = d_model/h, so the inner products are cheaper. The final projection Wᴼ recombines information across heads.
evaluation_criteria: States the Concat(...) formula
Explains that each head uses different projections
Notes that d_k = d_model/h keeps computation similar
Explains head specialisation with examples
common_mistakes: Saying each head 'sees different tokens' — they all see all tokens, but through different projections
Not mentioning the output projection Wᴼ

conceptual.question: Explain the Feed-Forward Network (FFN) sublayer in a Transformer block. What is its role compared to the attention sublayer?
conceptual.model_answer: Each Transformer layer has two sublayers: (1) Multi-head self-attention and (2) Position-wise FFN. The FFN is applied identically to each position independently: FFN(x) = max(0, xW₁ + b₁)W₂ + b₂. The inner dimension is typically 4× the model dimension (e.g., 4096 for d_model=1024). The attention sublayer routes information between positions — it decides 'what to look at' and mixes information from different positions. The FFN sublayer processes each position independently — it applies the same learned transformation to each token representation. Interpretations: (1) The FFN as a 'memory' — Geva et al. (2020) showed that FFN layers act as key-value memories, with the first layer as keys and the second as values, storing factual knowledge. (2) The FFN accounts for ~2/3 of the model's parameters in standard architectures. (3) Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) replaces the FFN with multiple expert FFNs, routing each token to top-k experts, enabling massive parameter counts without proportional compute.
evaluation_criteria: States the FFN formula
Distinguishes the role of FFN (per-token transformation) from attention (cross-token routing)
Notes the 4× expansion ratio
Mentions FFN as memory or MoE
common_mistakes: Treating the FFN as secondary or unimportant — it holds most of the model's parameters

conceptual.question: What is the computational complexity of self-attention? How does this limit Transformers for long sequences?
conceptual.model_answer: For a sequence of length n with model dimension d: Computing QKᵀ: O(n²·d) — every pair of tokens is compared. Applying softmax: O(n²). Computing the weighted sum with V: O(n²·d). Total attention complexity: O(n²·d) time and O(n²) memory (the attention matrix). For n=512 (BERT): 262k attention entries — manageable. For n=8192 (long documents): 67M entries per head. For n=100k (book-length): 10B entries — infeasible. This quadratic scaling is the central limitation of standard Transformers for long sequences. Solutions: Sparse attention (Longformer, BigBird): O(n·√n) or O(n). Linear attention (Performers): O(n) via kernel approximation of softmax. Sliding window (local) attention: O(n·w) where w is window size. FlashAttention: not asymptotically better (still O(n²)) but dramatically reduces memory I/O by tiling the computation, enabling 10x+ longer sequences in practice.
evaluation_criteria: States O(n²·d) time and O(n²) space
Quantifies with concrete n values
Names at least two approaches to address this
Distinguishes FlashAttention (IO efficiency) from true subquadratic methods
common_mistakes: Confusing FlashAttention with linear attention — FlashAttention is still O(n²) asymptotically

applied.question: You need to fine-tune BERT for a multi-label text classification task with 50 classes and only 2,000 labelled examples. Walk through your approach.
applied.model_answer: Multi-label = each example can have multiple of the 50 class labels. 2k examples is low-resource. Approach: (1) Model: BERT-base with a multi-label classification head: Linear(768 → 50) + sigmoid (not softmax — multi-label requires independent probabilities per class). Loss: Binary cross-entropy, summed over 50 heads. (2) Low-resource strategy: Use a smaller model (BERT-base, not large). Consider domain-adapted BERT if the text domain is specialised. (3) Regularisation: Dropout on the classification head (0.1-0.3). Label smoothing. (4) Fine-tuning strategy: Freeze lower layers initially, fine-tune top 2-3 layers first (prevents catastrophic forgetting). Then unfreeze all with discriminative learning rates (lower LR for lower layers). (5) Augmentation: Back-translation, synonym replacement, or EDA (Easy Data Augmentation) to expand the 2k samples. (6) Evaluation: Per-class and macro F1 (not accuracy). Check for class imbalance across the 50 labels. (7) Consider few-shot prompting with an LLM as a baseline — at 2k examples, prompt-based zero/few-shot may be competitive.
evaluation_criteria: Correctly uses sigmoid + BCE for multi-label
Addresses the low-resource setting with specific strategies
Mentions discriminative fine-tuning or layer freezing
Raises zero/few-shot prompting as an alternative
common_mistakes: Using softmax + cross-entropy for multi-label classification
Not addressing catastrophic forgetting in fine-tuning

applied.question: Your Transformer model's inference latency is too high for a production API (target: 50ms p99). The model is BERT-base running on CPU. What are your optimisation options?
applied.model_answer: Systematic optimisation hierarchy, from cheapest to most expensive: (1) Hardware: Move to GPU first — BERT-base inference is 10-50x faster on GPU vs CPU. If CPU-only is a hard constraint, optimise for it. (2) Batching: Batch requests together — even small batches (2-8) improve throughput significantly. Dynamic batching with a 5-10ms wait window. (3) Quantisation: INT8 quantisation (dynamic or static) via ONNX Runtime or TorchScript. Typical 2-4x speedup on CPU with < 1% accuracy loss. (4) ONNX export: Convert to ONNX and run with ONNXRuntime, which optimises graph execution. 1.5-2x speedup typically. (5) Knowledge Distillation: Distil into a smaller student (DistilBERT = 40% fewer params, 60% faster, 97% of BERT performance; TinyBERT for even smaller). This is a one-time training cost. (6) Sequence length reduction: Truncate to the minimum necessary length for the task. Attention is O(n²) — halving sequence length is 4x faster attention. (7) Layer pruning: Remove attention heads and FFN neurons with smallest activation magnitudes, fine-tune.
evaluation_criteria: Covers multiple optimisation levels (hardware, inference engine, model compression)
Quantifies expected speedups
Names DistilBERT or similar for distillation
Mentions sequence length impact on latency
common_mistakes: Starting with retraining before exploring inference-time optimisations
Not considering the accuracy-latency tradeoff for each option

applied.question: Compare BERT and GPT-2 for a question-answering task. Which would you choose and how would you adapt it?
applied.model_answer: Extractive QA (span extraction from a context paragraph, e.g., SQuAD): BERT is the natural choice. Its bidirectional attention lets every token attend to the full context, making it ideal for identifying the answer span within a passage. Fine-tuning: add a linear head predicting start/end token indices. BERT-base achieves 88% F1 on SQuAD 1.1. Generative QA (abstractive answers, not necessarily in the context): GPT-2 or a more capable decoder-only LLM is preferable. Can generate answers not verbatim in the context. Fine-tuning: frame as 'context + question → answer' generation. Modern practice: for generative QA, use a larger instruction-tuned model (GPT-3.5, Claude, Llama 2-chat) in a RAG pipeline rather than fine-tuning GPT-2 from scratch. For closed-domain extractive QA on a specific corpus: BERT/RoBERTa fine-tuned on domain data. For open-domain QA requiring reasoning or synthesis: decoder-only LLM + RAG.

Correctly recommends BERT for extractive, decoder-only for generative
Describes the fine-tuning mechanism for each

applied.question: You're building a semantic search system for 10M documents. Design the full pipeline from document ingestion to query serving.
applied.model_answer: Architecture: (1) Document ingestion: Chunk documents into 256-512 token segments with overlap (64 tokens) to preserve context across chunk boundaries. (2) Embedding generation: Use a sentence-transformer model (e.g., all-mpnet-base-v2 or E5-large) to embed each chunk. Batch process in parallel. Store embeddings in a vector database. (3) Vector database: FAISS for in-memory (fast, no infra overhead, good to ~10M), Qdrant or Weaviate for persistent scalable serving with filtering. Index type: HNSW (Approximate Nearest Neighbour) — O(log n) query time, high recall. (4) Query serving: Embed query with same model. ANN search for top-k (50-100) candidates. Optional reranking: pass top candidates + query to a cross-encoder reranker (e.g., ms-marco-MiniLM) for higher precision. (5) Hybrid search: Combine dense (embedding) retrieval with sparse (BM25) retrieval via reciprocal rank fusion — handles exact keyword matches that dense search misses. (6) Latency: Typical p99 latency: embedding (~20ms on GPU) + ANN search (~5ms) + reranking (50-100ms for top-50). Cache frequent queries.

applied.question: How would you handle a 128k token context window in a Transformer model? What are the engineering challenges?
applied.model_answer: At 128k tokens, standard attention is infeasible naively. Engineering challenges and solutions: (1) Memory: Standard attention stores O(n²) attention maps. For 128k tokens and h=32 heads, at float16: 32 × 128k² × 2 bytes ≈ 1TB. FlashAttention-2 computes attention in tiles without materialising the full matrix — memory becomes O(n) instead of O(n²), making 128k feasible on modern A100/H100 GPUs. (2) Positional encoding: Standard learned positional embeddings can't extrapolate. RoPE with extended theta (LLaMA's approach) or YaRN (a RoPE extension specifically for long contexts) needed. (3) KV cache: At 128k context length, the key-value cache becomes large. Multi-Query Attention (MQA) or Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) shares K,V heads across multiple Q heads, reducing KV cache size 8-32x. (4) Attention sink: Very long contexts exhibit 'attention sink' behaviour — tokens disproportionately attend to initial tokens. StreamingLLM handles this by always keeping initial tokens in the KV cache. (5) Retrieval augmentation: For truly long contexts, selectively routing only relevant sections to the LLM (via a retrieval step) can be more accurate and efficient than 128k brute-force attention.
