deep_dive.question: Derive the forward and backward pass of scaled dot-product attention in matrix form and identify the computational bottleneck.
deep_dive.model_answer: Forward pass: Given X ∈ ℝ^(n×d), projections Q=XWQ, K=XWK, V=XWV ∈ ℝ^(n×d_k). S = QKᵀ/√d_k ∈ ℝ^(n×n) — attention logits. A = softmax(S) row-wise ∈ ℝ^(n×n) — attention weights. O = AV ∈ ℝ^(n×d_k) — output. Backward pass: Given upstream gradient ∂L/∂O. ∂L/∂V = Aᵀ·(∂L/∂O). ∂L/∂A = (∂L/∂O)·Vᵀ. ∂L/∂S = A ⊙ (∂L/∂A - (∂L/∂A ⊙ A)·1·1ᵀ) — the Jacobian of row-wise softmax (requires the outer product computation). ∂L/∂Q = (∂L/∂S/√d_k)·K, ∂L/∂K = (∂L/∂S/√d_k)ᵀ·Q. Computational bottleneck: storing A ∈ ℝ^(n×n) is O(n²) memory. For n=8k, that's 64M floats × 32 heads × float16 = 4GB just for attention maps. This is the problem FlashAttention solves by fusing the softmax + V multiplication into a single tiled kernel pass, never materialising A in HBM.
evaluation_criteria: Correctly sets up the matrix dimensions throughout
Correctly derives the softmax Jacobian term in the backward pass
Identifies the n×n matrix as the bottleneck
Explains how FlashAttention addresses it
common_mistakes: Getting the backward pass through softmax wrong (common — the outer product term is non-obvious)
Confusing the attention matrix memory footprint with the weight matrix memory
deep_dive.follow_up: How does FlashAttention's tiling approach ensure numerical stability while avoiding storing the full attention matrix?

deep_dive.question: What is the relationship between Transformers and kernel methods? Explain the Performer and its FAVOR+ approximation.
deep_dive.model_answer: Standard attention: A(Q,K,V) = softmax(QKᵀ/√d_k)V. If we view softmax(qᵢkⱼᵀ/√d_k) as a similarity kernel, attention is a kernel regression where each output position is a kernel-weighted sum of values. The quadratic cost comes from evaluating this kernel for all n² pairs. Performer (Choromanski et al., 2021): approximates the softmax attention using a feature map φ such that softmax(qᵢkⱼᵀ) ≈ φ(qᵢ)ᵀφ(kⱼ). This factorises the n×n kernel matrix as Φ_Q·Φ_Kᵀ, allowing the computation to be rearranged: A(Q,K,V) ≈ Φ_Q·(Φ_Kᵀ·V). The parenthesised multiplication is computed first — O(n·d²) instead of O(n²·d). FAVOR+ (Fast Attention Via Orthogonal Random features): constructs unbiased estimates of softmax using random Fourier features with orthogonalisation. Standard random features have high variance — orthogonal random features reduce variance while maintaining the unbiased property. The approximation error and variance are bounded. Limitation: FAVOR+ approximates softmax — for tasks where exact attention patterns matter (e.g., long-range coreference), the approximation can hurt quality. For approximate tasks, it's highly effective.
evaluation_criteria: Frames attention as a kernel regression
Shows the n² → n algebraic factorisation trick
Explains FAVOR+ and why orthogonalisation reduces variance
Acknowledges the approximation quality tradeoff
common_mistakes: Confusing Performers with Linformers (a different linear attention approach via low-rank projection of K and V)
deep_dive.follow_up: How does the Linformer approach to linear attention differ from Performer's, and what are the tradeoffs?

deep_dive.question: Explain the training objective and architecture of BERT in detail. What specifically does masked language modelling force the model to learn?
deep_dive.model_answer: BERT architecture: L=12 (base) or 24 (large) Transformer encoder layers. d_model=768 or 1024. 12 or 16 heads. Input: [CLS] token₁ ... tokenₙ [SEP] token representations = token embeddings + segment embeddings + learned positional embeddings. Pretraining objectives: (1) Masked Language Modelling (MLM): 15% of tokens are selected. Of those: 80% replaced with [MASK], 10% replaced with a random token, 10% left unchanged. The 10% random and 10% unchanged prevent the model from learning to only attend to [MASK] tokens. The model must predict the original token. This forces: (a) bidirectional context integration — to predict a masked word, every other token must be attended to, (b) syntactic understanding — predicting masked verbs/nouns requires grammatical knowledge, (c) semantic knowledge — predicting masked entities requires world knowledge. (2) Next Sentence Prediction (NSP): predict whether sentence B follows sentence A. Later shown to be less useful; RoBERTa drops it entirely. Fine-tuning: [CLS] representation used for classification; per-token representations for NER/span prediction. The random 10% in masking is critical — without it, the model only learns about [MASK] tokens and fails to build general representations.
evaluation_criteria: States the 80/10/10 masking strategy
Explains why the 10/10 split is necessary
Describes what MLM forces the model to learn with specificity
Mentions NSP and that RoBERTa ablated it
common_mistakes: Saying BERT uses causal attention — it uses full bidirectional attention
Not explaining the rationale for the 10% random, 10% unchanged split
deep_dive.follow_up: Why does using whole-word masking instead of subword masking improve BERT's representations?

deep_dive.question: What is Flash Attention? Explain the tiling algorithm and how it achieves both memory efficiency and speed despite still being O(n²) in compute.
deep_dive.model_answer: Standard attention materialises the n×n attention matrix A in GPU High Bandwidth Memory (HBM). For n=8k, this is 8k² × 32 heads × 2 bytes = 4GB just in HBM reads/writes. Modern GPUs are compute-bound on small ops but memory-bandwidth-bound on large data movements. FlashAttention insight: the bottleneck is not FLOP count but HBM I/O. Algorithm: (1) Tile Q into blocks Q₁...Qₜ and K,V into blocks K₁...Kₛ. (2) Load one block of Q and one block of K,V into SRAM (which is 10-100x faster than HBM). (3) Compute partial attention scores and partial output in SRAM. (4) Use online softmax normalisation (the log-sum-exp trick) to accumulate the correct softmax across blocks without needing to see all K,V at once. (5) Write only the final output O back to HBM — never the n×n attention matrix. Result: HBM reads/writes reduced from O(n²) to O(n). Wall-clock time: 2-4x faster for long sequences. Memory: O(n) instead of O(n²). FLOPs: still O(n²·d) — compute is unchanged, I/O is what was reduced. FlashAttention-2 and 3 extend this with better parallelism over the sequence dimension and WGMMA instructions on H100.
evaluation_criteria: Correctly identifies HBM I/O as the bottleneck, not FLOPs
Explains the SRAM tiling concept
Describes the online softmax normalisation trick
States that compute is O(n²) but I/O is O(n)
common_mistakes: Saying FlashAttention is O(n) in compute — it's O(n) in memory I/O only
Not explaining why SRAM vs HBM matters (bandwidth gap)
deep_dive.follow_up: How does the online softmax computation work? Derive how it accumulates the correct normalised attention weights across tiles.

conceptual.question: Explain the pretraining objective of GPT-style models. What does next-token prediction force the model to learn?
conceptual.model_answer: GPT-style pretraining: maximise the log-likelihood of each token given all preceding tokens: L = Σₜ log P(xₜ | x₁,...,xₜ₋₁). This is causal language modelling (CLM). To predict the next token accurately, the model must learn: (1) Syntax and grammar — incorrect predictions for grammatically ill-formed continuations. (2) World knowledge — factual associations (e.g., 'The capital of France is...'). (3) Reasoning patterns — multi-step arithmetic, logical deductions that appear in text. (4) Style and discourse — coherent paragraph structure, argument flow. (5) Code — syntax, variable scoping, algorithm patterns when trained on code. The key insight: language modelling is a surprisingly complete proxy for intelligence because natural language encodes human knowledge, reasoning, and communication. Emergent capabilities (few-shot learning, chain-of-thought) arise when models are trained at sufficient scale, which was not predicted by the objective alone.
evaluation_criteria: States the CLM objective correctly
Identifies multiple distinct things the model must learn to predict tokens well
Mentions emergent capabilities and their relationship to scale
Distinguishes CLM (GPT) from MLM (BERT)
common_mistakes: Saying GPT 'just predicts words' without connecting this to the breadth of knowledge required
conceptual.follow_up: What is the scaling hypothesis and what evidence supports or challenges it?

conceptual.question: Explain Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF). What problem does it solve and what are its components?
conceptual.model_answer: Problem: A pretrained LLM optimised for next-token prediction is not optimised for being helpful, harmless, and honest. It may generate plausible text that is harmful, misleading, or unhelpful. RLHF aligns the model's outputs with human preferences. Components: (1) Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT): Fine-tune the pretrained LLM on a curated dataset of high-quality (prompt, response) pairs written by labellers. This gives the model the right format and basic behaviour. (2) Reward Model (RM): Present labellers with two responses to the same prompt; they indicate which is better. Train a reward model on these pairwise preferences to predict a scalar reward score for any (prompt, response) pair. (3) RL Optimisation (PPO): Use the reward model as the reward signal. Optimise the SFT model using Proximal Policy Optimisation (PPO) to maximise expected reward while staying close to the SFT policy via a KL penalty: reward = RM(x,y) - β·KL(π_RL || π_SFT). The KL term prevents reward hacking. Output: a model that scores highly on human preference comparisons.
evaluation_criteria: Names all three stages in order (SFT, RM, RL)
Explains what the reward model is trained on (pairwise comparisons)
States the KL penalty and explains its purpose (prevent reward hacking)
Identifies PPO as the RL algorithm
common_mistakes: Skipping the SFT stage and going straight to RL from the pretrained model
Not explaining why the KL constraint is necessary
conceptual.follow_up: What is Direct Preference Optimisation (DPO) and how does it simplify the RLHF pipeline?

conceptual.question: What is in-context learning (ICL) / few-shot prompting? How does it work mechanistically?
conceptual.model_answer: In-context learning: at inference, the model is given a prompt containing a few (k) examples of (input, output) pairs followed by a test input. Without any gradient updates, the model generates the correct output for the test input. Zero-shot: no examples, just task description. Few-shot: k examples (typically 1-10). Mechanistic understanding: Brown et al. (2020, GPT-3) showed few-shot performance scales dramatically with model size. Hypotheses: (1) Task identification — the examples let the model identify the task distribution and select appropriate text completion patterns from its pretraining distribution. (2) Format copying — the model learns output format from examples. (3) Implicit gradient updates — Akyürek et al. (2022) showed ICL is functionally equivalent to gradient descent on the context examples, implemented via the attention mechanism. (4) Head specialisation — certain attention heads in large models implement induction copying (attend to the token that followed the current token type previously), which is the mechanical substrate for ICL. Limitations: ICL performance is sensitive to example order, label format, and surface-level choices — it is not robust.
evaluation_criteria: Defines zero-shot vs few-shot correctly
Explains at least one mechanistic theory (induction heads or implicit gradient descent)
Notes that ICL requires no weight updates
Mentions sensitivity/fragility as a limitation
common_mistakes: Confusing ICL with fine-tuning — no weights are updated in ICL
conceptual.follow_up: What are induction heads and why are they considered the mechanical basis for in-context learning?

conceptual.question: Explain parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT). Compare LoRA, prefix tuning, and prompt tuning.
conceptual.model_answer: Full fine-tuning updates all model parameters — expensive (same parameter count as the model) and requires separate model copies per task. PEFT methods update only a small number of additional or selected parameters. LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation): freezes pretrained weights W and injects trainable low-rank decompositions ΔW = BA where B ∈ ℝ^(d×r), A ∈ ℝ^(r×k), rank r ≪ min(d,k). Typically r=4-64 for billion-parameter models. At inference, ΔW is merged into W, so no additional latency. Very effective: matches or exceeds full fine-tuning on many tasks with 0.1% of the parameters. Prefix Tuning: prepends trainable 'soft prompt' vectors to the key and value sequences in each attention layer. The prefix is not natural language — it's optimised directly in embedding space. More expressive than prompt tuning, but harder to train. Prompt Tuning: prepends trainable tokens only to the input embedding layer, not all attention layers. Simpler than prefix tuning, scales well with model size (matches fine-tuning for very large models). QLoRA: LoRA applied to a 4-bit quantised model — enables fine-tuning 65B models on a single 48GB GPU.
evaluation_criteria: Explains LoRA's BA decomposition and why r ≪ d matters
Distinguishes prefix tuning (all layers) from prompt tuning (input only)
Notes that LoRA merges at inference for zero latency overhead
Mentions QLoRA
common_mistakes: Confusing soft prompts with natural language prompt engineering
Forgetting that LoRA can be merged — thinking it always adds latency
conceptual.follow_up: Why does LoRA work well despite the low-rank constraint? What is the theoretical justification?

conceptual.question: What is hallucination in LLMs? What are the main causes and mitigation strategies?
conceptual.model_answer: Hallucination: the LLM generates confident, fluent, plausible-sounding statements that are factually incorrect or unsupported by the input. Types: (1) Factual hallucination — incorrect facts about the world. (2) Faithfulness hallucination — contradicts or goes beyond the provided source document. Causes: (1) Knowledge compression — pretraining compresses knowledge into weights; the model interpolates or extrapolates incorrectly for obscure facts. (2) RLHF reward hacking — reward models prefer confident, fluent text; models learn to generate confident-sounding text even without knowledge. (3) Sycophancy — models trained on human preferences learn to agree with users rather than be accurate. (4) Long-tail knowledge — rare facts are underrepresented in training data. (5) Attention limitations — model cannot properly integrate information across very long contexts. Mitigations: (1) RAG — ground responses in retrieved documents, forcing the model to cite sources. (2) Output verification — self-consistency checking (generate multiple responses and vote). (3) Uncertainty quantification — train models to express calibrated uncertainty. (4) Fine-tuning with factuality rewards. (5) Tool use — use search/calculators instead of relying on parametric memory.
evaluation_criteria: Distinguishes factual vs faithfulness hallucination
Gives multiple root causes beyond 'the model made it up'
Proposes at least 3 concrete mitigations
Mentions RLHF sycophancy as a cause
common_mistakes: Treating hallucination as purely a knowledge gap problem — it's also a confidence calibration problem
conceptual.follow_up: How does self-consistency sampling reduce hallucination and what are its limitations?

conceptual.question: What is the difference between zero-shot, few-shot, and fine-tuning? When would you choose each?
conceptual.model_answer: Zero-shot: Task is described in the prompt with no examples. No data or training required. Performance depends entirely on the model's pretraining. Best for: well-defined tasks that the model has seen in pretraining, quick prototyping, tasks where collecting labelled data is impossible. Few-shot / in-context learning: k examples are provided in the prompt. No gradient updates. Performance improves with k but is sensitive to example quality and order. Best for: tasks needing format specification, tasks where collecting a few examples is easy, when the model is too large to fine-tune. Fine-tuning: Update model weights on task-specific labelled data. Highest performance for specific tasks. Options range from full fine-tuning (all weights) to PEFT (LoRA, etc.) to just the classification head. Best for: production systems with stable, well-defined tasks and sufficient labelled data, where maximum accuracy on the target task is required. Decision framework: zero-shot first (cheapest), then few-shot if output is poor, then PEFT fine-tuning if few-shot is insufficient and you have 100-10k labelled examples, then full fine-tuning if you have 10k+ examples and need maximum performance.
evaluation_criteria: Clearly explains what happens to model weights in each case
Gives concrete guidance on when to choose each
Orders them by cost/effort vs performance
Mentions PEFT as the middle ground
common_mistakes: Treating fine-tuning as always better — zero/few-shot with GPT-4 often beats fine-tuned BERT
conceptual.follow_up: When can few-shot prompting outperform fine-tuning a smaller model?

applied.question: Design a system to reduce hallucinations in an LLM-based customer support bot. The bot must cite specific policy documents.
applied.model_answer: Architecture: RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) pipeline with citation enforcement. (1) Document preparation: Chunk policy documents into paragraphs (256-512 tokens), each with a unique chunk_id. Generate embeddings (E5-large or text-embedding-ada-002). Store in vector database (Qdrant/Weaviate) with chunk_id, source_doc, section metadata. (2) Query processing: Embed user query. Retrieve top-k (10-15) relevant chunks via ANN search. Optionally rerank with a cross-encoder. (3) Prompt construction: System prompt enforces citation: 'Answer ONLY using the provided documents. For every factual claim, cite the specific chunk_id.' Provide retrieved chunks with their IDs in the prompt. (4) Response generation: LLM generates with inline citations [chunk_id]. (5) Post-processing: Verify every claim is backed by a cited chunk (automated hallucination detection). Flag uncited claims. Optionally extract cited text and highlight it to the user. (6) Faithfulness evaluation: Use a second LLM as a judge — 'Is this claim supported by the cited text?' to automatically catch unfaithful citations. (7) Fallback: If retrieval finds nothing relevant (below threshold), return 'I couldn't find this in our documentation' rather than generating from parametric memory.
evaluation_criteria: Proposes RAG as the core approach
Includes chunk_id citation enforcement in the prompt
Proposes automated faithfulness verification
Includes a fallback for low-confidence cases
common_mistakes: Not addressing the case where the LLM cites a chunk but misrepresents it (faithfulness hallucination)
Using the same LLM for generation and verification without noting conflict of interest
applied.follow_up: How would you measure the hallucination rate of this system in production without labelling every response manually?

applied.question: You need to fine-tune Llama-3-8B on a custom dataset of 50,000 examples on a single A100 80GB GPU. Walk through the training setup.
applied.model_answer: Llama-3-8B in float32 = 32GB weights alone. On a single A100 80GB: (1) Quantisation: Load the model in 4-bit (QLoRA) using bitsandbytes NF4 quantisation. Model footprint: ~4-5GB. (2) LoRA config: Apply LoRA to query and value projections (and optionally all linear layers). rank=16 or 32, alpha=32, dropout=0.05. Trainable params: ~1-5% of base model. (3) Training framework: Use HuggingFace PEFT + trl (SFTTrainer) or LLaMA-Factory. (4) Gradient checkpointing: Trade compute for memory — don't store all intermediate activations, recompute on backward pass. Saves ~50-70% activation memory. (5) Batch size: With QLoRA + gradient checkpointing, can fit batch_size=4-8, gradient accumulation=4-8 steps for effective batch of 16-64. (6) Mixed precision: bf16 for LoRA adapter weights (the 4-bit base model stays quantised). (7) Sequence length: Start with 2048, increase to 4096 if memory allows — shorter sequences allow larger batches. (8) Optimizer: 8-bit AdamW (also from bitsandbytes) halves optimizer state memory. (9) Chat template: Format examples correctly for Llama-3's chat template; mask system + user tokens in loss (train only on assistant responses).
evaluation_criteria: Names QLoRA specifically and explains why it's necessary
Covers gradient checkpointing
Mentions 8-bit AdamW for optimizer state compression
Notes loss masking to train only on assistant tokens
common_mistakes: Attempting full fine-tuning without quantisation — won't fit in 80GB
Not masking the instruction/prompt tokens in the loss calculation
applied.follow_up: How would you evaluate whether your fine-tuned model is better than the base model without expensive human evaluation?

applied.question: Compare chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting, tree-of-thought (ToT), and ReAct. When would you use each for a reasoning-heavy task?
applied.model_answer: Chain-of-Thought (CoT): Prompts the model to generate intermediate reasoning steps before the final answer ('Let's think step by step'). Works because LLMs trained on text where reasoning is written out explicitly can activate latent reasoning capabilities. Best for: mathematical reasoning, multi-step logical deductions, tasks where the answer depends on sequential intermediate results. Simple to implement. Tree-of-Thought (ToT): Extends CoT to explore multiple reasoning branches. At each step, the model generates k candidate thoughts, a value function evaluates each, and search (BFS/DFS) selects the best path. Best for: problems with discrete decision points where backtracking is valuable — puzzles, multi-step planning, creative writing with structural constraints. Significantly more expensive (multiple LLM calls per step). ReAct (Reason + Act): Interleaves reasoning traces with actions (tool calls) and observations. The model reasons about what to do, calls a tool (search, calculator, code executor), observes the result, and continues reasoning. Best for: tasks requiring external knowledge (search), precise computation (calculator), or code execution. The foundation of most production AI agents. Decision: Use CoT for pure reasoning tasks. Use ReAct when the task needs external information or computation. Reserve ToT for problems where exploring multiple solution paths and backtracking is essential — it's expensive.
evaluation_criteria: Correctly describes each technique
Explains why CoT works (externalising reasoning steps)
Notes ToT's search mechanism and cost
Identifies ReAct as the basis for agents
Gives concrete decision guidance
common_mistakes: Conflating CoT with ReAct — CoT has no tool use
Recommending ToT without acknowledging its compute cost
applied.follow_up: What is the difference between tool use and function calling in modern LLM APIs?

applied.question: You're asked to evaluate whether GPT-4 or a fine-tuned open-source model is better for your production use case. Design the evaluation framework.
applied.model_answer: Evaluation framework: (1) Define success metrics for your specific task (F1 for extraction, BLEU/ROUGE for summarisation, custom rubric for generation quality). Never rely on a single metric. (2) Build an evaluation dataset: 200-500 representative examples with human-labelled ground truth. Include edge cases, adversarial examples, and common failure modes. (3) Automated evaluation: Task-specific metrics (accuracy, F1, ROUGE). LLM-as-judge: use a powerful LLM (GPT-4-turbo) to rate outputs on dimensions like accuracy, helpfulness, coherence. Pairwise comparison: show the judge two outputs, ask which is better — reduces position bias. (4) Human evaluation: Blind A/B comparison for a sample of examples. Have evaluators rate on your rubric. Use inter-annotator agreement to validate rubric clarity. (5) Practical evaluation: Latency: p50, p95, p99 latency under production load. Cost per 1000 requests: compute total cost including inference. Rate limits and reliability: API quota for GPT-4, self-hosted infrastructure for open-source. (6) Safety evaluation: Adversarial prompts, jailbreak attempts, PII leakage tests. (7) Decision: If fine-tuned open-source matches GPT-4 on your task metrics, it likely wins on cost and latency. If GPT-4 is significantly better and the task is business-critical, the API cost may be justified.
evaluation_criteria: Covers automated + human evaluation
Includes latency and cost in the framework
Uses LLM-as-judge approach
Includes safety/adversarial evaluation
common_mistakes: Evaluating only on accuracy without latency and cost
Using the model being evaluated as its own judge
applied.follow_up: What is LLM-as-judge bias and how do you mitigate it?

applied.question: Design an LLM-powered pipeline to extract structured data (company name, revenue, headcount) from unstructured earnings call transcripts at scale.
applied.model_answer: Scale assumption: thousands of transcripts per day. (1) Extraction approach: Use an LLM with structured output (JSON mode or function calling). System prompt: 'Extract the following fields from the transcript. Return valid JSON only. If a field is not mentioned, return null.' Schema: {company: str, fiscal_quarter: str, revenue_usd_millions: float, revenue_yoy_growth_pct: float | null, headcount: int | null, ...}. (2) Model selection: GPT-4o-mini or a fine-tuned Llama-3-8B via vLLM for cost at scale. GPT-4o-mini is ~20x cheaper than GPT-4 for extraction tasks. (3) Chunking: Transcripts can be 50-100 pages. Chunk into sections (operator remarks, Q&A). Extract per section, merge results with deduplication. Alternatively, identify the 'highlights' section first and extract from there. (4) Validation: Pydantic schema validation of the JSON output. Range checks (revenue > 0, headcount > 100). Regex cross-validation for numeric fields. Flag low-confidence extractions for human review. (5) Serving: Async Celery workers for batch processing. Redis for job tracking. Store results in PostgreSQL with source_chunk references for auditability. (6) Monitoring: Track extraction failure rate, null rate per field, human review rate. Alert if null rate spikes (model degradation or format change in transcripts).
evaluation_criteria: Uses structured JSON output / function calling
Addresses transcript length with chunking
Includes Pydantic validation and error handling
Considers cost-efficient model selection for scale
common_mistakes: Passing the full 100-page transcript to the LLM without chunking
No validation step — assuming LLM JSON output is always valid
applied.follow_up: How would you continuously monitor for data quality degradation if the format of earnings call transcripts changes over time?

deep_dive.question: Explain the scaling laws for LLMs (Chinchilla scaling laws). What are their implications for training compute-optimal models?
deep_dive.model_answer: Kaplan et al. (2020, OpenAI): Model loss L scales as a power law in model size N, data size D, and compute C: L(N) ∝ N^(-α), L(D) ∝ D^(-β). For fixed compute C, both N and D should be scaled together — earlier work (GPT-3) overparameterised models relative to data. Hoffmann et al. (2022, Chinchilla paper): Re-fit the scaling laws with more data points. Finding: for compute-optimal training, data tokens D should scale linearly with model parameters N: D ≈ 20·N. GPT-3 (175B params) was trained on ~300B tokens — Chinchilla-optimal would be 3.5T tokens. Chinchilla (70B params, 1.4T tokens) matches or exceeds GPT-3 at 1/3 the parameters. Implications: (1) Most pre-Chinchilla LLMs were undertrained — more data, same compute budget, smaller model is better. (2) Models trained Chinchilla-optimally are smaller and faster at inference for the same capability level. (3) Beyond compute-optimal training: models like Llama-2-7B trained on 2T tokens (far more than Chinchilla-optimal for inference-efficiency). For deployment, training longer on more data makes a smaller model competitive with a larger model — more practical.
evaluation_criteria: Describes Kaplan et al. power laws
States the 20·N Chinchilla finding
Explains that most pre-Chinchilla models were undertrained
Distinguishes compute-optimal for training vs inference-efficient
common_mistakes: Confusing compute-optimal training with optimal inference — they imply different model size choices
deep_dive.follow_up: How do the Chinchilla scaling laws apply to reasoning models like o1/o3 that use test-time compute scaling?

deep_dive.question: Explain KV caching in autoregressive Transformer inference. How does GQA (Grouped-Query Attention) reduce its memory footprint?
deep_dive.model_answer: Autoregressive inference: to generate token tₙ, the model runs a forward pass over [t₁,...,tₙ₋₁,tₙ]. Without caching, this would repeat all attention computations for previous tokens. KV cache: store the key and value projections for all previous tokens in all layers. At step n, only compute K,V for the new token and append to the cache. Attention over the full history is computed with cached K,V + new Q. Cache size for a single sequence: 2 × n_layers × seq_len × n_heads × d_head × dtype_bytes. For Llama-2-70B: 2 × 80 × 4096 × 8 × 128 × 2 bytes ≈ 1GB per sequence at 4k tokens. For batch_size=32 at 8k tokens: 64GB — the full GPU memory. Multi-Query Attention (MQA): use a single K,V head shared across all Q heads. Reduces KV cache size by n_heads times. Slight quality degradation. Grouped-Query Attention (GQA): compromise — group Q heads into G groups, each sharing one K,V head. n_kv_heads = n_q_heads / G. Llama-3 uses G=8, so 8 Q heads share 1 K,V head per group. Reduces KV cache 8x vs MHA with minimal quality loss vs MQA. GQA also improves decoding throughput because K,V loading from HBM is the bottleneck during decoding — fewer K,V heads = less bandwidth required.
evaluation_criteria: Explains why KV caching avoids recomputation
Quantifies the cache size with actual numbers
Correctly describes the MQA/GQA hierarchy
Explains the bandwidth bottleneck during decoding
common_mistakes: Not quantifying cache size — vague answers don't demonstrate engineering depth
Confusing MQA and GQA
deep_dive.follow_up: What is speculative decoding and how does it speed up autoregressive inference beyond KV cache?

deep_dive.question: What is Direct Preference Optimisation (DPO)? Derive why it is equivalent to RLHF with a closed-form optimal policy.
deep_dive.model_answer: RLHF objective: max_π E[r(x,y)] - β·KL(π || π_ref). The closed-form optimal policy is: π*(y|x) ∝ π_ref(y|x)·exp(r(x,y)/β). Rearranging: r(x,y) = β·log(π*(y|x)/π_ref(y|x)) + β·log Z(x). DPO insight (Rafailov et al., 2023): instead of learning r and then optimising π, substitute the optimal policy equation into the Bradley-Terry preference model directly. Bradley-Terry: P(yₗ ≻ yₗₒₛₑ|x) = σ(r(yₗ) - r(yₗₒₛₑ)). Substitute r(y) = β·log(π(y)/π_ref(y)) + const: P(yₗ ≻ yₗₒₛₑ|x) = σ(β·log(π(yₗ)/π_ref(yₗ)) - β·log(π(yₗₒₛₑ)/π_ref(yₗₒₛₑ))). DPO loss: L_DPO = -E[log σ(β·(log π(yₗ)/π_ref(yₗ) - log π(yₗₒₛₑ)/π_ref(yₗₒₛₑ)))]. This eliminates the separate reward model and RL loop entirely. Advantages: simpler training pipeline, no reward model needed, no PPO instability. Disadvantages: requires offline preference data (no online exploration), can be brittle if reference model is too far from the optimal policy.
evaluation_criteria: States the RLHF objective with KL constraint
Derives the closed-form optimal policy
Substitutes into Bradley-Terry to arrive at DPO loss
Compares RLHF vs DPO tradeoffs
common_mistakes: Presenting DPO as just 'simpler RLHF' without the derivation — the derivation shows they are theoretically equivalent
Not acknowledging DPO's limitations (offline data, no exploration)
deep_dive.follow_up: What is the token-level DPO extension and why might it be superior to the sequence-level formulation?

deep_dive.question: Explain the Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture. How does sparse MoE enable scaling model capacity without proportional compute?
deep_dive.model_answer: Standard dense Transformer: all parameters are used for every input token. MoE: replace the FFN sublayer with E expert FFNs and a router. For each token, the router selects the top-k experts (typically k=1 or 2). Only the selected experts process the token. Parameters: E × FFN parameters. FLOPs per token: k/E × E × FFN FLOPs = k × FFN FLOPs. Key: model capacity (parameters) scales with E, compute per token stays constant. Examples: Switch Transformer (k=1, E=128-2048), Mixtral-8x7B (k=2, E=8 — each 'expert' is a 7B FFN, active parameters per token = 12.5B, total parameters = 47B). Router: a linear layer computes softmax scores over all experts, selects top-k, applies scores as weights. Load balancing: without explicit balancing, a few experts dominate (expert collapse). Solutions: auxiliary loss penalising uneven expert utilisation, noise injection, expert capacity limit (drop tokens that exceed a per-expert budget). Engineering challenges: all-to-all communication across GPUs when experts are distributed — communication-heavy. Expert parallelism required at scale. Evaluation: Mixtral-8x7B matches Llama-2-70B performance at 1/4 the active parameters — 4x more efficient inference.
evaluation_criteria: Explains the router and top-k selection
Derives that compute scales with k, not E
Names load balancing as a key challenge and describes a solution
References a real MoE model (Mixtral, Switch Transformer)
common_mistakes: Saying MoE reduces all compute — it reduces only FFN compute; attention is still full
Not addressing expert collapse/load balancing
deep_dive.follow_up: How does the routing mechanism in Mixtral differ from the Switch Transformer, and what are the tradeoffs of k=1 vs k=2?

conceptual.question: What is Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)? What problem does it solve compared to pure LLM generation?
conceptual.model_answer: RAG combines information retrieval with language generation. The LLM's parametric memory (weights) is augmented with non-parametric memory (a retrieved document store). Query → Retriever → Top-k documents → LLM prompt with documents → Grounded response. Problems solved: (1) Knowledge cutoff — LLMs have static training data; RAG provides access to current or private information. (2) Hallucination — grounding in retrieved documents gives the LLM source material to cite, reducing confabulation. (3) Verifiability — responses can cite specific chunks, allowing users to verify claims. (4) Domain specificity — without fine-tuning, a general LLM can be specialised by constructing a domain-specific document store. (5) Cost — cheaper than fine-tuning for knowledge injection. Limitations: retrieval quality is the bottleneck; if the retriever fails to fetch the right documents, the generator cannot compensate. Garbage in, garbage out.
evaluation_criteria: Describes the retrieve-then-generate pipeline correctly
Identifies at least 3 problems RAG addresses
Distinguishes parametric vs non-parametric memory
Acknowledges retrieval quality as the bottleneck
common_mistakes: Treating RAG as primarily an anti-hallucination tool — it addresses multiple distinct problems
conceptual.follow_up: What is the difference between naive RAG and advanced RAG, and what does advanced RAG add?

conceptual.question: Explain dense vs sparse retrieval. What are the tradeoffs between BM25 and embedding-based approaches?
conceptual.model_answer: Sparse retrieval (BM25): bag-of-words model with TF-IDF weighting and length normalisation. BM25(q,d) = Σᵢ IDF(qᵢ)·(f(qᵢ,d)·(k₁+1))/(f(qᵢ,d)+k₁·(1-b+b·|d|/avgdl)). Strengths: exact keyword matching, interpretable, fast (inverted index lookup), no embeddings needed, works well for named entities and codes. Dense retrieval: embed query and documents into a vector space; find nearest neighbours by cosine/dot-product similarity. Models like DPR, E5, BGE. Strengths: semantic matching — 'car' matches 'vehicle', paraphrase handling, multilingual. Weaknesses: vocabulary mismatch with technical jargon, slower (ANN search), requires embedding infrastructure. Hybrid search: combine both via reciprocal rank fusion (RRF): score = Σ_r 1/(k + rank_r(d)). This consistently outperforms either alone, especially on heterogeneous queries (some need exact match, some need semantic match). Industry standard: most production RAG systems use hybrid retrieval.
evaluation_criteria: States the BM25 formula or at minimum its components
Identifies where each excels (exact match vs semantic)
Proposes hybrid search as the production recommendation
Describes RRF or another fusion method
common_mistakes: Saying dense retrieval is 'always better' — BM25 is hard to beat for exact technical terms
Not knowing RRF as the standard fusion technique
conceptual.follow_up: What is learned sparse retrieval (SPLADE) and how does it bridge dense and sparse approaches?

conceptual.question: What is an embedding model? How is it different from a generative LLM, and what makes a good embedding model?
conceptual.model_answer: An embedding model encodes text into a fixed-size dense vector that captures semantic meaning. The vector distance (cosine similarity or dot product) correlates with semantic similarity. Architecturally: typically a BERT-style encoder. The [CLS] token or mean-pooled output is the embedding. Unlike generative LLMs: no decoder, no autoregressive generation, no next-token objective. Trained on: (1) Contrastive learning — given (query, positive_doc, negative_docs), push the positive pair closer and negatives apart. Loss: InfoNCE / NT-Xent. (2) Sentence pair classification (NLI). (3) Hard negative mining — use BM25 or dense retrieval to find 'hard' negatives that are similar but wrong — crucial for quality. What makes a good embedding model: (1) Asymmetric encoding — query and document may have different characteristics; some models (like E5) use 'query: ...' and 'passage: ...' prefixes. (2) Training data quality and diversity. (3) Normalised embeddings for cosine similarity. (4) MTEB (Massive Text Embedding Benchmark) is the standard evaluation across 56 tasks. Top models: E5-mistral-7b, BGE-M3, GTE-Qwen2.
evaluation_criteria: Distinguishes encoder from generative model
Explains contrastive training and hard negatives
Names MTEB as the benchmark
Names at least one production-grade embedding model
common_mistakes: Using a generative LLM embedding (e.g., GPT-4 embeddings) without knowing it's a separate fine-tuned model
conceptual.follow_up: What is the matryoshka representation learning (MRL) approach and why is it useful for embedding models?

conceptual.question: What is a vector database? How do HNSW indices enable fast approximate nearest neighbour search?
conceptual.model_answer: A vector database stores and indexes high-dimensional embedding vectors, enabling fast similarity search. Beyond storage, it provides: ANN indexing, metadata filtering, hybrid search, and CRUD operations on vector collections. HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World): inspired by skip lists and small-world graph theory. Construction: vectors are organised into a multi-layer graph. Each layer is a subgraph where vertices are connected to k nearest neighbours, with fewer vertices at higher layers (exponentially decreasing probability of inclusion). Top layers are coarse, lower layers are dense. Query: start at the entry point in the top layer. Greedily traverse to the nearest neighbour at that layer. Descend to the next layer and repeat. At the bottom layer, collect the top-k candidates. Complexity: O(log n) query time. Parameters: M (edges per node, trades recall vs memory), ef_construction (search depth during build, trades build time vs quality), ef_search (query recall vs speed). Recall vs speed: at ef_search=100, HNSW achieves ~99% recall at ~1ms for 1M vectors. Limitation: HNSW is in-memory — for billion-scale, DiskANN (graph-based index on disk) or IVF-PQ (product quantisation for compression) are used.
evaluation_criteria: Explains the layered graph structure
Describes the greedy top-down query traversal
States O(log n) complexity
Names the key parameters and their tradeoffs
Mentions billion-scale alternatives
common_mistakes: Treating all vector databases as HNSW — IVF, ANNOY, ScaNN are also common index types
conceptual.follow_up: How does product quantisation (PQ) reduce the memory footprint of a vector index?

conceptual.question: What is chunking in RAG and why does chunking strategy significantly affect retrieval quality?
conceptual.model_answer: Chunking: documents are split into segments before embedding. Embeddings capture the semantic content of a chunk — if a chunk is too large, the embedding averages over unrelated information. If too small, it loses context. Effects on retrieval quality: (1) Granularity: Small chunks (50-100 tokens) give precise retrieval but may lose surrounding context needed to answer the question. Large chunks (500-1000 tokens) contain more context but produce noisier embeddings. (2) Boundary effects: Fixed-size character splitting can cut mid-sentence, creating incoherent chunks. Sentence-aware or semantic splitting produces cleaner embeddings. (3) Overlap: Sliding window with overlap (e.g., 20%) ensures that sentences near boundaries are covered in at least one chunk. (4) Structural chunking: Split by paragraph, section, or document structure rather than by character count — preserves natural semantic units. (5) Embedding mismatch: Embedding models are trained on specific input lengths — exceeding the model's sweet spot degrades embedding quality. Advanced strategies: (1) Parent-child chunking — embed small child chunks for precise retrieval, but return the full parent chunk to the LLM for context. (2) Proposition chunking — extract atomic factual propositions as chunks for maximum precision.
evaluation_criteria: Explains granularity tradeoff
Mentions overlap and its purpose
Describes at least one advanced chunking strategy
Connects to embedding model context window
common_mistakes: Treating chunking as a solved problem — it's one of the most impactful RAG hyperparameters
conceptual.follow_up: How does semantic chunking differ from fixed-size chunking and when is the overhead justified?

applied.question: Your RAG system retrieves relevant documents but the LLM still gives incorrect answers. How do you diagnose and fix this?
applied.model_answer: This is a 'retrieval is fine, generation is broken' pattern — but first verify the assumption. Diagnosis pipeline: (1) Retrieval quality check: Manually inspect the top-k retrieved chunks for 20-30 queries. Are the right documents actually being retrieved? Calculate retrieval recall (does the answer document appear in top-k?). If retrieval recall is low, the problem is not in the generator. (2) Context faithfulness: Given the retrieved context + query, does the LLM extract the correct answer from the context? Test with oracle context (manually provide the correct document). If it still fails with oracle context, the problem is the generator/prompt, not retrieval. (3) Failure mode categorisation: Retrieval precision failures (wrong docs retrieved). Faithfulness failures (LLM ignores retrieved context, uses parametric memory instead). Synthesis failures (answer requires combining info across multiple chunks). Reasoning failures (correct info retrieved but model can't reason over it). Fixes per failure mode: For faithfulness failures: stronger system prompt emphasising 'use only the provided documents'. Citation enforcement. Larger context window to fit more relevant chunks. For synthesis failures: multi-hop retrieval (retrieve, generate a sub-answer, retrieve again). Graph RAG for entity-relationship traversal. For reasoning failures: chain-of-thought prompting, or upgrade to a stronger LLM.
evaluation_criteria: Tests retrieval and generation independently before drawing conclusions
Proposes oracle context test
Categorises failure modes specifically
Provides targeted fixes per failure mode
common_mistakes: Immediately improving the LLM when the problem might be in the retriever
Not testing with oracle context to isolate the problem
applied.follow_up: How would you build an automated RAG evaluation pipeline using RAGAS?

applied.question: Design a RAG pipeline for a codebase Q&A system (e.g., 'How does our authentication module work?').
applied.model_answer: Code has unique structure unlike prose. Pipeline design: (1) Indexing strategy: Don't chunk by character — chunk by code structure: per-function, per-class, per-file module. Use tree-sitter to parse ASTs and extract logical units. For each function: store function signature, docstring, body, file path, and a natural language summary (generated by an LLM). (2) Metadata: File path, module name, language, last_modified. Enables metadata filtering ('only search Python files', 'only search auth module'). (3) Embedding: Use a code-specific embedding model (CodeBERT, UniXCoder, or text-embedding-3-large which handles code well). (4) Retrieval: Hybrid: code-specific dense embeddings + BM25 on function names and docstrings. Rerank with a code cross-encoder. (5) Context construction: When retrieving a function, also include: its docstring, calling functions (call graph), imported modules. This provides relational context. (6) Graph RAG: Build a call graph. When a function is retrieved, also retrieve its callees/callers to answer 'how does X work end-to-end'. (7) Query reformulation: Code questions often contain function/class names — extract these with NER and use them to filter the index before embedding search.
evaluation_criteria: Proposes AST-based chunking, not character-based
Includes code-specific metadata
Names a code-specific embedding model
Proposes call graph / relational context
common_mistakes: Using the same chunking strategy as prose
Not including natural language summaries for functions (embedding is poor on raw code for semantic search)
applied.follow_up: How would you handle code that spans multiple files through imports and class inheritance?

applied.question: Compare FAISS, Pinecone, Qdrant, and Weaviate for a production RAG system. How do you choose?
applied.model_answer: FAISS (Facebook AI Similarity Search): Library, not a database. In-memory (or mapped to disk). No built-in persistence, replication, or metadata filtering. Extremely fast for single-machine use cases. Best for: research, prototyping, or when you control the infrastructure and need maximum performance without managed overhead. Not suitable as a standalone production database. Pinecone: Fully managed SaaS vector database. No infrastructure to manage. Supports metadata filtering, namespaces, hybrid search. High write latency (~1-2s for ingestion). Good developer experience. Best for: teams that want zero infra overhead and can accept the cost and data residency constraints of a managed service. Qdrant: Open-source (Rust-based), self-hosted or cloud. Excellent performance, rich filtering, on-disk indexing, quantisation support. Strong Rust client. Best for: teams that need self-hosted for data privacy/compliance, want production-grade features without SaaS cost, and are comfortable with infrastructure. Weaviate: Open-source, self-hosted or cloud. Has built-in modules for vectorisation (can call embedding models directly). GraphQL API. Better for hybrid object + vector storage use cases. More opinionated architecture. Decision framework: Prototype → FAISS. Privacy/compliance required → Qdrant (self-hosted). No infra capacity → Pinecone. Need to store rich objects alongside vectors → Weaviate.
evaluation_criteria: Notes FAISS is a library not a database
Gives concrete strengths and weaknesses for each
Addresses the managed vs self-hosted dimension
Provides a clear decision framework
common_mistakes: Recommending FAISS for production without noting it's not a persistent database
applied.follow_up: How would you handle vector index updates (adds, deletes, updates) in a production system where the knowledge base changes daily?

applied.question: What is query rewriting / HyDE in RAG? When does it help and when does it hurt?
applied.model_answer: Query rewriting: transform the raw user query into a better form before retrieval. Motivations: conversational queries are often under-specified ('tell me more' after context), colloquial, or don't use the vocabulary present in documents. HyDE (Hypothetical Document Embeddings, Gao et al., 2022): instead of embedding the query directly, prompt the LLM to generate a hypothetical document that would answer the query. Embed that hypothetical document and use it as the retrieval query. Intuition: the hypothetical document lives in the same embedding space as real documents and uses the vocabulary and style of an answer, not a question. Works because: query-document embedding distance is often asymmetric — 'What is RLHF?' embeds differently from 'RLHF is a technique that...'. Other approaches: Step-back prompting — abstract the specific query to a more general one before retrieval. Sub-question decomposition — break complex queries into multiple simpler sub-queries and retrieve for each. Multi-query retrieval — generate k rephrased versions of the query, retrieve for all, merge results. When HyDE hurts: (1) Short factual queries where the query embedding is already close to the answer. (2) When the LLM hallucinates the hypothetical document in a misleading direction. (3) Adds latency (one LLM call per query before retrieval).
evaluation_criteria: Explains HyDE's core insight (embedding in answer space, not query space)
Names at least 2 other query rewriting strategies
Identifies when HyDE can hurt (hallucinated hypothetical, simple queries)
common_mistakes: Thinking HyDE always helps — it adds an LLM call and can mislead if the hypothetical is wrong
applied.follow_up: How would you A/B test whether HyDE improves retrieval quality in your specific system?

applied.question: Your RAG system has high retrieval recall but low precision — it retrieves too many irrelevant documents. How do you improve precision?
applied.model_answer: High recall, low precision: the relevant documents are in the top-k, but so are many irrelevant ones, which introduces noise and may confuse the LLM. Strategies: (1) Reranking: Pass the top-k (e.g., 50) candidates + query to a cross-encoder reranker (ms-marco-MiniLM, Cohere Rerank API). Cross-encoders are slower but more accurate because they jointly encode query + document. Keep only top-r (e.g., 5) for the LLM prompt. This is the single highest-impact improvement for precision. (2) Threshold filtering: Discard chunks below a similarity score threshold. Requires calibration — set threshold on a validation set. (3) Metadata filtering: If the query contains intent signals (date, document type, author), filter by metadata before or alongside embedding search. (4) Smaller chunks: More granular chunks improve precision but reduce context. Pair with parent-child retrieval for context. (5) Better embedding model: Switch to a domain-fine-tuned or higher-quality embedding model. (6) MMR (Maximal Marginal Relevance): Select diverse results rather than the top-k by similarity — avoids returning 10 similar chunks all covering the same subtopic.
evaluation_criteria: Proposes cross-encoder reranking as the primary solution
Distinguishes bi-encoder (embedding) from cross-encoder (reranker)
Names MMR for diversity
Mentions metadata filtering as complementary
common_mistakes: Reducing k to improve precision — this reduces recall without fixing the ranking problem
applied.follow_up: What is Cohere Rerank and how does it differ from training your own cross-encoder reranker?

deep_dive.question: Explain the RAGAS framework. What metrics does it define and how are they computed without ground truth labels?
deep_dive.model_answer: RAGAS (Retrieval-Augmented Generation Assessment) evaluates RAG pipelines using LLM-as-judge to avoid the need for expensive ground-truth annotations. Core metrics: (1) Faithfulness: Are all claims in the answer supported by the retrieved context? Process: decompose the answer into individual statements → for each statement, ask the LLM if it is entailed by the context → faithfulness = supported_statements / total_statements. (2) Answer Relevancy: Is the answer relevant to the question (ignoring whether it's factually correct)? Process: given the answer, generate k hypothetical questions that the answer could be responding to → embed all k questions and the original question → answer relevancy = mean cosine similarity between generated questions and original. (3) Context Precision: Are the retrieved chunks ranked such that relevant ones appear first? Computes average precision@k over the retrieved context list, with LLM judging chunk relevance. (4) Context Recall: Do the retrieved chunks cover all information needed to answer the question? Requires a ground truth answer. Process: decompose ground truth into statements → for each statement, check if any retrieved chunk supports it. Additional metrics: Context Entity Recall, Noise Sensitivity. RAGAS provides a pipeline evaluation score by combining these metrics. Limitation: LLM-as-judge introduces its own biases and errors — RAGAS scores correlate with, but are not equivalent to, human judgements.
evaluation_criteria: Correctly describes all four core metrics
Explains the computational process for each (not just what they measure)
Notes which metrics require ground truth and which don't
Acknowledges LLM-as-judge limitations
common_mistakes: Confusing faithfulness and answer relevancy
Not knowing the decompose-then-check approach for faithfulness
deep_dive.follow_up: How would you adapt RAGAS to evaluate a multi-turn conversational RAG system?

deep_dive.question: Explain Graph RAG. How does it extend traditional RAG for multi-hop reasoning and entity relationship queries?
deep_dive.model_answer: Traditional RAG: retrieve relevant chunks by embedding similarity → answer. Fails when the answer requires traversing relationships between entities across multiple documents. Example: 'Which companies did the founders of OpenAI go on to start?' requires identifying founders, then finding what else they founded — multi-hop. Graph RAG (Edge et al., Microsoft, 2024): (1) Knowledge graph construction: Extract entities and relationships from all documents using an LLM. Build a graph where nodes = entities (people, companies, concepts) and edges = relationships (founded, acquired, worked_at). (2) Community detection: Run graph clustering (Leiden algorithm) to identify communities of related entities. Generate a summary for each community. (3) Query routing: For queries about specific entities → retrieve relevant subgraphs. For broad thematic queries → use community summaries. (4) Multi-hop traversal: Start from entities mentioned in the query. Traverse the knowledge graph along relevant edges. Gather entity descriptions, relationship context, and neighbouring entities. Combine retrieved graph context with traditional chunk retrieval. Strengths: Multi-hop reasoning, entity disambiguation, global understanding of a corpus. Weaknesses: Expensive to build (many LLM calls for extraction). Knowledge graph quality depends on extraction quality. Adds latency for graph traversal.
evaluation_criteria: Explains why traditional RAG fails for multi-hop
Describes the knowledge graph construction process
Explains community detection and its role
Compares strengths and weaknesses vs traditional RAG
common_mistakes: Confusing Graph RAG with using a graph database as a vector store — they are different
deep_dive.follow_up: How would you evaluate whether Graph RAG outperforms naive RAG for a specific question type?

deep_dive.question: Derive why reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) is a robust score fusion method. What are its theoretical properties?
deep_dive.model_answer: RRF (Cormack et al., 2009): given rankings from multiple retrieval systems, RRF score for document d across R rankings: RRF(d) = Σ_r 1/(k + rank_r(d)), where k is a constant (typically 60). Documents not ranked by a system receive a score of 0. Why RRF is robust: (1) Rank-based, not score-based: Raw similarity scores from dense retrieval (e.g., cosine similarity) and sparse retrieval (BM25) are not on the same scale and cannot be directly combined. Normalising scores introduces sensitivity to score distribution. RRF uses only rank order, which is scale-invariant. (2) k smoothing: The constant k prevents single top-ranked documents from dominating when they appear at rank 1 in multiple systems. For k=60, the difference between rank 1 and rank 2 is 1/61 - 1/62 ≈ 0.0003 — small. Without k, rank 1 would be 3x more valuable than rank 3. (3) Theoretical property: Assume each ranker is a noisy estimate of the true relevance order. Under mild conditions, RRF converges to the true ranking with more rankers. Empirically: RRF outperforms linear interpolation of scores on most benchmarks. Limitations: cannot model that one ranker should be trusted more than another for specific query types.
evaluation_criteria: States the RRF formula with k
Explains why rank-based fusion avoids score normalisation issues
Derives the effect of k on the fusion weights
Acknowledges the uniform-trust limitation
common_mistakes: Treating k as a critical hyperparameter to tune — empirically, k=60 works well across many tasks
deep_dive.follow_up: How would you modify RRF to give higher weight to the dense retriever for semantic queries and BM25 for keyword queries?

deep_dive.question: What is ColBERT? How does its late interaction architecture improve upon bi-encoder and cross-encoder retrieval?
deep_dive.model_answer: Retrieval approaches spectrum: Bi-encoder: embed query to one vector qₑ, document to one vector dₑ. Score = qₑ·dₑ. Fast (ANN indexable) but lossy — compresses the full document into one vector. Cross-encoder: concatenate query + document, run through BERT, predict relevance score. Accurate but O(n) — must run the model for every query-document pair, can't precompute. ColBERT (Khattab & Zaharia, 2020): Late interaction. Separately encode all query tokens to {q₁,...,qₘ} and document tokens to {d₁,...,dₙ}. Score = Σᵢ max_j (qᵢ·dⱼ) — MaxSim: for each query token, find its best matching document token. Sum over query tokens. Advantages over bi-encoder: token-level interaction captures query-document term alignment better than a single vector. More expressive. Advantages over cross-encoder: document token embeddings {d₁,...,dₙ} can be precomputed and indexed (ColBERT builds a token-level IVFPQ index). At query time: only query tokens are computed fresh. Retrieval in two stages: first filter using compressed representations, then rerank with full MaxSim. Limitation: storage cost is n×d per document (one vector per token) — 100x more than bi-encoders. ColBERTv2 uses residual compression to reduce this 6-10x.
evaluation_criteria: States the MaxSim scoring function correctly
Explains why document embeddings can be precomputed
Compares to bi-encoder and cross-encoder on accuracy vs latency tradeoff
Notes the storage cost limitation
common_mistakes: Confusing ColBERT with a cross-encoder — the key is that document tokens are precomputed independently of the query
deep_dive.follow_up: What is the residual compression approach in ColBERTv2 and how does it reduce the storage overhead?

deep_dive.question: Explain the information retrieval theoretical foundations of RAG. How do the probability of relevance ranking and language modelling retrieval frameworks connect to modern dense retrieval?
deep_dive.model_answer: Classical IR theoretical frameworks: (1) Probability Ranking Principle (Robertson, 1977): documents should be ranked in decreasing order of their probability of relevance to the query: P(R=1|d,q). BM25 approximates this under a binary independence model. (2) Language Modelling approach (Ponte & Croft, 1998): rank documents by the probability of the query being generated by the document's language model: P(q|Mᵈ). The document model Mᵈ is estimated from document term frequencies with Dirichlet or Jelinek-Mercer smoothing. Smoothing is critical — it handles query terms that don't appear in the document by mixing with a collection-wide LM. Connection to dense retrieval: Dual-encoder retrieval (DPR, E5) computes: score(q,d) = fθ(q)ᵀ·gφ(d). This is a learned dot product — the encoder maps both the query and document into a shared embedding space where relevant pairs have high inner product. Formal connection: if we treat the encoder as computing a low-rank approximation of the relevance probability P(R=1|q,d) via log-bilinear factorisation, dense retrieval is a neural approximation of the Probability Ranking Principle. The contrastive training loss (InfoNCE) is equivalent to maximum likelihood estimation of P(d⁺|q) under a softmax over all documents in the batch. ANCE (Approximate Nearest Neighbour Negative Contrastive Estimation): offline hard negative mining by periodically refreshing the negative index — mines negatives that are near-misses in embedding space, training the model on its current hardest failures. This is an EM-like algorithm: E-step = mine hard negatives, M-step = update the encoder on those negatives.
evaluation_criteria: States the Probability Ranking Principle correctly
Explains the language modelling retrieval framework and the role of smoothing
Connects dual-encoder scoring to a log-bilinear P(R=1|q,d) factorisation
Explains ANCE's hard negative mining as an EM procedure
common_mistakes: Treating dense retrieval as purely empirical without connecting it to classical IR theory
Not knowing that Dirichlet smoothing in language model retrieval is the theoretical motivation for BM25's document length normalisation
deep_dive.follow_up: How does the theoretical connection between contrastive learning and mutual information maximisation (InfoNCE) explain why in-batch negatives are less effective than hard negatives?

conceptual.question: What is an AI agent? How does it differ from a standard LLM call?
conceptual.model_answer: A standard LLM call: single inference, stateless, produces one output given an input. An AI agent: an LLM in a loop that can take actions, observe results, and decide subsequent actions. Key properties: (1) Tool use: the agent can call external tools (search, code execution, APIs, databases). (2) Planning: multi-step reasoning about how to achieve a goal. (3) Memory: short-term (context window, conversation history) and long-term (external memory stores). (4) Decision-making: deciding when to use tools vs answer directly, choosing which tool, evaluating whether the goal is achieved. Agent loop: perceive (input + observations) → reason (LLM decides next action) → act (execute tool) → observe (get result) → repeat until goal met or stopping condition. Key distinction from simple tool-calling: an agent has agency over the sequence of actions — it decides what to do next based on observations, not a fixed pipeline.
evaluation_criteria: Distinguishes stateless LLM call from iterative agent loop
Names the key agent properties (tool use, planning, memory)

conceptual.question: What is LangGraph? How does it differ from LangChain's AgentExecutor and what problems does it solve?
conceptual.model_answer: LangChain's AgentExecutor: a relatively rigid loop that runs an agent by repeatedly calling the LLM with the tool results appended. Limited control over the flow — hard to implement branching, conditional paths, or different behaviour for different states. LangGraph: a framework for building LLM workflows as directed graphs (or directed acyclic/cyclic graphs). Core concepts: (1) State: a typed dictionary passed between nodes. Each node reads from and writes to the state. (2) Nodes: Python functions or LLM calls that transform the state. (3) Edges: directed connections between nodes. Conditional edges: route to different nodes based on state. (4) Persistence: built-in checkpointing of state to storage (Redis, Postgres) enabling resumability, human-in-the-loop, and long-running workflows. Problems solved: (1) Explicit control flow — you define exactly what happens and when, vs the LLM deciding everything. (2) Cycles — LangGraph natively supports cycles (agent loops), which DAG-based frameworks can't express. (3) Multi-agent: orchestrate multiple specialised agents as nodes in a graph. (4) Human-in-the-loop: pause execution at any node, wait for human input, resume. (5) Streaming: native SSE streaming of intermediate states.
evaluation_criteria: Contrasts AgentExecutor's rigidity with LangGraph's explicit control
Names the core abstractions: State, Nodes, Edges
Identifies checkpointing/persistence as a key differentiator
Mentions human-in-the-loop and multi-agent use cases
common_mistakes: Treating LangGraph as just a wrapper around LangChain — it's a lower-level graph execution engine
conceptual.follow_up: How does LangGraph handle cycles in the graph, and what prevents infinite loops?

conceptual.question: What is the ReAct pattern? How does it structure an agent's reasoning and action?
conceptual.model_answer: ReAct (Yao et al., 2022): Synergises Reasoning and Acting. The agent interleaves reasoning traces and actions in a structured format: Thought: [reasoning about what to do next] Action: [tool_name(args)] Observation: [tool result] Thought: [reasoning about the observation] Action: [next tool call or final answer] ...Final Answer: [response to user]. The interleaved structure forces the LLM to reason about each observation before taking the next action, rather than executing a fixed plan. Advantages over pure reasoning (CoT): can acquire external information via tools. Advantages over pure acting: each action is preceded by a reasoning step, making the chain debuggable and correctable. Advantages over Plan-then-Execute: replanning happens dynamically after each observation — if a tool returns unexpected results, the agent can adapt. Implementation in LangGraph: Thought is the LLM's internal output, Action is a function call / tool selection, Observation is the tool result appended to state.
evaluation_criteria: Shows the Thought-Action-Observation format explicitly
Explains why interleaved reasoning is better than pure planning
Distinguishes ReAct from Plan-and-Execute
Connects to LangGraph implementation
common_mistakes: Confusing ReAct with chain-of-thought — CoT doesn't have the action/observation loop
conceptual.follow_up: What are the failure modes of the ReAct pattern, and how does reflection (like Reflexion) address them?

conceptual.question: What is multi-agent architecture? When would you use a single agent vs multiple specialised agents?
conceptual.model_answer: Multi-agent: multiple AI agents, each with specific tools, instructions, or expertise, coordinated to solve complex tasks. Patterns: (1) Orchestrator + workers: a central LLM decides which specialised worker agent to call and synthesises results. (2) Supervisor: similar to orchestrator but with feedback loops — the supervisor evaluates worker output and can retry or route to different workers. (3) Peer-to-peer: agents communicate directly with each other, each solving sub-tasks. (4) Hierarchical: nested orchestrators, each managing a team of agents for sub-domains. Single agent: appropriate when the task fits in one context window, requires a small set of tools, and doesn't benefit from specialisation. Multi-agent: appropriate when: (1) Task exceeds context window limits — different agents handle different parts without needing the full context. (2) Parallelism — multiple agents can work simultaneously on independent sub-tasks. (3) Specialisation — a code agent, a research agent, and a writing agent each have tailored prompts, tools, and permissions. (4) Fault isolation — failure of one worker doesn't crash the whole pipeline. Tradeoffs: more complex to build and debug, higher latency from coordination overhead.
evaluation_criteria: Names multiple multi-agent patterns
Gives concrete criteria for single vs multi-agent choice
Mentions context window as a multi-agent motivator
Addresses coordination overhead
common_mistakes: Recommending multi-agent for all complex tasks — single agents with good tool use often suffice
conceptual.follow_up: How do you handle shared state and memory between agents in a multi-agent LangGraph workflow?

conceptual.question: What is an agent's memory architecture? Compare short-term, long-term, and semantic memory in practice.
conceptual.model_answer: Agent memory types: (1) Short-term / working memory: the context window — the running conversation, tool call history, and observations. Limited to the model's context length. Cleared between sessions unless persisted. (2) Long-term episodic memory: records of past interactions, actions, and outcomes. Stored externally (database). Retrieved by summarisation or vector search when relevant past episodes are needed. (3) Semantic/knowledge memory: factual knowledge about the world or domain. RAG over a knowledge base, or parametric memory baked into the LLM's weights. (4) Procedural memory: the agent's skills — embedded in the system prompt, tool definitions, and code. Retrieval from long-term memory: embedding past interactions → store in vector DB → retrieve semantically similar past experiences at the start of a new session. Memory compression: conversation history grows unbounded. Strategies: (1) Summarise and compress: periodically summarise earlier turns, discard raw history. (2) Sliding window: keep only the last k turns. (3) Importance-weighted: LLM identifies the most important facts to retain. In LangGraph: state is the short-term memory. External Redis/Postgres checkpointing enables persistence across sessions.
evaluation_criteria: Distinguishes all four memory types clearly
Explains how long-term memory is retrieved (vector search)
Addresses memory compression for unbounded conversations
Connects to LangGraph's checkpointing
common_mistakes: Treating the context window as unlimited — it's the central constraint in agent memory design
conceptual.follow_up: How would you implement a 'forget' mechanism for an agent that must comply with GDPR data deletion requests?

applied.question: Design a research agent that can answer questions by searching the web, reading papers, and synthesising information. Specify the LangGraph graph structure.
applied.model_answer: Graph structure: Nodes: (1) parse_query: Extract keywords, identify query type (fact lookup vs synthesis vs comparison). (2) plan: LLM generates a research plan — list of sub-questions to answer. (3) search: Web search (Tavily) for each sub-question. Returns URLs + snippets. (4) fetch_content: Fetch full page content for top-k URLs. (5) extract_relevant: LLM extracts relevant passages from fetched content, annotated with source URL. (6) synthesise: LLM synthesises all extracted passages into a coherent answer with citations. (7) evaluate_quality: LLM self-evaluates: 'Does this answer fully address the original question?' If not, routes back to plan with gaps identified. (8) format_output: Structure the final response with citation links. State: {query, plan, search_results, fetched_content, extracted_passages, draft_answer, evaluation, final_answer, iteration_count}. Edges: parse → plan → search → fetch → extract → synthesise → evaluate. Conditional edge from evaluate: if quality passes → format_output; if fails and iteration < 3 → plan (with gap context). Termination: max iterations = 3, or quality check passes. Tools: Tavily search, web fetch, optional: academic paper search (Semantic Scholar API).
evaluation_criteria: Specifies all major nodes with clear responsibilities
Defines the state schema
Includes a conditional self-evaluation loop
Adds iteration limit to prevent infinite loops
common_mistakes: Not including a quality evaluation / stopping condition
Forgetting to track sources for citations
applied.follow_up: How would you add a human-in-the-loop checkpoint before the agent starts fetching content from the web?

applied.question: How do you handle errors and retries in a LangGraph agent workflow? What patterns prevent cascading failures?
applied.model_answer: Error categories in LangGraph agents: (1) Tool errors: API rate limits, network timeouts, tool returning unexpected format. (2) LLM errors: model refuses to call a tool, generates malformed JSON, exceeds context length. (3) Logic errors: agent gets into an infinite loop, contradicts itself. Patterns: (1) Node-level try/catch: Each tool node wraps execution in try/catch. On failure, write an error message to state (rather than raising). The next reasoning node sees the error and decides how to proceed. (2) Retry with backoff: For transient errors (rate limits), retry with exponential backoff (max 3 retries). Use tenacity or a custom retry wrapper around tool calls. (3) Fallback tools: If primary search fails, fall back to a secondary search API. Model this as a conditional edge: primary_search → check_result; if error → fallback_search. (4) Circuit breaker: Track error count per tool in state. If a tool fails 3 times, mark it as unavailable and route around it. (5) Max iterations: Always set a hard limit on agent cycles. In LangGraph: `while_condition` or a recursion limit. (6) Checkpoint on success: After each successful major step, checkpoint the state. On resume after failure, start from the last checkpoint, not from scratch. (7) Graceful degradation: If the full research pipeline fails, return the best partial answer gathered so far rather than an empty error.
evaluation_criteria: Categorises different error types
Proposes retry with backoff for transient errors
Mentions circuit breaker or fallback patterns
Addresses checkpointing for resumability
common_mistakes: Letting unhandled exceptions propagate and crash the whole workflow
Not setting iteration limits
applied.follow_up: How would you implement observability for a LangGraph agent in production — what events would you log and what metrics would you track?

applied.question: Design a code review agent that takes a GitHub PR diff and produces a structured review with severity-labelled comments.
applied.model_answer: Inputs: PR diff, repository context (language, framework), optional PR description. Graph structure: (1) parse_diff: Parse the unified diff into per-file, per-hunk changes. Identify file types, added/removed lines. (2) classify_changes: Categorise changes: new feature, bug fix, refactor, dependency update. Route to appropriate specialist reviewers. (3) parallel_review: Fan out to specialised review nodes in parallel: security_reviewer: checks for SQL injection, XSS, hardcoded secrets, insecure dependencies. logic_reviewer: checks for off-by-one errors, null pointer risks, incorrect conditionals. style_reviewer: checks for code style, naming conventions, dead code. performance_reviewer: flags O(n²) loops, N+1 queries, unnecessary allocations. (4) merge_comments: Aggregate all review comments, deduplicate overlapping comments. (5) triage_severity: LLM assigns severity: CRITICAL (security/data loss risk), MAJOR (likely bugs), MINOR (style/performance), NITPICK. (6) format_output: Structure as GitHub-compatible review JSON with inline comments and file positions. State: {diff, parsed_hunks, change_type, review_comments_per_reviewer, merged_comments, final_review}. Tools: GitHub API for PR context, code execution sandbox for running tests on changed code, static analysis tool wrappers (bandit, semgrep).
evaluation_criteria: Proposes parallel specialised reviewers
Includes severity classification
Includes security as a distinct reviewer
Connects to GitHub API for output format
common_mistakes: Sending the full diff to a single LLM call without specialisation — misses nuanced review quality
applied.follow_up: How would you evaluate the quality of this agent's reviews compared to human code reviews?

applied.question: What is human-in-the-loop (HITL) in LangGraph? Design a content moderation workflow that requires human approval for borderline cases.
applied.model_answer: HITL: pausing agent execution at a specific node to await human input before proceeding. LangGraph supports this via interrupt_before and interrupt_after directives on nodes, combined with persistent state checkpointing. When the graph hits an interrupt, execution pauses and the thread_id is stored. A human reviewer can query the current state, provide input, and resume. Design: Content moderation workflow: Nodes: (1) classify_content: LLM classifies submitted content with confidence: {category: SAFE|BORDERLINE|UNSAFE, confidence: float, reason: str}. (2) route: Conditional edge based on classification: SAFE (confidence > 0.9) → approve_automatically. UNSAFE (confidence > 0.9) → reject_automatically. BORDERLINE or any (confidence < 0.9) → human_review_queue. (3) human_review_queue: Interrupt here. Write to a review queue table with the content, LLM's classification and reasoning, and a suggested decision. Human reviewer sees the queue, makes a decision (approve/reject/escalate), and resumes the thread via the LangGraph API. (4) apply_decision: Execute the human's decision (approve/reject/flag) and optionally feed the decision back as a training signal. State: {content_id, content, llm_decision, human_decision, reviewer_id, timestamp}. The checkpointing ensures the workflow can pause for hours and resume correctly.
evaluation_criteria: Describes the interrupt mechanism in LangGraph
Designs the confidence-based routing correctly
Includes training signal feedback
Handles the queue persistence aspect
common_mistakes: Thinking HITL requires a completely different architecture — LangGraph's interrupt is specifically designed for this
applied.follow_up: How would you prevent reviewer fatigue if the BORDERLINE queue consistently receives 10,000 items per day?

applied.question: How do you evaluate an AI agent's performance? What metrics and evaluation approaches are specific to agents vs standard LLM evaluation?
applied.model_answer: Agent evaluation differs from standard LLM eval in that we're evaluating a multi-step process, not a single output. Dimensions: (1) Task completion rate: Does the agent successfully complete the given task? Binary or partial credit. Gold standard: human evaluation of final output. Automated: check final state against expected state (for deterministic tasks). (2) Efficiency: Steps to completion: fewer tool calls = more efficient. Token usage: total tokens consumed across all LLM calls in the trajectory. Time to completion. (3) Tool use accuracy: Did the agent call the right tools? With the right arguments? Tool call precision/recall vs a reference trajectory. (4) Trajectory quality: Even if the final answer is correct, was the trajectory coherent? Did the agent take unnecessary detours? Evaluate using LLM-as-judge on the full trajectory. (5) Robustness: Performance on adversarial inputs, ambiguous queries, tool failures. (6) Agent-specific benchmarks: GAIA (general assistant benchmark), SWE-bench (code repair agents), WebArena (web navigation). Evaluation methodology: (1) Fixed-environment evaluation: deterministic environments where the same trajectory can be replayed. (2) Trajectory replay: save agent trajectories during eval, replay and compare. (3) LLM judge on trajectory: provide the full Thought-Action-Observation sequence to a judge LLM and ask for a quality rating.
