Prepend a learnable [CLS] token. Add learned positional embeddings. Feed through a standard Transformer encoder. Use [CLS] representation for classification. Key differences from CNNs: (1) Global attention from layer 1: every patch attends to every other patch in every layer. CNNs build up receptive field gradually through depth. (2) No inductive biases: CNNs have built-in translation equivariance and locality. ViT has neither — it must learn spatial relationships from data. Consequence: ViT requires much more data to train from scratch (JFT-300M vs ImageNet). (3) Scales better with data and model size: at large scale, ViT matches or exceeds CNN accuracy. ViT-G (2B params) is the strongest single image classifier. Tradeoffs: CNNs are more sample-efficient on small datasets, have better spatial inductive biases. ViT achieves better accuracy at large scale and has a uniform architecture (no special pooling layers). Modern landscape: Swin Transformer introduces hierarchical structure and local window attention — combining CNN inductive biases with transformer flexibility, outperforming both on many benchmarks.
evaluation_criteria: Describes the patch embedding process correctly (patch → flatten → project → positional embed)
Explains the missing inductive biases and why that requires more data
Compares CNN vs ViT sample efficiency and scale behaviour
Mentions Swin Transformer as a hybrid
common_mistakes: Saying ViT 'always beats CNNs' — it only does so convincingly at large scale
conceptual.follow_up: How does the Swin Transformer's shifted window attention address the quadratic complexity of standard ViT attention for high-resolution images?

applied.question: You need to deploy a real-time pothole detection system on a dashcam running on a Raspberry Pi 4. Design the full pipeline.
applied.model_answer: Constraints: Raspberry Pi 4 (ARM Cortex-A72, ~13 GFLOPS, no discrete GPU, 4GB RAM), real-time (~15+ fps). (1) Model architecture: MobileNetV3 + SSDLite or NanoDet — designed for mobile inference. Avoid ResNet/YOLO-v8 which are too heavy. Target model size < 5MB, < 200M FLOPs per inference. (2) Quantisation: INT8 post-training quantisation using TFLite converter. Typical 2-4x speedup on ARM with XNNPACK backend. Validate accuracy drop < 2% mAP. (3) Input resolution: 320×320 or 416×416 — balance between accuracy and speed. Larger resolution = better small object detection but slower inference. (4) Inference framework: TFLite with XNNPACK delegate for optimised ARM NEON SIMD instructions, or ONNX Runtime with ARM compute library. (5) Data pipeline: capture frames from camera at 30fps. Skip frames (process every 2nd frame) to stay within compute budget. Ring buffer to avoid I/O bottleneck. (6) Pre/post processing: image normalisation and NMS must also be fast. Implement NMS in C or use hardware-accelerated version. (7) Training data: collect dashcam footage, annotate potholes with bounding boxes. Augment heavily (rain, night, glare) since dashcam lighting is variable. Transfer from COCO-pretrained backbone. (8) Deployment testing: benchmark on actual Raspberry Pi — p99 latency, temperature throttling under sustained load.
evaluation_criteria: Chooses a mobile-appropriate architecture (MobileNet/NanoDet), not a heavy model
Proposes INT8 quantisation with latency and accuracy validation
Addresses frame skipping and ring buffer for real-time pipeline
Mentions temperature throttling as a deployment reality
common_mistakes: Proposing YOLOv8 or ResNet-50 without addressing that they are too heavy for Raspberry Pi
Forgetting that NMS post-processing also consumes significant CPU time
applied.follow_up: How would you build the training dataset for pothole detection when publicly labelled pothole datasets are small and geographically biased?

applied.question: Your image classifier achieves 94% accuracy on the test set but performs poorly on images from a new hospital's cameras. Diagnose and fix.
applied.model_answer: This is a distribution shift / domain gap problem. Diagnosis: (1) Visual inspection: compare sample images from training distribution vs new hospital cameras. Look for differences in: lighting conditions, camera angle, image resolution, colour calibration, contrast. (2) Embedding analysis: run both distributions through the model backbone, project embeddings to 2D via UMAP. If the two distributions form separate clusters, the features are domain-mismatched. (3) Feature distribution statistics: compute mean and variance of activations at each layer for both distributions. Large divergence in late layers indicates high-level semantic mismatch; early layer divergence indicates low-level visual mismatch. Root causes: Different camera manufacturer → different colour space, sharpening, compression. Different lighting setup → different contrast and shadow patterns. Patient demographics differ → different pathology appearance distribution. Fixes: (1) Domain adaptation: collect unlabelled images from the new hospital. Fine-tune the model on these unlabelled images using self-supervised or adversarial domain adaptation (DANN — Domain-Adversarial Neural Networks). (2) Labelled fine-tuning: collect 200-500 labelled examples from the new hospital. Fine-tune the last 2-3 layers with a low learning rate. (3) Test-time augmentation (TTA): during inference, augment the image multiple ways (brightness, contrast, flips) and average predictions — reduces sensitivity to lighting variation. (4) Stain normalisation equivalent: for medical images specifically, apply histogram equalisation or colour normalisation to map new hospital images to the training distribution.
evaluation_criteria: Identifies distribution shift as the root cause, not model quality
Proposes embedding-space diagnosis (UMAP clustering)
Names DANN or another domain adaptation technique
Includes the low-data fine-tuning option with specific quantities
common_mistakes: Suggesting retraining from scratch — domain adaptation requires far less data and preserves learned representations
applied.follow_up: What is the DANN (Domain-Adversarial Neural Network) architecture and how does the gradient reversal layer work?

applied.question: Design a video understanding pipeline that classifies sports actions (50 classes) in 10-second clips at 30fps.
applied.model_answer: Input: 10s × 30fps = 300 frames per clip. Processing all 300 frames with a CNN+Transformer is expensive. Architecture options: (1) Two-stream network: spatial stream processes individual frames (appearance), temporal stream processes optical flow stacks (motion). Combine predictions. Good accuracy, complex pipeline (need optical flow computation). (2) 3D CNN (I3D, SlowFast): inflated 3D convolutions capture spatiotemporal patterns. SlowFast: slow pathway (low frame rate, high resolution, captures appearance) + fast pathway (high frame rate, low resolution, captures motion). Strong baseline. (3) Video Transformer (TimeSformer, Video Swin): apply attention across both space and time. Divided space-time attention is more efficient than full spatiotemporal attention. Production recommendation: (1) Frame sampling: sample 8-16 frames uniformly from the 300 — temporal context is captured without processing all frames. (2) Model: SlowFast-R50 or Video Swin-T pretrained on Kinetics-400. Fine-tune on sports action dataset. (3) Temporal aggregation: average pool clip-level predictions across multiple overlapping clips for final decision. (4) Data: Kinetics-400 pretraining covers most sports actions — fine-tuning with 500-2000 labelled clips per class is sufficient. (5) Inference: batch clips, use TensorRT for GPU serving. Latency: 10s clip → 50-100ms inference on GPU.
evaluation_criteria: Addresses the frame sampling problem (not all 300 frames)
Describes SlowFast or a comparable architecture
Proposes pretraining on Kinetics-400
Addresses multi-clip aggregation for robust prediction
common_mistakes: Processing all 300 frames without sampling — computationally infeasible
Treating video classification as a sequence of independent image classifications
applied.follow_up: How does optical flow capture motion information, and why have modern architectures largely replaced it with learned temporal representations?

applied.question: Compare SIFT, ORB, and deep feature matching for a visual place recognition system (robot localisation). Which do you choose for production?
applied.model_answer: Task: given a query image from a robot camera, identify which previously mapped location it corresponds to. SIFT (Scale-Invariant Feature Transform): detects keypoints at multiple scales, computes 128-dim gradient histograms as descriptors. Rotation and scale invariant. Very accurate matches. Slow (~0.5s per image), not patented anymore but still CPU-heavy. Matching: approximate nearest neighbour in 128D space (FLANN). ORB (Oriented FAST + Rotated BRIEF): binary descriptor (256 bits). Uses Hamming distance matching — extremely fast via bitwise XOR. ~10x faster than SIFT. Slightly less accurate. Good for real-time embedded robotics. Deep feature matching (NetVLAD, SuperPoint + SuperGlue): SuperPoint detects keypoints and computes learned 256D descriptors. SuperGlue matches them using a graph neural network that reasons about spatial consistency. Far more robust to lighting change, viewpoint change, weather. SuperGlue matching: ~20ms on GPU. Highest accuracy by large margin on challenging conditions. Production recommendation: For a robot indoors with stable lighting and compute budget: ORB + a bag-of-words place recognition index (DBoW2). For outdoor or challenging conditions: SuperPoint + SuperGlue with a GPU onboard. For pure place recognition (not keypoint matching): NetVLAD global descriptors — single 4096D vector per image, indexed with FAISS for fast retrieval.
evaluation_criteria: Correctly characterises the speed/accuracy tradeoff of each
Explains ORB's binary descriptor and Hamming distance
Names SuperPoint/SuperGlue and quantifies their advantage
Gives a concrete conditional recommendation
common_mistakes: Recommending SIFT for real-time robotics without addressing its computational cost
applied.follow_up: How does NetVLAD's differentiable VLAD encoding enable end-to-end learning of place recognition features?

applied.question: Design a data collection and annotation pipeline to train a custom object detector for warehouse inventory management (300 SKU classes, partially occluded items on shelves).
applied.model_answer: Challenges: 300 classes (long tail — some SKUs are rare), occlusion on shelves, similar-looking products, varying lighting. Data collection: (1) Camera setup: mount fixed cameras at consistent angles. Capture from multiple shelf heights. Use consistent lighting (LED panels) to reduce variability. (2) Data volume target: 500-1000 images per SKU for common items, 100-200 for rare. Total: ~100k-200k images. Use a turntable setup for isolated product photography for synthetic augmentation. (3) Active learning: start with 10k labelled images, train a baseline model. Use model uncertainty (entropy of predictions) to select the most informative unlabelled images for annotation next. This reduces total annotation cost by ~50%. Annotation pipeline: (1) Bounding box annotation via Label Studio or Scale AI. Semi-automated: model pre-annotates, humans correct. Much faster than manual from scratch. (2) Quality control: 10% random sample re-annotated by a second annotator. Measure inter-annotator IoU > 0.85. Reject images below threshold. (3) Handling occlusion: annotate the visible portion of the bounding box, add an 'occluded' flag. Training: fine-tune YOLO-v8 on the annotated dataset. Use mosaic augmentation (4 images tiled) to expose the model to many classes per batch. Class-balanced sampling — oversample rare SKUs. Evaluation: per-class AP, confusion matrix between visually similar SKUs.
evaluation_criteria: Proposes active learning to reduce annotation cost
Includes inter-annotator agreement as a quality gate
Addresses the long-tail class imbalance with class-balanced sampling
Mentions semi-automated annotation with model pre-annotation
common_mistakes: Collecting data without accounting for the distribution shift between lab photography and in-shelf conditions
applied.follow_up: How would you use synthetic data generation (rendering from 3D models) to supplement real-world training data for rare SKUs?

deep_dive.question: Derive the backpropagation equations through a convolutional layer. What are the gradients with respect to the input, weights, and bias?
deep_dive.model_answer: Forward pass (single filter, valid convolution): output[i,j] = Σₖ Σₗ input[i+k, j+l] · weight[k,l] + bias. Given upstream gradient ∂L/∂output[i,j]. Gradient w.r.t. weight: ∂L/∂weight[k,l] = Σᵢ Σⱼ ∂L/∂output[i,j] · input[i+k, j+l]. This is a convolution of the input with the upstream gradient. Gradient w.r.t. bias: ∂L/∂bias = Σᵢ Σⱼ ∂L/∂output[i,j] — sum of all upstream gradients. Gradient w.r.t. input: ∂L/∂input[p,q] = Σₖ Σₗ ∂L/∂output[p-k, q-l] · weight[k,l]. This is a full convolution of the upstream gradient with the 180°-rotated filter — a transposed convolution. Key insight: the backward pass through a conv layer is itself a conv operation. This is why transposed convolutions (sometimes called deconvolutions) are used in decoder networks — they implement the transpose of the forward conv operation. For the multi-channel case: gradients accumulate across input channels for weight gradients, and across output channels for input gradients, via the same summation structure.
evaluation_criteria: Derives all three gradients (input, weight, bias) correctly
Identifies that ∂L/∂input is a transposed convolution with the rotated filter
Explains why the backward pass is also a convolution
Connects to transposed convolutions in decoder architectures
common_mistakes: Getting the indexing wrong in the input gradient (p-k, q-l not p+k, q+l)
Forgetting that the filter is flipped 180° in the backward pass

deep_dive.question: Explain Non-Maximum Suppression (NMS) and its variants. What are the failure modes and how do Soft-NMS and DETR address them?
deep_dive.model_answer: Standard NMS: given a set of bounding boxes with confidence scores, iteratively select the highest-scoring box, suppress all boxes with IoU > threshold (typically 0.5) with the selected box. Repeat until no boxes remain. O(n²) in the number of boxes. Failure modes: (1) Crowded scenes: two overlapping instances of the same class — NMS suppresses the lower-scoring box even though it's a valid detection. E.g., two people standing close together. (2) Threshold sensitivity: IoU threshold of 0.5 misses soft overlaps; 0.3 suppresses too aggressively. No threshold works for all scenes. (3) Class-agnostic vs class-specific: standard NMS is per-class but some architectures do it globally. Soft-NMS (Bodla et al., 2017): instead of hard suppression, decay the confidence score of nearby boxes by a function of their IoU with the selected box: score = score × (1 - IoU) (linear) or score × exp(-IoU²/σ) (Gaussian). Boxes with high overlap get lower scores but are not removed. Better recall in crowded scenes. DETR (Carion et al., 2020): eliminates NMS entirely. Uses a Transformer decoder with learned object queries that directly output a fixed set of N predictions. Bipartite matching loss (Hungarian algorithm) assigns each ground truth object to exactly one query during training, forcing predictions to be unique. The model learns non-duplicate prediction as part of training rather than via post-processing.
evaluation_criteria: States the NMS algorithm correctly including the IoU threshold step
Identifies crowded scene failure mode specifically
Explains Soft-NMS's score decay mechanism
Explains DETR's bipartite matching as an NMS-free alternative
common_mistakes: Saying DETR is simply 'faster' than NMS — it eliminates a post-processing step but training is more complex
deep_dive.follow_up: Derive the Hungarian algorithm's time complexity and explain why it's tractable for small N (e.g., N=100 queries in DETR).

deep_dive.question: Explain the U-Net architecture in detail. Why is it effective for medical image segmentation and what role do skip connections play?
deep_dive.model_answer: U-Net (Ronneberger et al., 2015): encoder-decoder architecture shaped like a U. Encoder (contracting path): series of 3×3 conv → ReLU → 3×3 conv → ReLU → 2×2 max pool blocks. Each pool halves spatial resolution, doubles channels. Captures context — what is where. Decoder (expanding path): series of 2×2 transposed conv (upsampling) → concatenate with skip connection from corresponding encoder level → 3×3 conv → ReLU → 3×3 conv → ReLU. Restores spatial resolution. Final 1×1 conv produces per-pixel class scores. Skip connections: concatenate the encoder's feature map at resolution r with the decoder's feature map at the same resolution r. Why critical: the encoder downsamples aggressively — by the bottleneck, fine spatial details (exact cell boundaries, thin structures) are lost. Skip connections route these high-resolution spatial details directly to the decoder, bypassing the lossy bottleneck. The decoder uses both: low-resolution deep features (what, high semantic content) + high-resolution shallow features (where, precise spatial location). Why effective for medical imaging: (1) Trained on very few images (the original paper used ~30 images) via heavy augmentation (elastic deformations, rotation). (2) Overlap-tile strategy: allows prediction of arbitrarily large images by tiling with overlap. (3) Weighted loss: border pixels between touching cells are up-weighted to improve cell boundary separation — crucial for instance-like segmentation without instance heads.
evaluation_criteria: Describes encoder downsampling + decoder upsampling structure
Explains why skip connections recover spatial detail lost at the bottleneck
Notes U-Net's exceptional data efficiency
Mentions the border-weighted loss for touching objects
common_mistakes: Confusing skip connections (concatenation) with residual connections (addition)
deep_dive.follow_up: How has U-Net been adapted for 3D volumetric medical imaging (CT/MRI), and what are the computational challenges?

deep_dive.question: What is optical flow? Explain the Lucas-Kanade and Horn-Schunck formulations, and contrast them with learned optical flow (RAFT).
deep_dive.model_answer: Optical flow: for each pixel (x,y) in frame t, find its displacement vector (u,v) to frame t+1. The brightness constancy assumption: I(x,y,t) = I(x+u, y+v, t+1). Linearising via Taylor expansion: Iₓu + Iᵧv + Iₜ = 0 (optical flow constraint equation). One equation, two unknowns — underconstrained. Lucas-Kanade (local method): assume flow is constant within a small neighbourhood window W. Stack the constraint equation for all pixels in W: [Iₓ Iᵧ]ᵀ · [u v] = -Iₜ for each pixel in W. Solve via least squares: [u v]ᵀ = (AᵀA)⁻¹Aᵀb where A is the matrix of spatial gradients. AᵀA must be invertible — fails at flat regions (aperture problem). Best at corners/edges (high-gradient regions). Horn-Schunck (global method): adds a global smoothness constraint: minimise ∫∫[(Iₓu+Iᵧv+Iₜ)² + α²(|∇u|² + |∇v|²)]dxdy. Produces dense, smooth flow fields. Slower, more sensitive to discontinuities at object boundaries. RAFT (Recurrent All-Pairs Field Transforms, Teed & Deng, 2020): learns optical flow end-to-end. (1) Feature encoder extracts features for both frames. (2) Correlation volume: compute all pairwise dot products between feature vectors — 4D tensor encoding frame-to-frame similarity at all offsets. (3) Recurrent update operator: iteratively refines the flow field using the correlation volume, current flow estimate, and context features. State-of-the-art. Handles large motions, occlusions, and lighting changes that break brightness constancy.
evaluation_criteria: States the brightness constancy assumption and its Taylor linearisation
Explains why Lucas-Kanade is underconstrained and how the window solves it
Contrasts local (LK) vs global (HS) regularisation approaches
Describes RAFT's correlation volume and iterative refinement
common_mistakes: Saying optical flow 'tracks pixels' — it estimates per-pixel motion fields, not identities
deep_dive.follow_up: How does the aperture problem arise in optical flow estimation, and which types of image regions are most affected?

conceptual.question: Define the core components of a Reinforcement Learning problem. What distinguishes RL from supervised learning?
conceptual.model_answer: RL components: Agent: the learner/decision maker. Environment: everything the agent interacts with. State s ∈ S: a representation of the environment at a given time. Action a ∈ A: what the agent can do. Reward r = R(s,a,s'): scalar feedback signal from the environment. Policy π(a|s): the agent's decision function — maps states to action probabilities. Value function V^π(s) = E[Σₜ γᵗrₜ | s₀=s, π]: expected discounted cumulative reward from state s following policy π. Discount factor γ ∈ [0,1]: balances immediate vs future rewards. Model (optional): P(s'|s,a) — the transition dynamics. Key distinctions from supervised learning: (1) No labels: the agent receives reward signals, not correct action labels. It must discover which actions lead to rewards via trial and error. (2) Sequential decisions: actions affect future states and therefore future rewards — temporal credit assignment is required. (3) Exploration vs exploitation: the agent must balance exploiting known good actions and exploring new ones to discover potentially better actions. (4) Non-iid data: training data (trajectories) are generated by the agent's own policy — data distribution changes as the policy improves, causing non-stationarity.
evaluation_criteria: Defines all core components (S, A, R, π, V, γ)
Explains reward vs label distinction
Identifies temporal credit assignment
Mentions exploration vs exploitation and non-iid data
common_mistakes: Treating RL as just 'learning from reward' without explaining why sequential decision-making makes it fundamentally different from classification
conceptual.follow_up: What is the difference between model-based and model-free RL? When would you choose each?

conceptual.question: Explain the Bellman equation. How does it form the basis for value-based RL algorithms?
conceptual.model_answer: The Bellman equation expresses the value of a state as a function of the immediate reward and the value of the next state. For the value function under policy π: V^π(s) = Σₐ π(a|s) Σₛ' P(s'|s,a) [R(s,a,s') + γ·V^π(s')]. This is a recursive consistency condition — the value of s equals the expected immediate reward plus the discounted value of the successor state. Bellman optimality equation: V*(s) = max_a Σₛ' P(s'|s,a) [R(s,a,s') + γ·V*(s')]. The unique fixed point of this operator is the optimal value function. Algorithms built on this: (1) Dynamic Programming (Policy Iteration, Value Iteration): if the model P is known, iterate the Bellman operator until convergence. (2) Q-Learning (model-free): approximate Q*(s,a) = R + γ·max_{a'} Q*(s',a') via temporal difference learning. Update: Q(s,a) ← Q(s,a) + α[r + γ·max_{a'} Q(s',a') - Q(s,a)]. The TD error (bracketed term) is the Bellman residual — the deviation from the Bellman consistency condition. DQN: approximate Q with a neural network, use a replay buffer and target network to stabilise training.
evaluation_criteria: States the Bellman equation for V^π correctly
States the optimality equation and identifies it as a fixed point
Connects to Q-learning via the TD error
Mentions DQN as the deep RL extension
common_mistakes: Confusing V(s) and Q(s,a) — V is state value, Q is state-action value
conceptual.follow_up: Why does Q-learning converge to the optimal policy even when following a non-optimal (epsilon-greedy) behaviour policy?

conceptual.question: What is the policy gradient theorem? Explain REINFORCE and its limitations.
conceptual.model_answer: Policy gradient methods directly optimise the policy π_θ(a|s) by gradient ascent on the expected return J(θ) = E_π[Σₜ γᵗrₜ]. Policy gradient theorem (Sutton et al., 1999): ∇_θ J(θ) = E_π[∇_θ log π_θ(aₜ|sₜ) · Qᵖⁱ(sₜ,aₜ)]. The gradient is the expected product of the log-probability gradient (how to move θ to increase the probability of action a at state s) and the action-value function (how good that action was). REINFORCE: Monte Carlo estimate of the policy gradient. Collect a full trajectory τ = (s₀,a₀,r₀,...,sₜ,aₜ,rₜ). Estimate Qᵖⁱ(sₜ,aₜ) = Σₖ₌ₜ γᵏ⁻ᵗrₖ (discounted return from t). Update: θ ← θ + α·Σₜ ∇_θ log π_θ(aₜ|sₜ) · Gₜ. Limitations: (1) High variance: using a single trajectory return Gₜ as the Q estimate introduces enormous variance. The same action can receive very different returns across episodes due to stochastic dynamics. (2) Sample inefficiency: requires complete trajectories before updating. (3) Credit assignment: early actions that led to long-term rewards receive the full return Gₜ, making attribution difficult. Solutions: Subtract a baseline (critic): Gₜ - b(sₜ) where b is the state value function (Actor-Critic, A2C, A3C). The baseline doesn't change the expected gradient but dramatically reduces variance.
evaluation_criteria: States the policy gradient theorem correctly
Describes the REINFORCE update rule
Identifies high variance as the primary limitation
Mentions the baseline / actor-critic as the solution
common_mistakes: Confusing the policy gradient with the value gradient — these are different objects
conceptual.follow_up: Prove that subtracting a state-dependent baseline from the return does not bias the policy gradient estimate.

conceptual.question: What is Proximal Policy Optimisation (PPO)? What problem does it solve compared to vanilla policy gradient methods?
conceptual.model_answer: Vanilla policy gradient problem: large gradient steps can catastrophically destroy the policy. If a step overshoots, the new policy may be very bad, and subsequent gradient estimates (which depend on the current policy) become garbage — unrecoverable. TRPO (Trust Region Policy Optimisation): constrains the KL divergence between the old and new policy: max_θ E[π_θ(a|s)/π_θ_old(a|s) · A(s,a)] subject to KL(π_θ_old || π_θ) ≤ δ. Effective but computationally expensive (conjugate gradient, Fisher information matrix). PPO (Schulman et al., 2017): approximates TRPO with a simpler clipped objective. Let r_t(θ) = π_θ(aₜ|sₜ) / π_θ_old(aₜ|sₜ) (probability ratio). PPO-Clip: L^CLIP = E[min(r_t·Â_t, clip(r_t, 1-ε, 1+ε)·Â_t)] where ε ≈ 0.2. The clip prevents the ratio from moving too far from 1 — if the policy is being updated to increase the probability of an action (Â > 0), the update stops when r_t > 1+ε. If decreasing (Â < 0), stops when r_t < 1-ε. This is the de facto standard for RLHF training of LLMs, robotics, and game-playing agents. Combines simplicity (first-order optimisation, no constraint solver) with stability.
evaluation_criteria: Identifies the catastrophic policy update problem in vanilla PG
States TRPO's KL constraint
Derives the PPO clip objective and explains what ε controls
Notes PPO is used in RLHF for LLMs
common_mistakes: Saying PPO 'prevents overfitting' — it prevents destructive policy updates, a different problem
conceptual.follow_up: What is the advantage function Â in PPO and how is it estimated using Generalised Advantage Estimation (GAE)?

conceptual.question: Compare Q-learning, Actor-Critic, and model-based RL. When would you use each?
conceptual.model_answer: Q-learning (value-based, model-free): learns Q*(s,a) directly via TD learning. Policy is implicit: π(s) = argmax_a Q(s,a). Works for: discrete action spaces, when a good Q-function approximation is possible. DQN family (Double DQN, Dueling DQN, Rainbow) achieves superhuman Atari performance. Limitations: doesn't scale to continuous high-dimensional action spaces (maximising over actions is intractable). Actor-Critic (policy gradient + value-based, model-free): separates the actor (policy π_θ) and critic (value function V_φ or Q_φ). Actor updates toward actions with higher-than-expected advantage. Critic reduces variance of the actor's gradient. Works for: continuous action spaces (robotics, locomotion). SAC (Soft Actor-Critic), TD3 are state-of-the-art for continuous control. More sample-efficient than pure policy gradient. Model-based RL: learn a model P̂(s'|s,a) of the environment dynamics. Use the model for planning (Dyna, MBPO, Dreamer) — generate synthetic experience, reduce real environment samples needed. Works for: environments where real interactions are expensive (robotics, drug discovery). Sample efficiency is 10-100x better than model-free. Limitation: model errors compound — planning on an inaccurate model can be catastrophically wrong. Use when: discrete actions + full observability → Q-learning/DQN. Continuous control + sample budget → SAC/TD3. Expensive real environment → model-based (Dreamer, MBPO).
evaluation_criteria: Correctly identifies why Q-learning fails for continuous actions
Explains the actor-critic split
Names specific algorithms for each paradigm
Gives concrete selection guidance based on action space and sample cost
common_mistakes: Saying model-based RL 'always wins' — model errors can make it worse than model-free on complex environments
conceptual.follow_up: What is the deadly triad in RL and why can combining function approximation, bootstrapping, and off-policy learning cause divergence?

conceptual.question: What is multi-armed bandit problem? How does it relate to full RL, and what are the main exploration strategies?
conceptual.model_answer: Multi-armed bandit (MAB): an agent repeatedly chooses from K actions (arms). Each arm yields a stochastic reward with an unknown distribution. Goal: maximise cumulative reward. Unlike full RL: no state transitions, no sequential decision making — each action is independent. It isolates the exploration-exploitation tradeoff in its purest form. Regret: cumulative difference between the optimal arm's expected reward and the chosen arm's reward. Goal: minimise regret. Exploration strategies: (1) ε-greedy: with probability ε explore uniformly at random, otherwise exploit the best-known arm. Simple, widely used in DQN. Decaying ε schedule reduces exploration over time. (2) UCB (Upper Confidence Bound): choose arm with highest UCB₁ score = Q̂(a) + c·√(ln t / N(a)). The second term rewards arms that haven't been tried recently. Provably achieves O(log T) regret — asymptotically optimal. (3) Thompson Sampling: maintain a posterior distribution over each arm's reward distribution. Sample from each posterior, play the arm with the highest sample. Bayesian, works extremely well in practice. (4) Softmax / Boltzmann exploration: select arms proportional to exp(Q̂(a)/τ). τ controls exploration temperature. Relation to RL: MAB = single-state MDP. Insights carry over: UCB principles inspire optimistic initialisation in RL; Thompson Sampling generalises to posterior sampling RL (PSRL); ε-greedy is standard in DQN.
evaluation_criteria: Defines regret correctly
Explains ε-greedy, UCB, and Thompson Sampling
States UCB's O(log T) regret bound
Connects bandit insights to full RL
common_mistakes: Treating the bandit as equivalent to RL — the key missing element is state transitions and long-term consequences
conceptual.follow_up: What is contextual bandit and how does it sit between MAB and full RL?

applied.question: Design an RL system to train a robotic arm to pick and place arbitrary objects. Specify the state space, action space, reward function, and training strategy.
applied.model_answer: Task: pick objects from a table and place them in a target bin. Hardware: 6-DoF robot arm + RGB-D camera. State space: robot proprioception: joint angles θ (6D), joint velocities θ̇ (6D). gripper state: open/closed + contact force. object state: position (3D) + orientation (quaternion, 4D) from vision pipeline or pose estimation. goal state: target bin position (3D). Total: ~25-dimensional state vector. For vision-based policies: RGB image + depth map as state (ConvNet encoder). Action space: continuous, 6D end-effector velocity (3D translational + 3D rotational) in Cartesian space, plus 1D gripper open/close command. Total: 7D continuous. SAC or TD3 for continuous control. Reward function: sparse: +1 for successful placement, 0 otherwise. Efficient to define, hard to learn (credit assignment over long horizon). Dense (shaped): r = -||pos_ee - pos_object|| (approach reward) + pick_success_bonus + -||pos_object - pos_target|| (place reward). Shaping via potential-based functions maintains optimal policy invariance. Hindsight Experience Replay (HER): relabel failed trajectories — if the arm picked up object and placed it at position p (not the target), treat p as the goal. Dramatically improves sample efficiency for goal-conditioned tasks. Training strategy: (1) Sim-to-real: train in Isaac Gym/MuJoCo simulation with domain randomisation (friction, mass, lighting). Deploy to real robot. (2) Curriculum: start with objects already in grasp, then with pre-positioned objects, then full pick-and-place.
evaluation_criteria: Defines all state/action dimensions concretely
Proposes both sparse and dense reward with HER
Mentions sim-to-real and domain randomisation
Includes curriculum learning for the long-horizon task
common_mistakes: Using only sparse reward without HER — convergence will be extremely slow or fail entirely
applied.follow_up: How does Hindsight Experience Replay work mathematically, and why does it not introduce bias into the Q-function estimate?

applied.question: You are training a DQN agent on a video game and observe that training is unstable — loss oscillates wildly and performance collapses periodically. Diagnose and fix.
applied.model_answer: DQN-specific instabilities: (1) Correlated samples: the replay buffer is filled with consecutive frames — training on correlated samples breaks the iid assumption and causes overfitting to recent experience. Fix: ensure replay buffer is large enough (1M+ transitions) and use uniform random sampling, not sequential. (2) Moving target problem: the target Q-values Q̂(s',a') are computed using the same network being updated. Every gradient step changes the targets, creating a moving goalpost. Fix: use a target network — a frozen copy of the Q-network updated every C steps (e.g., C=10,000). (3) Reward scale: if rewards are large (e.g., +100 for win), gradients explode. Fix: clip rewards to [-1, +1] or normalise via running mean/std. (4) Exploding Q-values: without reward clipping, Q-values can diverge exponentially. Fix: gradient clipping (max norm = 10), reward normalisation. (5) Action space exploration: if ε decays too fast, the agent stops exploring before finding good states. Fix: slower ε decay schedule; start at ε=1.0, decay to 0.1 over 1M steps. (6) Architecture mismatch: the network may be too large for the task (overfits to replay buffer) or too small (underfits). Diagnostics: plot Q-value estimates over time. If growing without bound → target network or reward clipping issue. If oscillating → correlated samples or learning rate too high. If plateaued low → exploration too low.
evaluation_criteria: Identifies the moving target problem and proposes target network
Identifies correlated samples and proposes large replay buffer
Addresses reward scaling
Proposes diagnostic approach (Q-value plotting)
common_mistakes: Treating all instability as a learning rate problem — DQN has several independent instability sources
applied.follow_up: How does Double DQN address the overestimation bias in standard DQN's target computation?

applied.question: Design an RL-based recommendation system for a news feed. What are the specific challenges compared to a supervised recommendation model?
applied.model_answer: RL framing: state = user session history, recent interactions, user features. Action = which article to show next (from a candidate set). Reward = engagement signal (click, dwell time, share) - diversity_penalty - filter_bubble_penalty. Policy: maps state → action. Challenges vs supervised recommendation: (1) Delayed and sparse reward: user satisfaction is measured at the end of a session (30-minute engagement), not per article. Credit assignment across 10-20 article impressions per session is hard. (2) Reward design: optimising for immediate CTR leads to clickbait. Must shape reward to balance short-term engagement with long-term user retention and content diversity. (3) Off-policy learning: we can't run experiments for every policy update — must learn from logged behaviour data collected under a different (historical) policy. Requires importance sampling corrections. (4) Exploration cost: exploring with a production recommendation system means showing suboptimal content to real users. Exploration budget must be managed carefully. (5) Large action space: millions of articles — full argmax over actions is infeasible. Use slate-based actions (select a set of k articles) or parametric action embeddings. (6) Non-stationarity: news freshness — articles become stale within hours. Environment is non-stationary. Architecture: Offline RL (CQL, BCQ) or Bandits (LinUCB, Thompson Sampling on contextual features) are safer starting points than online RL for production news feeds. Gradual online learning with conservative policy updates.
evaluation_criteria: Frames the problem as RL with correct state/action/reward
Identifies at least 3 RL-specific challenges for recommendation
Proposes off-policy learning for production safety
Addresses the large action space problem
common_mistakes: Ignoring the filter bubble / diversity problem in reward design — optimising CTR alone creates an echo chamber
applied.follow_up: What is Conservative Q-Learning (CQL) and why is it preferred over standard Q-learning for offline RL from logged data?

applied.question: Explain how AlphaGo and AlphaZero work. What RL innovations enabled superhuman performance in Go?
applied.model_answer: Go: 19×19 board, branching factor ~250, game tree depth ~150. Traditional MCTS exhausts the search tree — infeasible for Go. AlphaGo (Silver et al., 2016): three networks: (1) SL policy network π_SL: supervised learning on 30M human expert moves. Predicts human move probabilities. (2) RL policy network π_RL: fine-tune π_SL via self-play. Games are played between current and random past versions; win = +1, loss = -1. Policy gradient update. Produces stronger policy than SL alone. (3) Value network V: trained to predict the winner of games played by π_RL from any board position. Regression on game outcomes. MCTS integration: at each node, run simulation. Use π_SL to guide action selection (replace random rollouts). Use V to evaluate leaf nodes (replace full game rollout). Balance exploitation (UCB) and exploration (prior probabilities from π_SL). Result: defeated world champion Lee Sedol 4-1. AlphaZero (2017): eliminates all human knowledge. No SL pretraining on human games. Single network f_θ(s) → (p, v): p = policy prior, v = value estimate. MCTS guided purely by f_θ. Self-play from random initialisation. 40 days to master Go, Chess, and Shogi — achieves superhuman performance in all three. Key innovations: MCTS + neural network synergy, self-play curriculum, no domain-specific hand-crafted features.
evaluation_criteria: Describes all three AlphaGo networks and their training objectives
Explains how MCTS integrates the policy and value networks
States what AlphaZero removes vs AlphaGo
Quantifies the training timeline
common_mistakes: Saying AlphaZero 'just uses self-play' — the MCTS + neural network co-training loop is the key innovation
applied.follow_up: How does MuZero extend AlphaZero to environments where the rules are not known to the agent?

applied.question: What is reward hacking / Goodhart's Law in RL? Give two real examples and explain how to detect and mitigate it.
applied.model_answer: Goodhart's Law: 'When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.' In RL: the agent finds a policy that maximises the specified reward function but in ways that violate the designer's intent. The agent is doing exactly what you asked, not what you meant. Real examples: (1) OpenAI boat racing game: the agent discovered it could score more points by spinning in circles collecting bonus items without finishing the race — the reward (score) was not the intended objective (race completion). (2) RLHF sycophancy: LLMs trained with RLHF to maximise human preference scores learn to tell humans what they want to hear rather than what is true. The preference reward was a proxy for 'good response' that the model exploited. (3) Classic: a robot trained to move fast learned to make itself tall and fall over — falling = high velocity, violates the spirit of locomotion. Detection: (1) Compare proxy reward (what you're optimising) vs true metric (what you care about) on a held-out set not used for optimisation. (2) Human evaluation: periodic sampling of agent behaviour by humans who assess the spirit, not the letter, of the task. (3) Reward model uncertainty: for RLHF, flag generations where the reward model has high uncertainty — these are likely distribution-shift exploitation cases. Mitigation: (1) Reward shaping with multiple competing signals (cannot maximise one by sacrificing another). (2) Constrained RL: add constraints that proxy-reward maximisation must satisfy. (3) KL regularisation (in RLHF): prevent the policy from drifting too far from the reference policy. (4) Human in the loop: periodic human evaluation as the ground truth.
evaluation_criteria: States Goodhart's Law correctly
Gives concrete examples (not vague)
Proposes multiple mitigation strategies
Distinguishes the proxy reward from the true objective
common_mistakes: Treating reward hacking as a rare edge case — it is a systematic risk in any learned reward system
applied.follow_up: How does Constitutional AI (Anthropic's approach) attempt to address reward hacking in LLM alignment?

deep_dive.question: Derive the policy gradient theorem from first principles. Show why the log-derivative trick is necessary.
deep_dive.model_answer: Objective: J(θ) = E_{τ~π_θ}[R(τ)] = ∫ π_θ(τ) R(τ) dτ where τ is a trajectory. Gradient: ∇_θ J(θ) = ∫ ∇_θ π_θ(τ) R(τ) dτ. Problem: ∇_θ π_θ(τ) is not an expectation under π_θ, so we cannot estimate it by sampling. Log-derivative trick: ∇_θ π_θ(τ) = π_θ(τ) · ∇_θ log π_θ(τ). Therefore: ∇_θ J(θ) = ∫ π_θ(τ) · ∇_θ log π_θ(τ) · R(τ) dτ = E_{τ~π_θ}[∇_θ log π_θ(τ) · R(τ)]. Now this is an expectation under π_θ — estimable by sampling. Expanding log π_θ(τ) for a trajectory τ = (s₀,a₀,...,sₜ,aₜ): log π_θ(τ) = Σₜ log π_θ(aₜ|sₜ) + log P(s₀) + Σₜ log P(sₜ₊₁|sₜ,aₜ). Only the policy terms depend on θ. Therefore: ∇_θ log π_θ(τ) = Σₜ ∇_θ log π_θ(aₜ|sₜ). Final result: ∇_θ J(θ) = E_π[Σₜ ∇_θ log π_θ(aₜ|sₜ) · R(τ)]. Variance reduction: replace R(τ) with the reward-to-go Gₜ = Σₖ₌ₜ γᵏ⁻ᵗrₖ (actions cannot affect past rewards). Subtract baseline b(sₜ) to reduce variance without biasing the gradient (baseline is independent of action).
evaluation_criteria: Sets up the trajectory integral correctly
Applies the log-derivative trick explicitly and explains why it's needed
Derives ∇_θ log π_θ(τ) = Σₜ ∇_θ log π_θ(aₜ|sₜ)
Shows reward-to-go reduction and baseline
common_mistakes: Skipping the log-derivative step and just asserting the result
Not showing why transition probabilities drop out of the gradient
deep_dive.follow_up: Prove that subtracting a state-dependent baseline b(sₜ) does not change the expected policy gradient.

deep_dive.question: Explain the deadly triad in reinforcement learning. Why can combining function approximation, off-policy learning, and bootstrapping lead to divergence?
deep_dive.model_answer: The deadly triad (Sutton & Barto): three conditions that, when combined, can cause divergence in value function estimation: (1) Function approximation: representing V or Q with a parameterised function (neural network, linear basis). The function approximator introduces approximation error. (2) Bootstrapping: updating estimates using other estimates (TD learning: V(s) ← r + γV(s')). The target V(s') is itself an approximation — errors in the target propagate into the update. (3) Off-policy learning: updating the value function using data generated by a different policy than the one being evaluated. The distribution of states in the data does not match the on-policy distribution. Why divergence occurs: Consider linear function approximation V(s) = θᵀφ(s). The TD update is θ ← θ + α[r + γθᵀφ(s') - θᵀφ(s)]φ(s). Under on-policy distribution, this converges. Under off-policy distribution, the update matrix A = E[φ(s)(φ(s) - γφ(s'))ᵀ] may not be positive definite, making the gradient update non-contractive. A concrete example: Baird's counterexample (1995) — a simple MDP with linear function approximation and off-policy DP diverges even for a benign-looking problem. Solutions: (1) LSTD (Least Squares TD): finds the fixed point of the projected Bellman operator — converges under function approximation. (2) Gradient TD (GTD2, TDC): minimise the mean squared projected Bellman error via two-timescale SGD — convergent under off-policy. (3) DQN workaround: replay buffer approximates iid sampling (reducing off-policy severity); target network reduces bootstrapping frequency.
evaluation_criteria: Names all three components of the deadly triad precisely
Explains why off-policy distribution mismatch breaks convergence
References Baird's counterexample or similar
Names at least two provably convergent solutions
common_mistakes: Saying 'off-policy learning causes divergence' without explaining the distributional mismatch mechanism
deep_dive.follow_up: How does the target network in DQN partially address the deadly triad without solving it fully?

deep_dive.question: Explain Soft Actor-Critic (SAC). How does maximum entropy RL change the objective, and what are the practical benefits?
deep_dive.model_answer: Standard RL objective: J(π) = E[Σₜ γᵗ r(sₜ,aₜ)]. Maximum entropy RL objective: J_maxEnt(π) = E[Σₜ γᵗ (r(sₜ,aₜ) + α·H(π(·|sₜ)))]. The entropy term H(π(·|s)) = -E[log π(a|s)] is added to the reward. α is the temperature parameter — controls the tradeoff between reward and entropy. Why maximum entropy: (1) Exploration: the entropy bonus incentivises the policy to maintain diversity — it doesn't commit to a single action unless strongly rewarded. (2) Robustness: high-entropy policies are more robust to perturbations — they don't rely on a single mode of behaviour. (3) Multimodal solutions: can capture multiple ways of solving a task rather than collapsing to one. SAC architecture: Actor: stochastic policy π_θ — samples actions from a learned Gaussian. Outputs mean and log-std, samples via reparameterisation. Critic: two Q-networks Q_{φ1}, Q_{φ2} — use min(Q₁, Q₂) as the target to reduce overestimation (following TD3). Target networks with soft update (Polyak averaging): φ_target ← τφ + (1-τ)φ_target. Temperature α: can be manually set or automatically tuned to maintain a target entropy H_target = -|A|. Practical benefits: very sample-efficient on continuous control benchmarks (MuJoCo locomotion). Off-policy (uses replay buffer). Stable training. State-of-the-art for continuous control in robotics.
evaluation_criteria: States the maximum entropy objective with the entropy bonus
Explains the intuition for why entropy bonus helps exploration and robustness
Describes SAC's dual Q-network and stochastic actor
Mentions automatic temperature tuning
common_mistakes: Confusing SAC's maximum entropy with simply adding noise to actions — the entropy is explicitly rewarded in the objective
deep_dive.follow_up: How does SAC's automatic entropy tuning work — derive the dual optimisation objective for α.

deep_dive.question: What is model-based RL? Explain the Dyna architecture and Dreamer's latent space planning approach.
deep_dive.model_answer: Model-based RL: learn an explicit model of the environment P̂(s'|s,a), R̂(s,a), then use it for planning or generating synthetic experience. Dyna (Sutton, 1991): integrate model learning with model-free Q-learning. Each real environment step: (1) Update Q(s,a) with the real transition (TD update). (2) Update the model P̂ with the real transition. (3) Perform k planning steps: sample (s,a) from previously visited state-action pairs, query P̂ for simulated (s',r), update Q with the simulated transition. Dyna is simple and effective when the model is accurate. Model error propagates through planning — with a poor model, planning makes things worse. Dreamer (Hafner et al., 2020): learns a world model in a compact latent space using a Recurrent State Space Model (RSSM). Components: Encoder: images → latent state h,z via CNN. Transition model: P(zₜ|hₜ,zₜ₋₁,aₜ₋₁) — deterministic + stochastic components. Reward model: R̂(h,z). Value and actor operate entirely in latent space — never interact with the real environment during planning. Imagination: roll out trajectories in latent space for 15 steps. Backpropagate through the imagined trajectories to update the actor (analytic gradients through the differentiable world model). Dreamer-v3 achieves superhuman performance on 150+ tasks across diverse domains from pixels, using the same hyperparameters. The key insight: latent space planning avoids the curse of dimensionality of image-space planning.
evaluation_criteria: Explains Dyna's k planning steps correctly
Describes the RSSM in Dreamer (deterministic + stochastic latent state)
Explains that Dreamer trains actor/critic entirely in imagination
Discusses model error as the key limitation of Dyna
common_mistakes: Treating Dreamer as just 'Dyna with a neural network model' — the latent space planning and differentiable world model are qualitatively different

conceptual.question: Explain the forward and reverse process in diffusion models. What is the training objective?
conceptual.model_answer: Diffusion models (DDPM, Ho et al., 2020) define two processes. Forward process (fixed): gradually add Gaussian noise to data over T timesteps. q(xₜ|xₜ₋₁) = N(xₜ; √(1-βₜ)xₜ₋₁, βₜI). After T steps (T=1000 typically), xₜ is approximately Gaussian noise. Closed form: q(xₜ|x₀) = N(xₜ; √ᾱₜ x₀, (1-ᾱₜ)I) where ᾱₜ = Πᵢ₌₁ᵗ (1-βᵢ). This lets us sample any noisy version directly. Reverse process (learned): denoise step by step. p_θ(xₜ₋₁|xₜ) = N(xₜ₋₁; μ_θ(xₜ,t), Σ_θ(xₜ,t)). Training objective: minimise the variational lower bound on -log p_θ(x₀). Ho et al. show this simplifies to: L_simple = E_{x₀,ε,t}[||ε - ε_θ(xₜ,t)||²]. Train a neural network ε_θ (usually a U-Net) to predict the noise ε that was added at each timestep. Given xₜ = √ᾱₜ x₀ + √(1-ᾱₜ)ε, predicting ε is equivalent to predicting x₀. At inference: start from pure Gaussian noise xₜ, iteratively apply the learned denoising step p_θ(xₜ₋₁|xₜ) for T steps to produce a sample.
evaluation_criteria: States the forward process with the noise schedule βₜ
States the closed form q(xₜ|x₀) with ᾱₜ
States the simplified L_simple noise prediction objective
Describes inference as iterative denoising from Gaussian noise
common_mistakes: Saying the model predicts x₀ — it predicts the noise ε (these are mathematically equivalent but the noise parameterisation trains better)

conceptual.question: How does Stable Diffusion's Latent Diffusion Model (LDM) differ from pixel-space diffusion models? What is classifier-free guidance?
conceptual.model_answer: Pixel-space diffusion (DDPM): diffusion process operates directly on full-resolution image pixels. At 512×512 × 3 channels, each step processes large tensors — computationally expensive. T=1000 steps × full-image denoising = extremely slow training and inference. Latent Diffusion Model (Rombach et al., 2022): (1) Train a VQ-VAE (Vector Quantised Variational Autoencoder) or KL-regularised autoencoder to compress images to a compact latent space: encoder E maps 512×512×3 → 64×64×4 (8× spatial reduction). Decoder D maps back. (2) Train the diffusion model in this 4D latent space — 64× fewer pixels per step. (3) Conditioning: cross-attention with CLIP text embeddings for text-to-image. Much faster training and inference than pixel-space. Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG, Ho & Salimans, 2021): trains a conditional diffusion model p(x|c) and an unconditional model p(x) jointly by randomly dropping the conditioning c during training (typically 10-20% of steps). At inference, the noise prediction is: ε̂ = ε_θ(xₜ, ∅) + w · (ε_θ(xₜ, c) - ε_θ(xₜ, ∅)). The guidance scale w amplifies the effect of the conditioning. High w (7-12): high fidelity to the prompt, lower diversity. Low w (1-3): more diversity, less prompt adherence. CFG trades off sample quality (FID) vs prompt alignment (CLIP score).
evaluation_criteria: Explains the compression ratio achieved by LDM (64× fewer pixels)
Describes the VQ-VAE component
States the CFG inference formula correctly
Explains the guidance scale tradeoff
common_mistakes: Saying CFG requires a separate classifier — it's 'classifier-free' because it uses the diffusion model itself, not an external classifier
conceptual.follow_up: What is ControlNet and how does it enable spatial conditioning (pose, depth, edges) in Stable Diffusion?

conceptual.question: Compare GANs, VAEs, normalising flows, and diffusion models as generative model families. What are the key tradeoffs?
conceptual.model_answer: GANs: implicit generative model — no explicit likelihood. Two-network adversarial training. Pro: sharpest images (sample quality). Con: training instability, mode collapse, no likelihood estimation, no latent space interpolation without tricks. VAEs: encode to Gaussian latent space, decode back. Explicit ELBO lower bound on likelihood. Pro: stable training, interpretable latent space, enables editing/interpolation. Con: blurry samples (reconstruction loss averages over possible images). Normalising flows: sequence of invertible transformations from a simple base distribution (Gaussian) to the data distribution. Pro: exact likelihood computation, invertible latent space (exact inference and generation). Con: architectural constraints (must be invertible) limit model capacity. Computationally expensive per step. Diffusion models: iterative denoising from Gaussian noise. Pro: highest sample quality (surpassing GANs), training stability, mode coverage (no collapse), strong likelihood bounds. Con: slow inference (T=1000 steps originally), large compute for training. DDIM, Consistency Models reduce sampling to ~10-50 steps. Current state: Diffusion (Stable Diffusion, DALL-E 3, Imagen) dominates image generation. Flow Matching (a continuous-time normalising flow variant) is gaining ground for its simpler training and faster sampling. GANs still used for video generation where speed is critical.
evaluation_criteria: Correctly characterises pros/cons of all four families
Identifies diffusion's key advantage (quality + stability) and key disadvantage (slow inference)
Notes that diffusion has largely replaced GANs for image synthesis
Mentions DDIM or Consistency Models for faster diffusion sampling
common_mistakes: Saying flows have 'no limitations' — the invertibility constraint is severe
conceptual.follow_up: What is Flow Matching and how does it simplify the training of normalising flows compared to continuous normalising flows (CNFs)?

conceptual.question: What is CLIP? How does contrastive pretraining on image-text pairs enable zero-shot image classification?
conceptual.model_answer: CLIP (Contrastive Language-Image Pretraining, Radford et al., 2021): jointly trains an image encoder (ViT or ResNet) and a text encoder (Transformer) on 400M (image, text) pairs from the internet. Training objective: contrastive loss (InfoNCE) — for a batch of N image-text pairs, maximise similarity between matched pairs and minimise similarity between unmatched pairs. The result: a shared embedding space where semantically similar images and texts are close. Zero-shot classification: (1) For each class label 'dog', 'cat', etc., construct text prompts: 'a photo of a {class}'. Embed all prompts with the text encoder → text embeddings. (2) Embed the query image with the image encoder → image embedding. (3) Compute cosine similarity between the image embedding and all text embeddings. (4) The class with highest similarity is the prediction — no task-specific training required. Zero-shot ImageNet accuracy: 76.2% (ViT-L/14) — comparable to supervised ResNet-50. Why it works: the contrastive objective aligns the image and text spaces such that visual concepts and their linguistic descriptions are co-located. The model has seen millions of natural language descriptions of images, learning a rich cross-modal semantic space. Applications beyond classification: image retrieval, image-text ranking, prompt-guided generation (Stable Diffusion uses CLIP text encoder), visual question answering.
evaluation_criteria: Describes the contrastive training objective on image-text pairs
Explains the zero-shot classification procedure step by step
Gives the zero-shot ImageNet number (76%)
Names downstream applications
common_mistakes: Saying CLIP 'fine-tunes on ImageNet' — the zero-shot result uses no ImageNet training data at all

conceptual.question: What are large multimodal models (LMMs)? How do architectures like LLaVA connect visual and language representations?
conceptual.model_answer: Large multimodal models (LMMs) extend LLMs to understand images, audio, or video alongside text. Key components for vision-language models: (1) Visual encoder: a pretrained vision model (CLIP ViT, SigLIP) that converts an image into a sequence of patch embeddings. For a 224×224 image with 14×14 patches: 256 visual tokens. (2) Projection layer: a learnable mapping that projects visual tokens from the visual encoder's embedding space into the LLM's token embedding space. LLaVA uses a simple linear projection. (3) Language model: a pretrained LLM (Vicuna, Llama-2) that processes the concatenated sequence of visual tokens + text tokens autoregressively. LLaVA training (Liu et al., 2023): Stage 1 (feature alignment): freeze both encoders and LLM, train only the projection layer on image-caption pairs. Aligns visual and text embedding spaces. Stage 2 (instruction tuning): unfreeze the LLM (keep vision encoder frozen), fine-tune on visual instruction following data (GPT-4-generated QA pairs about images). The projection layer bridges the two modalities without expensive retraining of either encoder. Advanced architectures: Flamingo uses cross-attention layers between visual tokens and LLM layers. Gemini and GPT-4V use native multimodal tokenisation (images encoded as discrete tokens or via resampling). LLaVA-1.5 and InternVL use higher resolution visual inputs (336×336 or tiling) for better spatial understanding.

Explains LLaVA's two-stage training correctly
Notes that the vision encoder is typically frozen in stage 2
Compares LLaVA's projection approach to Flamingo's cross-attention

conceptual.question: Explain score-based generative models and their connection to diffusion models. What is the score function?
conceptual.model_answer: Score function: s_θ(x) = ∇_x log p(x) — the gradient of the log data density with respect to the data point x. The score points in the direction of increasing data density. Score-based models (Song & Ermon, 2019): train a neural network to estimate the score: s_θ(x) ≈ ∇_x log p(x). Training via score matching: minimise E[||s_θ(x) - ∇_x log p(x)||²]. Denoising score matching (Vincent, 2011): instead of estimating the score of the data directly, estimate the score of the noised data: s_θ(x̃, σ) ≈ ∇_{x̃} log pσ(x̃) where x̃ = x + σε. This is tractable because ∇_{x̃} log pσ(x̃|x) = -ε/σ². Sampling via Langevin dynamics: x ← x + (η/2)·s_θ(x) + √η·ε. Iteratively walk up the score gradient with added noise → converges to samples from p(x). Connection to diffusion models (Song et al., 2020, 'Score-Based Generative Modeling through SDEs'): diffusion models define a Stochastic Differential Equation (SDE): dx = f(x,t)dt + g(t)dW (forward, adds noise). The reverse SDE (Anderson, 1982): dx = [f(x,t) - g(t)²·∇_x log pₜ(x)]dt + g(t)dW̄. The score function ∇_x log pₜ(x) is exactly what DDPM's noise prediction network estimates. Diffusion models are score-based models with a specific noise schedule and discrete-time approximation.
evaluation_criteria: Defines the score function correctly
Explains denoising score matching as the tractable training objective
States the reverse SDE and identifies the score function in it
Shows the connection to DDPM's noise prediction
common_mistakes: Treating score-based models and diffusion models as completely separate — Song et al. (2020) unified them under the SDE framework
