applied.question: Design a text-to-image generation system for an e-commerce platform that generates product lifestyle images. What are the specific requirements and how do you meet them?
applied.model_answer: Requirements: product must be accurate (no hallucinated features), brand-consistent style, commercially licensable outputs, latency < 10s per image, content safety. Architecture: (1) Base model: Stable Diffusion XL (SDXL) or FLUX — both produce high-quality, commercially permissive images (check licence carefully — SDXL's base model is open weight, FLUX.1 [dev] has restrictions). (2) Product accuracy: product image + text prompt → model must depict the correct product. Approach: ControlNet with product image as reference. Or: IP-Adapter to inject product appearance into the generation. (3) Brand consistency: fine-tune SDXL on a curated dataset of brand-approved lifestyle images using DreamBooth or LoRA (20-50 reference images). The fine-tuned model learns the brand's aesthetic (colour palette, composition style). (4) Content safety: (a) Prompt filtering — block prompts that contain disallowed content before generation. (b) Post-generation NSFW classifier on outputs. Flag any that score > threshold for human review. (5) Latency: SDXL on A10G GPU: ~6-8s for 30 DDIM steps at 1024×1024. Use SDXL-Turbo (adversarial diffusion distillation) for ~1s inference at slight quality cost. (6) Evaluation: human evaluation panel rates brand consistency, product accuracy, and photorealism on 50-image test sets. CLIP score for prompt alignment. (7) Output management: watermark outputs with a forensic watermark (SynthID) for accountability.
evaluation_criteria: Proposes ControlNet or IP-Adapter for product accuracy
Addresses brand consistency via DreamBooth/LoRA fine-tuning
Includes content safety (both input and output filtering)
Addresses latency with a specific model and step count
common_mistakes: Not addressing product accuracy — vanilla text-to-image will hallucinate product details
Forgetting content safety requirements for a production system
applied.follow_up: How does DreamBooth enable few-shot personalisation of a diffusion model, and what is the prior preservation loss?

applied.question: You are building a video generation system using a diffusion model. What are the key challenges compared to image generation, and how do state-of-the-art systems address them?
applied.model_answer: Video generation challenges: (1) Temporal consistency: frames must be consistent — no flickering, no object teleportation. The model must understand that the same object persists across frames. (2) Compute: a 10s video at 24fps = 240 frames. Naively applying image diffusion to each frame: 240× the compute of a single image. (3) Motion modelling: must generate plausible motion (a person walking, water flowing). Motion has its own statistics beyond frame-by-frame appearance. (4) Long-range temporal dependencies: objects must remain consistent across distant frames (same car colour at frame 1 and frame 200). Approaches: (1) Temporal attention: extend spatial attention to attend across frames. 3D attention: each spatial token attends to the same spatial location across all frames. Computationally expensive at high frame counts. (2) Temporal convolutional layers: add 1D temporal convolutions to propagate information across time while keeping spatial processing in 2D (VideoCrafter, AnimateDiff). (3) Video latent space: encode temporal sequences into a shared latent space with a video VAE. Run diffusion in compressed video latent space (Sora approach — space-time patches). (4) Motion prior: separate motion encoder/decoder (human pose sequences, optical flow) as conditioning. State-of-the-art: Sora uses video diffusion Transformers operating on space-time patches. Stable Video Diffusion fine-tunes image diffusion with temporal layers. Gen-2 and Kling use proprietary architectures. Runway, Pika are leading commercial systems.
evaluation_criteria: Identifies temporal consistency and compute as the core challenges
Explains temporal attention or temporal convolutions as solutions
Describes the compressed latent space approach
References Sora's space-time patch approach
common_mistakes: Treating video generation as just 'generate each frame independently' — temporal consistency is the central unsolved challenge
applied.follow_up: How does AnimateDiff enable motion generation without retraining the base image diffusion model?

applied.question: How would you fine-tune Stable Diffusion to generate images of a specific person's face consistently? Discuss DreamBooth, LoRA, and textual inversion.
applied.model_answer: Task: few-shot personalisation — given 5-20 images of a specific person, generate them in novel contexts. Textual Inversion (Gal et al., 2022): introduce a new pseudo-word token S* into the text encoder's vocabulary. Optimise only the embedding of S* to minimise the diffusion reconstruction loss on the reference images. Everything else frozen. Pro: very lightweight (only one embedding vector changed). Con: limited expressiveness — one embedding can't capture complex appearance. Best for style or object tokens, not faces. DreamBooth (Ruiz et al., 2023): fine-tune the full UNet (and optionally text encoder) on the reference images, binding a rare identifier token [V] to the subject ('a photo of [V] person'). Prior preservation loss: simultaneously train on class-level images ('a photo of a person') to prevent catastrophic forgetting of the general class concept. Pro: highest fidelity to the subject, novel pose generation. Con: full model fine-tune (≈5GB VRAM for SDXL), separate model per person. LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) for fine-tuning: apply LoRA to the UNet's attention layers only. Rank 4-16. ~5-30MB adapter per person instead of full model copy. Quality close to DreamBooth at a fraction of the storage and compute. Production recommendation: LoRA for face personalisation at scale — one base model + N lightweight adapters, one per user. DreamBooth when maximum fidelity is needed and compute is not a constraint. Safety: face personalisation raises serious consent and deepfake concerns. Require explicit consent, watermark outputs, and block celebrity/public figure identities.
evaluation_criteria: Correctly describes all three approaches and their tradeoffs
Explains DreamBooth's prior preservation loss
Recommends LoRA for production at scale with justification
Raises ethical/safety concerns around face generation
common_mistakes: Not explaining the prior preservation loss — it's the key innovation that prevents catastrophic forgetting in DreamBooth
applied.follow_up: How would you detect whether an image was generated by a fine-tuned model vs a real photograph?

applied.question: Design an evaluation framework for a text-to-image model. What metrics would you use and what are their limitations?
applied.model_answer: Evaluation dimensions: (1) Fidelity (image quality): FID (Fréchet Inception Distance) — measures the distance between the distribution of generated images and real images in Inception-v3 feature space. Lower is better. Standard benchmark but sensitive to the reference set. CLIP-FID: same but using CLIP features — better correlated with human quality ratings. IS (Inception Score) — measures sharpness and diversity via KL divergence of class predictions; less used now. (2) Prompt alignment (text faithfulness): CLIP Score = cosine similarity between CLIP image embedding and CLIP text embedding of the prompt. Measures how well the image matches the prompt. DrawBench / T2I-CompBench: structured prompts testing compositional understanding (attributes, spatial relations, counting). (3) Diversity: standard deviation of embeddings across samples. High-quality models that sacrifice diversity (mode collapse equivalent) will score well on FID but low on diversity. (4) Human evaluation: the gold standard. Use a structured rubric: photorealism (1-5), prompt faithfulness (1-5), aesthetic quality (1-5). Run blind A/B comparisons between model versions. HEIM (Holistic Evaluation of Text-to-Image Models) benchmark: standardised human eval across many dimensions. (5) Safety metrics: NSFW classifier rate on standard prompts. Bias audit: does the model produce stereotyped outputs for gender, race, profession? (6) Limitations: FID requires a large reference set and is sensitive to resolution. CLIP score saturates — it doesn't capture fine-grained compositional accuracy. Human eval is expensive and slow.
evaluation_criteria: Names FID and explains what it measures
Explains CLIP score for prompt alignment
Includes human evaluation as the gold standard
Includes safety and bias evaluation
common_mistakes: Relying only on FID — it doesn't capture prompt alignment and can be gamed
applied.follow_up: How does T2I-CompBench evaluate compositional text-to-image generation, and why is it harder than standard prompt following?

applied.question: Your diffusion model generates photorealistic images but has a disturbing failure mode: it generates recognisable faces of real people from the training set. How do you diagnose and mitigate this?
applied.model_answer: This is a training data memorisation problem — the model has overfit to specific training examples and can reproduce them. Diagnosis: (1) Membership inference: generate images with prompts related to suspected individuals. Compare to training data using perceptual similarity metrics (LPIPS, SSID). If generated images are within a threshold of training images, memorisation is confirmed. (2) Extraction attack: generate many images from a range of prompts. Run face detection and recognition (ArcFace, FaceNet) against a known faces database. Count recognition hits. (3) Duplication analysis: scan the training dataset for near-duplicate images of the same person (same face multiple times). Repeated examples are much more likely to be memorised. Root causes: (1) Training data contains many near-duplicate images of specific individuals (data imbalance). (2) Model is large enough to memorise rather than generalise. (3) Insufficient differential privacy during training. Mitigations: (1) Training data deduplication: remove near-duplicate images before training (using perceptual hashing or embedding similarity). (2) Differential privacy: add calibrated Gaussian noise to gradients during training (DP-SGD). Prevents memorisation with provable guarantees at the cost of some model quality. (3) Face blurring in training data: detect and blur faces in training images for models not intended for face generation. (4) Inference-time filtering: run face recognition on every generated image. Block outputs that match known individuals. (5) Model auditing: test for memorisation regularly using membership inference attacks as part of the release process.
evaluation_criteria: Identifies memorisation (not just 'the model learned faces')
Proposes a concrete diagnostic via membership inference or extraction attacks
Identifies training data duplication as a root cause
Proposes DP-SGD and deduplication as mitigations
common_mistakes: Proposing only inference-time filtering without addressing the root cause in the training data
applied.follow_up: What formal guarantees does differential privacy provide, and what is the privacy-utility tradeoff in DP-SGD for diffusion model training?

deep_dive.question: Derive the ELBO (Evidence Lower BOund) for a VAE and show how the reparameterisation trick makes it tractable.
deep_dive.model_answer: Goal: train a generative model p_θ(x) = ∫ p_θ(x|z) p(z) dz. Direct maximisation of log p_θ(x) is intractable (integral over z). Introduce approximate posterior q_φ(z|x). log p_θ(x) = log ∫ p_θ(x|z) p(z) dz = log E_{q_φ}[p_θ(x|z) p(z) / q_φ(z|x)] ≥ E_{q_φ}[log(p_θ(x|z) p(z) / q_φ(z|x))] (Jensen's inequality, since log is concave). ELBO = E_{q_φ}[log p_θ(x|z)] - KL(q_φ(z|x) || p(z)). First term: reconstruction — expected log-likelihood under the encoder's distribution. Second term: KL divergence — pushes the approximate posterior toward the prior (typically N(0,I)). For Gaussian encoder q_φ(z|x) = N(μ_φ(x), diag(σ²_φ(x))) and Gaussian prior p(z) = N(0,I): KL = -½ Σⱼ (1 + log σ²_j - μ²_j - σ²_j). Closed form — no sampling needed for KL. Reparameterisation trick for reconstruction term: E_{q_φ}[log p_θ(x|z)] = E_{ε~N(0,I)}[log p_θ(x | μ_φ(x) + σ_φ(x)⊙ε)]. z = μ + σ⊙ε — the randomness is moved into the fixed auxiliary variable ε. Gradients ∂/∂φ now pass through the deterministic function μ_φ(x) + σ_φ(x)⊙ε with respect to φ. Without reparameterisation, ∂/∂φ E_{q_φ}[f(z)] requires the REINFORCE estimator (high variance). With reparameterisation: low-variance pathwise gradient.
evaluation_criteria: Derives the ELBO via Jensen's inequality starting from log p_θ(x)
Identifies the two terms (reconstruction + KL) and their roles
States the closed-form KL for Gaussians
Explains why reparameterisation reduces variance compared to REINFORCE
common_mistakes: Starting from the ELBO without deriving it from log p_θ(x)
deep_dive.follow_up: What is the posterior collapse problem in VAEs and how do β-VAE and cyclical annealing address it?

deep_dive.question: What is DDIM sampling? Derive the deterministic sampling trajectory and explain how it enables fewer function evaluations.
deep_dive.model_answer: DDPM sampling: xₜ₋₁ = (1/√αₜ)(xₜ - ((1-αₜ)/√(1-ᾱₜ))·ε_θ(xₜ,t)) + σₜ·z. This is a stochastic process — ε_θ evaluations must proceed sequentially through all T=1000 timesteps. DDIM (Song et al., 2020): observes that DDPM's forward process doesn't need to be Markovian. Defines a family of non-Markovian forward processes q_σ(xₜ₋₁|xₜ,x₀) that have the same marginals q(xₜ|x₀) as DDPM. The reverse process for σ=0: xₜ₋₁ = √ᾱₜ₋₁ · (xₜ - √(1-ᾱₜ)·ε_θ(xₜ,t)) / √ᾱₜ + √(1-ᾱₜ₋₁)·ε_θ(xₜ,t). For σ=0: fully deterministic. Given xₜ and ε_θ(xₜ,t), we can compute x̂₀ = (xₜ - √(1-ᾱₜ)·ε_θ) / √ᾱₜ. Then xₜ₋₁ = √ᾱₜ₋₁·x̂₀ + √(1-ᾱₜ₋₁)·ε_θ(xₜ,t). Key insight: since the mapping is deterministic, we can skip timesteps. Instead of stepping t=1000→999→...→1, step through a subsequence τ = {τ₁,...,τS} with S=50. The trajectory is an ODE (probability flow ODE) — any ODE solver can be used. Consistency: starting from the same xₜ with σ=0, DDIM always produces the same image — enabling image interpolation by interpolating in the initial noise space.
evaluation_criteria: States the DDIM update equation with σ=0
Explains that the deterministic trajectory allows timestep skipping
Connects to the probability flow ODE
Notes the latent space consistency property
common_mistakes: Saying DDIM 'uses a different model' — it uses the same trained ε_θ as DDPM with a different sampling procedure
deep_dive.follow_up: How does consistency training (Consistency Models) further accelerate diffusion sampling to 1-2 steps?

deep_dive.question: Explain classifier-free guidance from the perspective of score functions. How does it implicitly combine a conditional and unconditional score?
deep_dive.model_answer: Score function perspective: the score of the conditional distribution is ∇_x log p(x|c). By Bayes: log p(x|c) = log p(c|x) + log p(x) - log p(c). Therefore: ∇_x log p(x|c) = ∇_x log p(c|x) + ∇_x log p(x). Classifier guidance (Dhariwal & Nichol, 2021): use ∇_x log p(c|x) from a separately trained classifier, scaled by guidance strength w: guided score = ∇_x log p(x) + w · ∇_x log p(c|x). At w=1: recovers the conditional score. At w>1: amplifies the classifier gradient, trading diversity for class adherence. Classifier-free guidance: train a single model that predicts both ε_θ(xₜ, c) (conditional) and ε_θ(xₜ, ∅) (unconditional, by dropping c). The conditional score ≈ -ε_θ(xₜ,c)/√(1-ᾱₜ) and unconditional score ≈ -ε_θ(xₜ,∅)/√(1-ᾱₜ). Guided score: ε̂ = ε_θ(xₜ, ∅) + w·(ε_θ(xₜ, c) - ε_θ(xₜ, ∅)) = (1-w)·ε_θ(xₜ, ∅) + w·ε_θ(xₜ, c). At w=1: pure conditional. At w>1: extrapolates beyond the conditional toward the high-density region of p(x|c) — sharpens the conditional distribution. This is score extrapolation — the same principle as reward upweighting in RLHF (emphasising the direction of improvement).
evaluation_criteria: Derives the conditional score decomposition via Bayes
States the guided score formula for CFG
Explains that w>1 extrapolates beyond the conditional distribution
Connects to classifier guidance as the predecessor
common_mistakes: Treating CFG as a simple interpolation — the w>1 extrapolation beyond p(x|c) is the key insight
deep_dive.follow_up: What is negative prompting in diffusion models and how does it relate to classifier-free guidance?

deep_dive.question: What is the architecture of a modern text-to-image Transformer (DiT)? How does it differ from UNet-based diffusion models?
deep_dive.model_answer: UNet-based diffusion (DDPM, SDXL): the denoising network is a UNet with: (1) Conv encoder (downsampling path). (2) Conv decoder (upsampling path) with skip connections. (3) Attention blocks at multiple scales. (4) Conditioning via cross-attention to text embeddings. Strong inductive biases (locality, translation equivariance). Hard to scale — the UNet architecture is relatively fixed. DiT (Diffusion Transformer, Peebles & Xie, 2023): replaces the UNet with a pure Transformer. Input: (1) Patchify the noisy latent xₜ (e.g., 32×32 latent with 2×2 patches → 256 tokens). (2) Add timestep embedding (sinusoidal + MLP) to each token via adaLN-Zero (adaptive layer normalisation): scale and shift the LayerNorm outputs based on the timestep conditioning. (3) Add class/text conditioning via adaLN-Zero. (4) L Transformer blocks (self-attention + FFN). (5) Unpatchify: linear layer maps tokens back to patch predictions. Advantages over UNet: (1) Clean, scalable architecture — can scale model size by adding blocks (DiT-S, DiT-B, DiT-L, DiT-XL). (2) Gflops ∝ model parameters — predictable scaling behaviour. (3) Isotropic (same resolution throughout) — no downsampling/upsampling complexity. Scaling results: DiT-XL/2 achieves state-of-the-art FID on ImageNet class-conditional. FLUX and SD3 use Multi-Modal DiT (MM-DiT) which processes image and text tokens jointly in the same Transformer layers via bidirectional attention.
evaluation_criteria: Explains patchification + unpatchification correctly
Describes adaLN-Zero for timestep/class conditioning
Contrasts with UNet on scalability and inductive biases
Mentions MM-DiT (FLUX/SD3) as the state of the art
common_mistakes: Treating DiT as just 'a Transformer version of UNet' without noting the architectural implications of isotropic resolution
deep_dive.follow_up: How does the adaLN-Zero initialisation strategy help stabilise training of deep DiT networks?

conceptual.question: Explain the Central Limit Theorem and its relevance to machine learning. Where does it break down?
conceptual.model_answer: CLT: for iid random variables X₁,...,Xₙ with mean μ and variance σ², the sample mean X̄ₙ = (1/n)Σ Xᵢ satisfies: √n(X̄ₙ - μ)/σ → N(0,1) as n → ∞. In machine learning relevance: (1) Mini-batch gradient estimation: the mini-batch gradient is an average of per-sample gradients. By CLT, this average is approximately normally distributed around the true gradient, with variance decreasing as 1/batch_size. This justifies using mini-batches as unbiased gradient estimators. (2) Loss convergence analysis: CLT underpins most PAC-learning generalisation bounds which assume iid samples. (3) Bootstrap: resampling-based confidence intervals for model evaluation rely on CLT for validity. Where it breaks down: (1) Heavy-tailed distributions: CLT requires finite variance. Gradient distributions in deep networks can be heavy-tailed (power law) — CLT convergence is extremely slow. Motivates gradient clipping. (2) Correlated data: CLT assumes iid. Time series, graph data, and sequential RL trajectories are correlated — standard CLT doesn't apply. Need mixing conditions. (3) Small n: CLT is asymptotic. For n < 30 (small batch sizes or evaluation sets), normality approximation may be poor. (4) Infinite-dimensional parameters: CLT in function spaces (Donsker theorem) requires different conditions.
evaluation_criteria: States the CLT correctly including the normalisation by √n
Connects to mini-batch gradient estimation
Identifies at least 2 breakdown conditions relevant to ML
Mentions heavy-tailed gradients and gradient clipping
common_mistakes: Saying CLT requires normally distributed inputs — it only requires finite mean and variance
conceptual.follow_up: What is the law of large numbers and how does it differ from the CLT in what it guarantees?

conceptual.question: Explain eigendecomposition and PCA from first principles. What do the eigenvalues and eigenvectors represent in the context of data?
conceptual.model_answer: Eigendecomposition: for a symmetric matrix A, A = QΛQᵀ where Q's columns are orthonormal eigenvectors and Λ = diag(λ₁,...,λₙ). Each eigenvector qᵢ satisfies Aqᵢ = λᵢqᵢ — it is a direction that A only stretches, not rotates. PCA from first principles: given data X ∈ ℝ^(n×d) (n samples, d features), centred so that Xᵀ1 = 0. The sample covariance matrix: C = (1/n)XᵀX ∈ ℝ^(d×d). Eigendecompose C = QΛQᵀ. The eigenvectors (principal components) q₁,...,qd are the directions of maximum variance in the data. λᵢ is the variance of the data projected onto qᵢ. The fraction of variance explained by the first k PCs: Σᵢ₌₁ᵏ λᵢ / Σᵢ₌₁ᵈ λᵢ. Projection: Z = XQ_k ∈ ℝ^(n×k) — the lower-dimensional representation. What eigenvalues/vectors mean: eigenvector = direction of a coherent pattern of variation in the data. For face images (Eigenfaces), PC1 captures the mean face variation (lighting), PC2 captures pose variation, etc. Eigenvalue = amount of variance along that direction. Near-zero eigenvalues indicate near-collinear features. Connection to SVD: X = UΣVᵀ. The right singular vectors V are the eigenvectors of XᵀX (= n·C). PCA via SVD is more numerically stable than explicitly forming C.
evaluation_criteria: States the eigendecomposition A = QΛQᵀ for symmetric matrices
Connects PCA to the covariance matrix eigendecomposition
Interprets eigenvalues as variance and eigenvectors as principal directions
Notes the SVD connection for numerical stability
common_mistakes: Saying PCA 'removes correlated features' — it finds orthogonal directions of maximum variance; removing correlation is a consequence
conceptual.follow_up: Why is PCA not appropriate as a preprocessing step for supervised learning in all cases? When can it hurt performance?

conceptual.question: What is Jensen's inequality? Give three examples of where it appears in ML theory.
conceptual.model_answer: Jensen's inequality: for a convex function f and a random variable X: f(E[X]) ≤ E[f(X)]. For concave f, the inequality reverses. Intuition: the function value at the average is less than or equal to the average of function values (for convex f). Three ML applications: (1) ELBO derivation in VAEs: log p(x) = log E_{q(z)}[p(x|z)p(z)/q(z)] ≥ E_{q(z)}[log(p(x|z)p(z)/q(z))] = ELBO. Since log is concave, Jensen gives the lower bound. The ELBO is maximised as a proxy for the intractable log p(x). (2) EM algorithm: in the E-step, Jensen's inequality bounds log p(x|θ) ≥ Σ_z q(z) log[p(x,z|θ)/q(z)] = Q(θ,θ_old) + H(q). Maximising Q in the M-step guarantees monotonic improvement of the log-likelihood. (3) KL divergence non-negativity: KL(p||q) = E_p[log p(X)/q(X)] = -E_p[log q(X)/p(X)] ≥ -log E_p[q(X)/p(X)] = -log 1 = 0 (by Jensen, since -log is convex). This proves KL(p||q) ≥ 0, with equality iff p=q.
evaluation_criteria: States Jensen's inequality correctly for both convex and concave f
Derives the ELBO application
Shows the EM application
Proves KL ≥ 0 via Jensen
common_mistakes: Applying Jensen in the wrong direction (confusing convex and concave cases)
conceptual.follow_up: When does equality hold in Jensen's inequality, and what does this imply for when the ELBO equals log p(x)?

conceptual.question: Explain the concepts of conjugate priors in Bayesian statistics. Give two examples and explain why they are computationally convenient.
conceptual.model_answer: Conjugate prior: a prior distribution p(θ) is conjugate to a likelihood p(x|θ) if the posterior p(θ|x) is in the same distributional family as the prior. The update is closed-form — no MCMC or variational inference needed. Example 1: Beta-Binomial. Likelihood: X ~ Binomial(n, θ). Prior: θ ~ Beta(α, β). Posterior: θ|X ~ Beta(α + X, β + n - X). The Beta parameters update by adding observed successes and failures. Widely used for A/B testing (click-through rate estimation). Example 2: Gaussian-Gaussian. Likelihood: X ~ N(μ, σ²) with known σ². Prior: μ ~ N(μ₀, τ²). Posterior: μ|X ~ N(μₙ, τₙ²) where μₙ = (μ₀/τ² + X/σ²) / (1/τ² + 1/σ²). The posterior mean is a precision-weighted average of prior and observed means. Why computationally convenient: (1) O(1) update: each new observation updates the sufficient statistics analytically. No optimisation required. (2) Sequential learning: natural online learning — process one observation at a time, updating the posterior. (3) Interpretable: Beta(α, β) can be interpreted as 'α successes and β failures' prior experience. In ML relevance: Bayesian linear regression (Gaussian prior on weights), Thompson Sampling for bandits (Beta-Binomial), Naive Bayes (Dirichlet-Categorical for text), Gaussian Mixture Models with Bayesian updates.
evaluation_criteria: States the definition of conjugate prior (posterior in same family as prior)
Correctly works through Beta-Binomial update
Correctly works through Gaussian-Gaussian update
Explains the O(1) sequential update advantage
common_mistakes: Saying conjugate priors are always 'the right choice' — they impose distributional assumptions that may not match reality
conceptual.follow_up: What is the Dirichlet distribution and why is it the conjugate prior for the categorical/multinomial likelihood?

conceptual.question: Explain the Expectation-Maximisation (EM) algorithm. Derive it for Gaussian Mixture Models.
conceptual.model_answer: EM: optimise log p(x|θ) = log Σ_z p(x,z|θ) when z is a latent variable (unobserved). Direct optimisation is hard due to the sum inside the log. EM: iteratively construct a lower bound (Jensen) and maximise it. E-step: compute responsibilities rᵢₖ = P(zᵢ=k|xᵢ, θ_old) — the posterior probability that sample i belongs to component k. M-step: maximise the expected complete-data log-likelihood Q(θ, θ_old) = E_z[log p(x,z|θ)]. Converges monotonically to a local maximum. GMM application: K Gaussian components with parameters θ = {πₖ, μₖ, Σₖ}ₖ₌₁ᴷ (mixing weights, means, covariances). E-step: rᵢₖ = πₖ N(xᵢ; μₖ, Σₖ) / Σⱼ πⱼ N(xᵢ; μⱼ, Σⱼ). M-step: Nₖ = Σᵢ rᵢₖ (effective count of samples in component k). πₖ = Nₖ/N. μₖ = (1/Nₖ) Σᵢ rᵢₖ xᵢ (responsibility-weighted mean). Σₖ = (1/Nₖ) Σᵢ rᵢₖ (xᵢ - μₖ)(xᵢ - μₖ)ᵀ (responsibility-weighted covariance). Repeat until convergence. Practical issues: initialisation matters (random init vs K-means init). Can converge to poor local optima. Covariance matrix can become singular if a component collapses to a single point — add regularisation (Σₖ + εI).
evaluation_criteria: States both E-step and M-step correctly in terms of the lower bound
Derives the GMM E-step (responsibilities) formula
Derives all three M-step updates (π, μ, Σ)
Addresses practical issues (initialisation, singularity)
common_mistakes: Confusing EM with K-means — K-means is a hard-assignment EM with unit covariance and hard cluster assignments
conceptual.follow_up: Prove that each EM iteration monotonically increases (or maintains) log p(x|θ).

conceptual.question: What are Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods? Explain the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm and its role in Bayesian ML.
conceptual.model_answer: MCMC: a class of algorithms for sampling from a complex probability distribution p*(x) known only up to a normalisation constant: p*(x) = p̃(x)/Z where Z = ∫p̃(x)dx is intractable. Used in Bayesian ML when the posterior p(θ|D) has no closed form. Metropolis-Hastings (MH): (1) Initialise θ₀. (2) At step t, propose θ' ~ q(θ'|θₜ) (a proposal distribution, e.g., Gaussian centred at θₜ). (3) Compute acceptance ratio: A = min(1, p̃(θ')q(θₜ|θ') / p̃(θₜ)q(θ'|θₜ)). (4) Accept: θₜ₊₁ = θ' with probability A, else θₜ₊₁ = θₜ. After a burn-in period, {θₜ} are samples from p*(x). Key property: detailed balance — the algorithm ensures the stationary distribution is p*. Normalisation constant Z cancels in the acceptance ratio — only p̃ is needed. Role in Bayesian ML: enables sampling from posterior distributions over model parameters when the posterior is complex (non-conjugate likelihoods, high-dimensional parameters). Used for: Bayesian neural networks (posterior over weights), Bayesian nonparametric models, exact Bayesian inference for small models. Limitations: slow mixing in high dimensions, correlated samples, requires many evaluations of p̃(θ) (expensive for neural networks). Alternatives: variational inference (faster, approximate), HMC (Hamiltonian MC — uses gradient information for faster mixing), NUTS (No-U-Turn Sampler, used in Stan and PyMC).
evaluation_criteria: States the MH acceptance ratio correctly
Explains that Z cancels in the ratio
Describes burn-in and correlated samples as limitations
Names HMC/NUTS as improved alternatives
common_mistakes: Saying MCMC 'requires the normalised distribution' — the normalisation constant cancels, which is the entire point
conceptual.follow_up: How does Hamiltonian Monte Carlo use gradient information to propose better moves and why does it mix faster than random walk MH?

applied.question: A model's predicted probabilities are systematically overconfident. How do you detect and fix calibration issues?
applied.model_answer: Calibration: a model is perfectly calibrated if P(correct | predicted probability p) = p for all p. Overconfident = predicted probability > actual accuracy at that confidence level. Detection: (1) Reliability diagram (calibration plot): bin predictions by confidence (e.g., 10 bins). For each bin, plot mean predicted confidence vs fraction of correct predictions. A perfectly calibrated model lies on the diagonal. Overconfident model lies above the diagonal. (2) Expected Calibration Error (ECE): ECE = Σₖ (nₖ/n)|acc(Bₖ) - conf(Bₖ)|. Weighted average absolute difference between accuracy and confidence per bin. (3) Brier score: mean squared error of probability predictions. Decomposes into calibration + resolution components. Causes of overconfidence: (1) NLL training without temperature scaling. (2) Small models trained on large datasets memorise training labels. (3) Label noise — model learns to be overconfident on noisy labels. Fixes: (1) Temperature scaling (Guo et al., 2017): post-hoc calibration — divide logits by a learned scalar T before softmax: p_calibrated = softmax(z/T). T > 1 makes distribution softer (less confident). T is tuned on a held-out calibration set (minimise NLL). Simple, effective, doesn't change accuracy. (2) Platt scaling: fit a logistic regression on the model's logits. (3) Isotonic regression: non-parametric calibration on the calibration set. (4) Label smoothing during training: prevents the model from driving log-probabilities to extremes.
evaluation_criteria: Describes the reliability diagram construction
Defines ECE
Proposes temperature scaling as the primary fix
Mentions label smoothing as a training-time prevention
common_mistakes: Conflating accuracy with calibration — a model can be 95% accurate and poorly calibrated
applied.follow_up: Why does temperature scaling preserve accuracy while improving calibration?

applied.question: Walk through a hypothesis test to determine whether Model A is significantly better than Model B on your evaluation dataset. What tests apply and what are the pitfalls?
applied.model_answer: Scenario: compare accuracy of Model A vs Model B on n test examples. Each example is correctly classified or not — Bernoulli outcome. Tests: (1) McNemar's test (recommended for paired classifiers): the test statistic focuses on the discordant pairs — examples where A is right and B is wrong (n₀₁) and where B is right and A is wrong (n₁₀). χ² = (|n₀₁ - n₁₀| - 1)² / (n₀₁ + n₁₀). Under H₀ (models are equivalent), this follows χ²(1). McNemar's is more powerful than a simple proportion test because it uses the paired structure. (2) Bootstrap confidence interval: resample the test set 1000 times with replacement. Compute accuracy difference on each resample. The 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles give a 95% CI for the true accuracy difference. If CI doesn't include 0, reject H₀. (3) Wilcoxon signed-rank test: non-parametric, for continuous metrics (F1, AUC) rather than binary correct/incorrect. Pitfalls: (1) Multiple comparisons: if you test many model variants, the probability of a false positive increases. Apply Bonferroni correction: p-value threshold = 0.05/K for K comparisons. (2) Test set reuse: if you've used the test set to tune Model A and B, it's no longer a held-out set. Need a fresh test set or adjust for adaptive data analysis. (3) Effect size vs statistical significance: with large n, even trivial differences (0.001%) become statistically significant. Always report effect size alongside p-value.
evaluation_criteria: Names McNemar's test and explains the discordant pairs
Proposes bootstrap as an alternative
Identifies multiple comparisons problem
Distinguishes statistical significance from practical effect size
common_mistakes: Using a t-test for binary accuracy differences — t-test assumes normally distributed continuous outcomes
applied.follow_up: How does adaptive data analysis (Dwork et al.) formalise the risk of test set reuse, and what is the holdout reuse theorem?

applied.question: Explain the mathematical intuition behind why neural networks trained with SGD generalise well despite being overparameterised. What does the loss landscape look like?
applied.model_answer: Classical theory: VC dimension of neural networks scales with the number of parameters — an overparameterised network can fit any labelling of n training points, implying zero generalisation guarantee from VC theory. Yet empirically, overparameterised networks generalise extremely well. Explanations: (1) Double descent: as model size increases beyond the interpolation threshold (where training loss = 0), generalisation error first rises then falls — the 'modern' overfitting regime. Overparameterised models interpolate in a way that is smooth (minimum norm interpolation), not arbitrary. (2) Implicit bias of SGD: gradient descent with small step sizes converges to solutions with minimum ℓ₂ norm in linearly overparameterised models. This is equivalent to the maximum margin solution, which generalises well. SGD has an implicit regularisation effect even without explicit regularisation. (3) Loss landscape: for wide networks, the loss landscape has many global minima (all achieving zero training loss) connected by paths of low loss ('loss valleys'). SGD finds a flat minimum — a region of the parameter space where the loss is low and insensitive to small parameter perturbations. Flat minima correlate with good generalisation (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997; Keskar et al., 2017). Sharpness-aware minimisation (SAM) explicitly searches for flat minima and improves generalisation. (4) Neural tangent kernel (NTK): in the infinite-width limit, NNs become linear in their parameters (kernel regime), where generalisation theory is well-understood. Practical takeaway: overparameterisation is not the enemy — the combination of overparameterisation + SGD + small step size creates an implicit bias toward solutions that generalise.
evaluation_criteria: Identifies the contradiction with classical VC theory
Explains double descent
Describes the implicit bias of SGD toward minimum norm / flat solutions
Mentions NTK or SAM
common_mistakes: Saying 'bigger models always overfit' — this is the classical view that double descent empirically refutes
applied.follow_up: What is the neural tangent kernel (NTK) and in what limit does it exactly characterise neural network training dynamics?

applied.question: Explain information theory concepts (entropy, mutual information, KL divergence) and their specific roles in ML algorithms.
applied.model_answer: Entropy H(X) = -Σ p(x) log p(x): measure of uncertainty/randomness in a distribution. High entropy = high uncertainty (uniform distribution). Low entropy = predictable (peaked distribution). In ML: (1) Decision tree splitting: maximise information gain = H(parent) - Σ wₖH(child_k). This greedily splits on the feature that most reduces uncertainty. (2) Maximum entropy principle: among all distributions consistent with constraints, choose the one with maximum entropy. Motivates softmax, logistic regression. Cross-entropy H(p,q) = -Σ p(x) log q(x): the average code length under q when the true distribution is p. In ML: the cross-entropy loss for classification = H(y_true, y_pred) = -Σ y_true log y_pred. Minimising cross-entropy loss ≡ MLE under the model. KL divergence KL(p||q) = Σ p(x) log(p(x)/q(x)) = H(p,q) - H(p): the 'extra bits' needed to encode samples from p using a code optimal for q. Always ≥ 0, not symmetric. In ML: VAE KL term, RLHF KL penalty (prevents policy from drifting), knowledge distillation loss. Mutual information I(X;Y) = H(X) - H(X|Y) = KL(p(x,y) || p(x)p(y)): amount of information X and Y share. Zero if independent. In ML: (1) Feature selection — select features with highest MI with the target. (2) ICA (Independent Component Analysis) — find components that minimise MI. (3) Representation learning (InfoNCE, MINE) — maximise MI between views of the same data.
evaluation_criteria: Defines entropy, cross-entropy, KL, and MI correctly
Gives concrete ML algorithm connections for each
Notes KL is not symmetric
Connects cross-entropy loss to MLE
common_mistakes: Conflating cross-entropy and KL divergence — they differ by H(p), which is a constant w.r.t. the model parameters
applied.follow_up: Why is forward KL (KL(p||q)) different from reverse KL (KL(q||p)) in terms of what behaviour they encourage in variational inference?

applied.question: What is the matrix rank, and how does low-rank structure arise and get exploited in ML systems?
applied.model_answer: Matrix rank: the number of linearly independent rows (= columns) in a matrix. A matrix M ∈ ℝ^(m×n) has rank r ≤ min(m,n). A rank-r matrix can be exactly factored as M = ABᵀ where A ∈ ℝ^(m×r), B ∈ ℝ^(n×r). Where low-rank structure arises in ML: (1) Weight matrices in neural networks: empirically, fine-tuned weight updates ΔW often have low intrinsic rank. LoRA exploits this — instead of updating W, update W + BA where rank(BA) = r ≪ min(m,n). r=4-64 instead of min(m,n)=768-4096. ~99% parameter reduction. (2) Recommendation systems: the user-item interaction matrix R ∈ ℝ^(|users| × |items|) is low rank — users share preferences, items share properties. Matrix factorisation: R ≈ UVᵀ where U ∈ ℝ^(|users|×k), V ∈ ℝ^(|items|×k), k=50-200. Collaborative filtering. (3) Attention matrices: the empirical attention matrix A ∈ ℝ^(n×n) is often low-rank — most attention patterns can be approximated with far fewer components. Linformer exploits this with a low-rank projection of K and V. (4) PCA/SVD: dimensionality reduction finds the best rank-k approximation to the data covariance. Eckart-Young theorem: the best rank-k approximation (in Frobenius or spectral norm) is given by the top k singular vectors/values of the SVD. (5) Neural network weight pruning: weights with small singular values contribute little to the output — truncate the SVD of each layer for compression.
evaluation_criteria: Defines rank correctly
Explains LoRA's low-rank factorisation of weight updates
Describes collaborative filtering as low-rank matrix factorisation
States the Eckart-Young theorem
common_mistakes: Confusing rank with the Frobenius norm — rank is the number of independent directions, not the magnitude of the matrix
applied.follow_up: How does the Eckart-Young theorem guarantee that PCA gives the optimal low-rank approximation to the data matrix?

deep_dive.question: Derive the EM algorithm's monotonic convergence property. Why does each iteration guarantee non-decreasing log-likelihood?
deep_dive.model_answer: Goal: maximise log p(x|θ) = log Σ_z p(x,z|θ). Introduce any distribution q(z). Decompose: log p(x|θ) = Σ_z q(z) log p(x|θ) (constant in z) = Σ_z q(z) log [p(x,z|θ)/q(z)] + Σ_z q(z) log [q(z)/p(z|x,θ)] = L(q,θ) + KL(q || p(z|x,θ)). Since KL ≥ 0: log p(x|θ) ≥ L(q,θ) for all q. L is a lower bound on the log-likelihood. E-step: set q(z) = p(z|x,θ_old). This makes KL = 0, so L(q,θ_old) = log p(x|θ_old) — the bound is tight. M-step: maximise L(q,θ) over θ with q fixed. This gives θ_new = argmax_θ L(q,θ) ≥ L(q,θ_old) = log p(x|θ_old). Monotonicity: log p(x|θ_new) ≥ L(q,θ_new) (KL ≥ 0) ≥ L(q,θ_old) (M-step maximises) = log p(x|θ_old) (E-step made bound tight). Therefore log p(x|θ_new) ≥ log p(x|θ_old). Each EM iteration increases (or maintains) the log-likelihood. Convergence to a local maximum: EM converges to a stationary point of the log-likelihood. Not necessarily the global maximum — initialisation matters.
evaluation_criteria: Derives the log p = L + KL decomposition
Shows that the E-step makes KL = 0 (tightens the bound)
Shows that the M-step increases L
Chains the inequalities to prove monotonicity
common_mistakes: Asserting monotonicity without the KL decomposition proof
deep_dive.follow_up: How does variational inference relate to EM — what happens when you can't compute the E-step exactly?

deep_dive.question: Explain the Cramér-Rao lower bound. What does it tell us about the efficiency of estimators, and why is MLE asymptotically efficient?
deep_dive.model_answer: Cramér-Rao Lower Bound (CRLB): for any unbiased estimator θ̂ of a parameter θ: Var(θ̂) ≥ 1/I(θ). Where I(θ) is the Fisher information: I(θ) = E[(∂/∂θ log p(x|θ))²] = -E[∂²/∂θ² log p(x|θ)]. The Fisher information measures how much information a single observation carries about θ. An estimator achieving Var(θ̂) = 1/I(θ) is called efficient. Derivation sketch: for any unbiased estimator, Cov(θ̂, s(x;θ)) ≤ √(Var(θ̂)·Var(s)) where s = ∂/∂θ log p(x|θ) is the score function. Since E[s]=0 (regularity condition), Cov(θ̂, s) = ∂/∂θ E[θ̂] = 1. By Cauchy-Schwarz: 1 ≤ Var(θ̂)·I(θ) → Var(θ̂) ≥ 1/I(θ). MLE asymptotic efficiency: √n(θ̂_MLE - θ₀) → N(0, 1/I(θ₀)) as n → ∞ (by the delta method and consistency of MLE). The asymptotic variance is 1/I(θ₀) — exactly the CRLB. MLE achieves the CRLB asymptotically — no unbiased estimator can do better in the limit. ML relevance: (1) Fisher information matrix (FIM) for neural networks: block-diagonal approximation (KFAC, EWC). (2) Natural gradient: scale gradient updates by the inverse FIM — updates in distribution space rather than parameter space. (3) EWC (Elastic Weight Consolidation): penalise changes to parameters with high Fisher information (important parameters) to prevent catastrophic forgetting.
evaluation_criteria: States the CRLB Var(θ̂) ≥ 1/I(θ)
Defines Fisher information correctly
States MLE's asymptotic efficiency
Connects FIM to natural gradient and EWC in ML
common_mistakes: Saying MLE is always efficient — it's only asymptotically efficient; for finite samples other estimators can be better
deep_dive.follow_up: What is the natural gradient and why does it converge faster than vanilla gradient descent for optimising the log-likelihood?

deep_dive.question: Explain singular value decomposition (SVD) in full. How does the truncated SVD provide the optimal low-rank approximation, and where is this used in ML?
deep_dive.model_answer: SVD: any matrix M ∈ ℝ^(m×n) can be decomposed as M = UΣVᵀ where U ∈ ℝ^(m×m) (orthogonal, left singular vectors), Σ ∈ ℝ^(m×n) (diagonal, singular values σ₁ ≥ σ₂ ≥ ... ≥ σᵣ ≥ 0, r = rank(M)), V ∈ ℝ^(n×n) (orthogonal, right singular vectors). The SVD always exists. Geometric interpretation: M transforms a unit sphere to an ellipsoid. Singular values are the semi-axis lengths. Left singular vectors are the output directions; right singular vectors are the input directions. Truncated SVD: keep only the top k singular values and vectors: Mₖ = UₖΣₖVₖᵀ. Eckart-Young theorem: Mₖ is the best rank-k approximation to M in both the Frobenius norm (||M-Mₖ||_F = √(σₖ₊₁² + ... + σᵣ²)) and spectral norm (||M-Mₖ||₂ = σₖ₊₁). No other rank-k matrix does better. ML applications: (1) PCA: data matrix X = UΣVᵀ. The top-k right singular vectors Vₖ are the principal components. Compressed representation Zₖ = XVₖ ∈ ℝ^(n×k). (2) Collaborative filtering: approximate user-item matrix R ≈ UₖΣₖVₖᵀ. (3) Word embeddings: GloVe uses SVD on the PMI (Pointwise Mutual Information) matrix of word co-occurrences. (4) LoRA: approximates ΔW ≈ BAᵀ with rank r — same as computing a rank-r SVD of ΔW. (5) Randomised SVD: for very large matrices, efficient approximation using random projections — O(mnk) instead of O(mn·min(m,n)).
evaluation_criteria: States the SVD decomposition with correct matrix dimensions
States the Eckart-Young theorem with both Frobenius and spectral norms
Connects to PCA, collaborative filtering, and LoRA
Mentions randomised SVD for large matrices
common_mistakes: Confusing eigendecomposition with SVD — eigendecomposition requires a square symmetric matrix; SVD works for any matrix
deep_dive.follow_up: How does the randomised SVD algorithm use random projections to efficiently compute the truncated SVD of a very large matrix?

deep_dive.question: Explain Gaussian Processes (GPs) as a Bayesian non-parametric model. What is the kernel function's role, and how does GP regression work?
deep_dive.model_answer: A Gaussian Process is a collection of random variables, any finite subset of which has a joint Gaussian distribution. Formally: f ~ GP(m(x), k(x,x')) where m(x) is the mean function (usually 0) and k(x,x') is the kernel (covariance function). The kernel encodes our prior beliefs about the function's properties: RBF kernel k(x,x') = σ² exp(-||x-x'||²/(2l²)): smooth, stationary functions. l is the length-scale (how quickly the function varies). Matérn kernel: less smooth, with controllable differentiability. Linear kernel: linear functions only. GP regression (GPR): observe n training points D = {X, y} where y = f(X) + ε, ε ~ N(0, σ_n²I). Prior: f ~ GP(0, K) where K[i,j] = k(xᵢ,xⱼ). Posterior (by Gaussian conditioning): P(f*|x*, D) = N(μ*, Σ*). μ*(x*) = k(x*, X) [K + σ_n²I]⁻¹ y (posterior mean). Σ*(x*, x*) = k(x*, x*) - k(x*, X) [K + σ_n²I]⁻¹ k(X, x*) (posterior variance). The posterior mean is the prediction; posterior variance is the uncertainty. Uncertainty decreases near training points. Hyperparameter learning: maximise the log marginal likelihood log p(y|X, θ) = -½ yᵀ(K+σ_n²I)⁻¹y - ½ log|K+σ_n²I| - n/2 log(2π). Computational bottleneck: inverting (K + σ_n²I) is O(n³). Sparse GP approximations (Nyström, inducing points) scale to larger datasets.
evaluation_criteria: Defines GP as a distribution over functions via the kernel
Derives the posterior mean and variance formulas
Explains the kernel's role (encoding function properties)
Identifies the O(n³) bottleneck and sparse GP solutions
common_mistakes: Saying GPs 'don't scale' without mentioning sparse approximations — they scale to millions of points with inducing point methods
deep_dive.follow_up: How do deep kernel learning and deep GPs extend GPs to handle complex, high-dimensional input spaces?

conceptual.question: What is AI alignment? Explain the core challenge and why it is considered an important problem.
conceptual.model_answer: AI alignment: the problem of ensuring that AI systems pursue goals that are consistent with human values and intentions. The core challenge: as AI systems become more capable, the gap between what we specify (the reward/objective) and what we actually want grows more consequential. Goodhart's Law: any measure used as an optimisation target ceases to be a good measure. Three levels of misalignment: (1) Specification misalignment: the objective we give the system doesn't capture what we actually want. Example: a cleaning robot that turns off the dirt sensor to report a clean house. (2) Robustness misalignment: the system behaves correctly in training distribution but fails under distribution shift or adversarial inputs. (3) Goal misgeneralisation: a system trained to achieve goal G in context C learns a proxy goal G' that correlates with G in C but diverges in new contexts. Why it's important at scale: a sufficiently capable system optimising even slightly misaligned goals can cause significant harm. The instrumental convergence thesis (Omohundro, Bostrom): capable AI systems pursuing almost any goal will converge on instrumental sub-goals like self-preservation, resource acquisition, and goal content integrity — potentially conflicting with human values. Current approaches: RLHF, Constitutional AI, interpretability research, scalable oversight (debate, recursive reward modelling).
evaluation_criteria: Distinguishes specification, robustness, and goal misgeneralisation
States Goodhart's Law and applies it
Explains instrumental convergence
Names current alignment approaches
common_mistakes: Treating alignment as purely a technical problem — value specification is fundamentally a philosophical and social problem
conceptual.follow_up: What is the orthogonality thesis and what does it imply about the relationship between intelligence and values?

conceptual.question: What is algorithmic fairness? Explain the three main fairness definitions and why they can be mutually incompatible.
conceptual.model_answer: Algorithmic fairness: ensuring that ML model decisions do not systematically disadvantage protected groups (race, gender, age, etc.). Three main definitions: (1) Demographic parity (statistical parity): P(Ŷ=1|A=0) = P(Ŷ=1|A=1). The positive prediction rate must be equal across groups A. Criticism: doesn't account for base rate differences between groups. Can require accepting lower accuracy for both groups to achieve parity. (2) Equalized odds (Hardt et al., 2016): TPR and FPR must be equal across groups: P(Ŷ=1|Y=1,A=0) = P(Ŷ=1|Y=1,A=1) and P(Ŷ=1|Y=0,A=0) = P(Ŷ=1|Y=0,A=1). Allows different base rates, ensures equal true positive and false positive rates. (3) Calibration (individual fairness proxy): P(Y=1|Ŷ=p, A=0) = P(Y=1|Ŷ=p, A=1) = p. The predicted probability p is accurate for all groups. The incompatibility result (Chouldechova, 2017; Kleinberg et al., 2016): when the base rates differ between groups (P(Y=1|A=0) ≠ P(Y=1|A=1)), demographic parity, equalized odds, and calibration cannot all be simultaneously satisfied except in degenerate cases. Implication: there is no one-size-fits-all fairness criterion — the choice depends on the application and whose error we care more about. Healthcare: equalized false negative rate (not missing disease). Lending: equalized false positive rate (not wrongly denying credit).
evaluation_criteria: States all three definitions correctly with formulas
Names the impossibility theorem and the condition (different base rates)
Explains why the incompatibility exists intuitively
Gives application-specific guidance
common_mistakes: Saying 'just remove the protected attribute' — protected attributes are often recoverable from correlated features, and removing them can hurt calibration
conceptual.follow_up: What is counterfactual fairness and how does it differ from statistical fairness definitions?

conceptual.question: What is model interpretability vs explainability? Compare LIME, SHAP, and attention-based explanations.
conceptual.model_answer: Interpretability: the degree to which a human can understand the model's internal mechanism — white-box, by design. Examples: linear models (coefficient = feature importance), shallow decision trees (follow the path), logistic regression. Explainability (XAI): post-hoc methods applied to black-box models to explain specific predictions. Does not make the model interpretable — it provides approximate explanations. LIME (Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations): for a specific prediction, perturb the input (randomly mask or substitute features), query the black-box model on perturbed inputs, fit a simple linear model to these local perturbations weighted by similarity to the original input. Output: linear feature importances for that specific prediction. Limitation: unstable — small changes to the input can produce very different explanations. SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations): computes the Shapley value of each feature — the average marginal contribution of that feature across all possible subsets of features. Theoretically grounded (satisfies efficiency, symmetry, dummy, additivity axioms). Consistent and locally accurate. TreeSHAP: O(TLD²) exact computation for tree ensembles. KernelSHAP: model-agnostic approximation. Limitation: expensive for large feature sets; assumes feature independence (can be misleading for correlated features). Attention-based explanations: visualise attention weights as feature importance. Limitation: attention is not explanation — high attention weight on a token doesn't mean that token is causal for the prediction. Jain & Wallace (2019) showed attention can be misleading.
evaluation_criteria: Distinguishes interpretability (by design) from explainability (post-hoc)
Describes LIME's local perturbation approach
Explains SHAP's Shapley value foundation and its axioms
Notes that attention ≠ explanation with citation
common_mistakes: Saying attention weights are feature importances — this is a widely cited misunderstanding
conceptual.follow_up: What are the four Shapley axioms and why do they make SHAP's feature attributions uniquely well-founded?

conceptual.question: What is differential privacy? Explain the (ε, δ)-DP definition and how it provides formal privacy guarantees.
conceptual.model_answer: Differential privacy (Dwork et al., 2006): a formal mathematical framework for privacy. Definition: a randomised mechanism M satisfies (ε, δ)-differential privacy if for all datasets D and D' differing in one record, and for all possible outputs S: P(M(D) ∈ S) ≤ exp(ε) · P(M(D') ∈ S) + δ. ε (privacy budget): controls how much the output distribution can differ between neighbouring datasets. Smaller ε = stronger privacy. ε=0 would mean identical output distributions (useless mechanism). ε ≈ 1-3 is considered strong privacy in practice. δ: a small probability of a complete privacy failure. Typically δ ≤ 1/n. For δ=0, pure DP is achieved (stricter). Interpretation: an adversary observing the output cannot determine with high confidence whether any individual was in the dataset. Key property: composability — the total privacy budget compounds across multiple analyses: (ε₁+ε₂, δ₁+δ₂)-DP for sequential composition. Mechanism: add calibrated Gaussian noise to the result: σ² = 2 ln(1.25/δ) · Δf² / ε² where Δf is the sensitivity (max change in the function due to one record). DP-SGD: clip per-sample gradients to bound sensitivity Δf = C, then add Gaussian noise N(0, σ²C²I) to the aggregated gradient. Enables DP training of neural networks at the cost of some model accuracy.
evaluation_criteria: States the (ε,δ)-DP definition correctly
Interprets ε as the maximum log-ratio of output probabilities
Explains δ as the catastrophic failure probability
Describes the Gaussian mechanism and DP-SGD
common_mistakes: Saying 'DP ensures data is anonymous' — DP provides probabilistic guarantees about what an adversary can infer, not full anonymisation
conceptual.follow_up: What is the privacy amplification by subsampling theorem and how does mini-batch training reduce the effective ε per step?

conceptual.question: What is adversarial robustness? Explain adversarial examples, why they exist, and what defenses are currently most effective.
conceptual.model_answer: Adversarial examples: inputs crafted by adding small, imperceptible perturbations (||δ||_p ≤ ε) to cause the model to misclassify: x_adv = x + δ such that f(x_adv) ≠ f(x). The perturbation is typically bounded in L∞ (max absolute pixel change) or L₂ norm. Why they exist: (1) High-dimensional input space: in d dimensions, many directions are nearly perpendicular to the decision boundary. A small step in these directions can cross the boundary with imperceptible visual change. (2) Linear hypothesis: Goodfellow et al. showed that a linear model with high-dimensional inputs is naturally susceptible — the dot product wᵀδ can be large even if each δᵢ is small (if w is large in many dimensions). (3) Non-smooth decision boundaries: neural networks learn piecewise linear decision boundaries — tiny input changes can jump across boundaries. Attacks: FGSM (Fast Gradient Sign Method): δ = ε · sign(∇_x L(x,y)). One-step gradient. PGD (Projected Gradient Descent): multi-step FGSM with projection back to the ε-ball. Strongest first-order attack. C&W attack: optimisation-based, finds minimum norm adversarial perturbation. Defenses: (1) Adversarial training (most effective): augment training data with adversarial examples. min_θ E[max_{||δ||≤ε} L(x+δ,y,θ)]. Expensive but provides certified robustness in some regimes. (2) Certified defenses: randomised smoothing — add Gaussian noise to inputs and certify predictions within a radius. Provides provable robustness guarantees. (3) Input preprocessing: JPEG compression, denoising — breaks gradient-based attacks but often vulnerable to adaptive attacks.
evaluation_criteria: Defines adversarial examples with the perturbation bound
Explains the linear model intuition for why they exist
Names FGSM and PGD attacks
Identifies adversarial training as the most effective defense
common_mistakes: Saying preprocessing defenses (JPEG, denoising) provide robust security — they typically fail against adaptive attacks
conceptual.follow_up: What is the certified robustness of randomised smoothing, and how does it provide provable guarantees?

conceptual.question: What is the AI risk taxonomy? Distinguish between near-term AI risks and long-term/catastrophic risks.
conceptual.model_answer: Near-term AI risks (present and emerging): (1) Bias and discrimination: models trained on biased data perpetuate or amplify societal biases in hiring, lending, criminal justice, healthcare. (2) Privacy violations: models that memorise training data, enable re-identification, or enable surveillance at scale. (3) Misinformation and deepfakes: generative AI enables synthetic media that deceives at scale. (4) Concentration of power: AI capabilities concentrated in few organisations creates economic inequality and geopolitical risk. (5) Job displacement: automation of cognitive tasks displacing knowledge workers faster than retraining can occur. (6) Safety-critical failures: autonomous vehicles, medical AI, infrastructure AI making errors with physical consequences. Long-term / catastrophic risks: (1) Misaligned superintelligence: a system more capable than humans optimising for a slightly misaligned objective could cause large-scale harm before humans could correct it. (2) Weaponisation: AI-enabled bioweapon design, autonomous weapons systems without human oversight. (3) Erosion of human autonomy: sufficiently capable AI systems making high-stakes decisions removes meaningful human agency. (4) Goal preservation and power-seeking: a capable AI system might resist shutdown or modification to preserve its goals (instrumental convergence). Frameworks for risk governance: EU AI Act (risk-based tiering: unacceptable, high, limited, minimal risk). NIST AI Risk Management Framework. Constitutional AI (Anthropic). Responsible Scaling Policies (RSPs).
evaluation_criteria: Clearly distinguishes near-term from long-term risk categories
Names at least 4 near-term risks with specificity
Describes at least 2 long-term risks with the underlying mechanism
Names a governance framework
common_mistakes: Treating AI risk as purely speculative (long-term only) or purely practical (near-term only) — both timescales are important
conceptual.follow_up: What is Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy (RSP) and how does it operationalise AI safety commitments?

applied.question: You are auditing a hiring algorithm used by a large employer. Design a complete fairness audit. What data do you need, what tests do you run, and what do you recommend?
applied.model_answer: A hiring algorithm audit has legal and ethical implications. Data needed: (1) Model predictions: scores/decisions for all applicants in the audit period. (2) Outcomes: who was hired, who progressed to interview — ground truth labels where available. (3) Protected attributes: gender, race, age, disability status — collected separately from the selection process for audit purposes. (4) Features used by the model: to check for proxy discrimination. Audit tests: (1) Disparate impact analysis: compute the selection rate for each protected group. The '4/5ths rule' (EEOC): if the selection rate for a protected group is < 80% of the majority group's rate, adverse impact is indicated. (2) Equalized odds check: compare true positive rates (qualified candidates selected) and false positive rates across groups. (3) Proxy feature analysis: run a feature attribution analysis (SHAP). If features highly correlated with protected attributes (zip code → race, name → gender) have high importance, the model may be discriminating via proxies. (4) Calibration check: is the score equally predictive of job performance across groups? (5) Intersectionality: audit not just single-attribute groups but intersections (e.g., Black women). Recommendations: (1) If adverse impact found: conduct adversarial debiasing or threshold adjustment per group. (2) Require post-hoc human review for any candidate rejected in a borderline score range. (3) Implement ongoing monitoring — run the audit quarterly. (4) Document the audit trail for regulatory compliance (GDPR Art.22, EEOC). (5) Consider whether the model should be used at all for this decision, given the high-stakes nature.
evaluation_criteria: Includes the 4/5ths rule for adverse impact
Checks for proxy discrimination via feature attribution
Includes intersectional analysis
Recommends ongoing monitoring, not just one-time audit
common_mistakes: Auditing only demographic parity without checking equalized odds — the two can give conflicting conclusions
applied.follow_up: What is the legal distinction between disparate treatment and disparate impact, and how do they each apply to AI hiring systems?

applied.question: Your company is deploying an LLM-powered medical information chatbot. What safety measures must be in place before deployment?
applied.model_answer: Medical chatbot risks: hallucination of medical facts, failure to recognise emergencies, providing inappropriate advice, patient reliance replacing professional care. Safety measures: Pre-deployment: (1) Red-teaming: hire clinical professionals and adversarial testers to find failure modes. Test: emergency recognition (suicidal ideation, chest pain), medication interactions, dangerous advice scenarios. Document all failures. (2) Clinical review: have medical professionals review the chatbot's responses across 500+ test cases covering the intended scope. Achieve a minimum acceptable accuracy threshold on factual medical questions. (3) Hallucination testing: specifically test for confident wrong answers on known medical facts. Measure factual error rate. (4) Scope limitation: define a strict scope (general health information only, not diagnosis or treatment advice). Implement prompt-level and output-level classifiers to detect out-of-scope queries. (5) Refusal calibration: the chatbot must appropriately refuse to diagnose, prescribe, or replace professional medical advice. Test that refusals are triggered correctly and not over-triggered on benign queries. At deployment: (6) Mandatory disclaimers: every response must include 'This is general health information only. Consult a healthcare professional for personalised medical advice.' (7) Emergency detection: a separate, reliable classifier detects mentions of suicidal ideation, chest pain, stroke symptoms, etc. These trigger immediate redirection to emergency services before any generated response. (8) Human escalation path: a clear 'talk to a nurse/doctor' button on every page. (9) Audit logging: every conversation logged (with consent) for retrospective review of adverse outcomes. (10) Staged rollout: limited beta with clinical oversight before full deployment.
evaluation_criteria: Includes clinical red-teaming and professional review
Specifies emergency detection as a separate classifier
Requires mandatory disclaimers
Proposes staged rollout with oversight
common_mistakes: Treating medical chatbot safety as just 'add a disclaimer' — the emergency detection and professional review requirements are non-negotiable
applied.follow_up: How would you design an evaluation benchmark to continuously monitor the medical chatbot's safety in production?

applied.question: A facial recognition system deployed by law enforcement has a false positive rate 5x higher for Black faces than white faces. Walk through the diagnosis and your recommendations.
applied.model_answer: This is a documented, real-world problem (NIST FRVT study confirmed this disparity across many commercial systems). Diagnosis: (1) Training data audit: what is the racial composition of the training set? Systems trained predominantly on lighter-skinned faces generalise poorly to darker-skinned faces. Check the label accuracy across demographic groups — annotation errors may be more common for minority groups. (2) Feature analysis: at what stage does the model diverge? Compare embedding space separability for images of different demographic groups. If embeddings for darker-skinned faces have higher within-class variance and lower between-class separation, the embedding model is undertrained for this group. (3) Evaluation breakdown: compute FAR (False Accept Rate) and FRR (False Reject Rate) separately for all demographic groups. Is it the embedding model or the matching threshold that's causing the disparity? (4) Vendor audit: request the vendor's internal NIST FRVT benchmark results by demographic group — this data should be publicly available. Recommendations: (1) Immediate: if the system is already deployed, impose a moratorium on using it for any decision that could result in arrest or detention until the disparity is addressed. (2) Re-evaluation: require threshold recalibration per demographic group to equalise false positive rates. (3) Retraining: augment training data with demographically balanced and high-quality datasets (including diverse skin tones, lighting conditions). (4) Human review mandate: require human officer review of all matches before any action is taken — no automated action on facial recognition alone. (5) Policy: consider whether law enforcement use of facial recognition should be limited or banned pending demonstrated equity across all groups.
evaluation_criteria: Identifies training data imbalance as the root cause
Proposes a moratorium on deployment pending investigation
Recommends per-group threshold recalibration
Advocates for human review as a mandatory safeguard
common_mistakes: Recommending only technical fixes without addressing the policy question of whether the system should be deployed at all
applied.follow_up: What is the NIST FRVT study and what did it find about demographic disparities in commercial facial recognition systems?

deep_dive.question: Explain mechanistic interpretability. What has it revealed about transformer circuits, and what is the importance of induction heads?
deep_dive.model_answer: Mechanistic interpretability: reverse-engineer neural networks to understand the algorithms implemented in their weights — not just what they do but how. Goal: identify circuits — subgraphs of attention heads and MLP neurons that implement specific computational functions. Key findings from Anthropic, Redwood, and collaborators: (1) Superposition: neural networks represent more features than they have dimensions by encoding many sparse features in superposition — features interfere but minimally. This means individual neurons are rarely monosemantic — they respond to many unrelated concepts. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are used to disentangle superposed features. (2) Induction heads: a specific two-attention-head circuit that implements the following algorithm: 'if I've seen [A][B] before in the context, and I currently see [A], predict [B].' The first head (previous-token head) attends to the previous token. The second head (induction head) attends to tokens that follow the same token as the previous-token head points to. Induction heads are the primary circuit underlying in-context learning — they implement pattern completion. They form at a specific training step ('phase change') and their formation coincides with the model's acquisition of ICL ability. (3) Curve detectors in CNNs: specific neurons in ResNets implement curve detection and colour detection in a human-interpretable way. (4) Indirect Object Identification (IOI) circuit: Olsson et al. identified the complete circuit in GPT-2 that identifies the indirect object in sentences like 'Mary and John went to the store. Mary gave [John] a bottle.' — spanning ~30 attention heads. Importance: mechanistic interpretability provides the only path to verified trust in AI systems — if we can understand the algorithm, we can audit it. Critical for AI safety.
evaluation_criteria: Explains the circuit concept in mechanistic interpretability
Describes induction heads and their two-head mechanism
Connects induction heads to in-context learning
Mentions superposition and sparse autoencoders
common_mistakes: Confusing attention visualisation with mechanistic interpretability — visualising attention weights is not the same as identifying circuits
deep_dive.follow_up: What are sparse autoencoders (SAEs) and how do they help identify monosemantic features in a superposition-compressed representation?

deep_dive.question: What is scalable oversight? Explain the debate, recursive reward modelling, and AI Safety via Debate approaches.
deep_dive.model_answer: Scalable oversight problem: as AI systems become more capable than human evaluators at many tasks, how do we verify that their outputs are correct and aligned? A human supervisor cannot directly evaluate the quality of a superhuman AI's reasoning. Three approaches: (1) Debate (Irving et al., 2018): two AI agents argue opposite positions to a human judge. The judge evaluates the debate, not the answer directly. Key insight: even if the judge cannot evaluate the answer directly, a dishonest agent must defend false claims against a capable adversary who can expose lies. If the judge can evaluate which agent's arguments are more compelling, and if the honest agent can always expose dishonest claims, then debate converges on truth. Limitation: requires the judge to correctly identify which argument is stronger, which may itself be difficult for complex claims. (2) Recursive Reward Modelling (RRM, Leike et al., 2018): break complex tasks into subtasks that humans can evaluate. A human evaluates decomposed sub-answers; a reward model is trained on these evaluations. The reward model is then used to train an AI that decomposes tasks for the human to evaluate. Recursive: the AI itself can help humans evaluate intermediate steps. (3) Weak-to-strong generalisation (Burns et al., 2024, OpenAI): train a strong model to be supervised by a weaker model. The strong model often generalises beyond what the weak supervisor can verify — suggesting that capability generalises even when training signal is weak. Bootstrapping technique for scalable oversight. Constitutional AI (Anthropic): use the AI itself to evaluate its outputs against a set of principles, reducing the human oversight bottleneck.
evaluation_criteria: States the scalable oversight problem clearly
Explains debate and the honesty assumption
Describes RRM's recursive decomposition
Mentions weak-to-strong generalisation
common_mistakes: Treating scalable oversight as a solved problem — all current approaches have significant limitations and open research questions
deep_dive.follow_up: What is the eliciting latent knowledge (ELK) problem and why does it present a fundamental challenge for scalable oversight approaches?

deep_dive.question: Explain the theoretical basis for why neural networks can exhibit emergent capabilities. What does emergence mean formally and what are the debates around it?
deep_dive.model_answer: Emergent capabilities (Wei et al., 2022): abilities that are not present (or near-zero performance) at small scale but appear sharply at larger scale — as if appearing discontinuously. Examples: multi-step arithmetic, chain-of-thought reasoning, calibration, multilingual translation without multilingual training. Formal definition: a capability is emergent if it is not predictable by smooth extrapolation from smaller models' performance. Theoretical explanations: (1) Metric discontinuity (Schaeffer et al., 2023 critique): many 'emergent' capabilities are artifacts of non-linear metrics. When evaluated with continuous metrics, the improvement is smooth. Multi-step tasks measured by exact-match accuracy (0 or 1 per task) show apparent emergence because the task requires all steps to be correct — a model at 90% per-step accuracy gets 0.9^10 = 34% overall, while a model at 95% gets 59%. The phase transition is in the metric, not the model. (2) Phase transitions in the loss landscape: neural network training can exhibit phase transitions — sudden changes in learned representations at specific scales. The formation of induction heads at a specific training step is an example. These are true discontinuities. (3) Critical phenomena: analogies to statistical physics — emergent behaviour in complex systems arises from phase transitions near critical points. (4) Task complexity: some tasks genuinely require a minimum level of representational capacity — below which they're impossible, above which they're achievable. Not a smooth transition. The debate: Schaeffer et al. argue most emergence is illusory (metric artifact). Others argue some emergence (induction head formation) is real. The distinction matters for AI safety — if capabilities emerge discontinuously, pre-emptive safety measures are harder to deploy.
evaluation_criteria: Defines emergence as absence of smooth extrapolation from smaller models
Presents the metric discontinuity critique (Schaeffer et al.) fairly
Explains the phase transition argument for real emergence
Notes why emergence matters for AI safety
common_mistakes: Accepting either extreme — claiming all emergence is real or all is illusory — without acknowledging the empirical nuance
deep_dive.follow_up: How do interpretability findings about induction head formation provide evidence for true (non-metric-artifact) emergence?

deep_dive.question: What is model cards and datasheets for datasets? Explain the information they capture and why they are necessary for responsible AI deployment.
deep_dive.model_answer: Model Cards (Mitchell et al., 2019): standardised documentation for ML models, capturing: (1) Model details: architecture, training procedure, evaluation metrics, contact information. (2) Intended use: primary use cases and out-of-scope uses. (3) Factors: relevant demographic or environmental factors that affect model performance. (4) Evaluation data: what test sets were used, how they were constructed. (5) Performance metrics: disaggregated across subgroups (gender, race, age, geography). (6) Ethical considerations: potential harms, potential biases, caveats. (7) Recommendations: deployment guidance, mitigation strategies. Datasheets for Datasets (Gebru et al., 2018): documentation for training/evaluation datasets, capturing: (1) Motivation: why was the dataset created? Who funded it? (2) Composition: what is in it? Who are the subjects? Are there sensitive data types? (3) Collection process: how was it collected? Over what time period? Is there consent? (4) Preprocessing: what was done to the data? (5) Uses: appropriate and inappropriate uses. (6) Distribution: how is it distributed? Under what licence? (7) Maintenance: who maintains it? What's the update policy? Why necessary: (1) Audibility: model cards enable external auditors to understand what a model can and cannot do. (2) Accountability: documents who is responsible for the model. (3) Bias disclosure: disaggregated metrics surface disparate performance. (4) Informed deployment: deployers can assess suitability for their context. (5) Regulatory compliance: increasingly required by law (EU AI Act requires technical documentation). Limitations: model cards can be incomplete, self-reported, and not independently verified.
evaluation_criteria: Names the key sections of both model cards and datasheets
Explains why disaggregated metrics in model cards are critical
Connects to regulatory requirements
Notes the self-reporting limitation
common_mistakes: Treating model cards as just marketing documents — their value is specifically in documenting limitations and failure modes
deep_dive.follow_up: What additional documentation is required under the EU AI Act for high-risk AI systems beyond what a standard model card provides?

conceptual.question: Explain the Fourier transform and the Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT). Why is the spectrogram used as input to speech models?
conceptual.model_answer: Fourier Transform: decomposes a signal f(t) into its frequency components. F(ω) = ∫ f(t) e^(-iωt) dt. For a pure sine wave at frequency ω₀: F(ω) is a delta spike at ω₀. Limitation for speech: global Fourier transform loses temporal information — a speech signal has different frequencies at different times (consonants, vowels, intonation changes). Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT): divide the signal into short overlapping frames (typically 25ms duration, 10ms hop), apply a window function (Hann, Hamming) to each frame to reduce edge artifacts, compute the DFT of each frame. STFT(t, ω) = ∫ f(τ) w(τ-t) e^(-iωτ) dτ. Output: 2D time-frequency representation. Magnitude |STFT(t,ω)|² = power spectrogram. Mel spectrogram: map the frequency axis to the Mel scale (logarithmic, matching human auditory perception). Mel scale emphasises lower frequencies where speech energy is concentrated. Apply a filterbank of triangular filters at Mel-spaced frequencies. Log-Mel spectrogram: take log of the Mel power — further compresses the dynamic range, matching human loudness perception (Weber-Fechner law). Why used for speech models: (1) Compact representation: reduces 16kHz raw audio (~16k values/sec) to ~100 frames/sec × 80 Mel bins = 8k values/sec. (2) Perceptually meaningful: Mel scale and log compression match how humans perceive pitch and loudness. (3) Translation-equivariant for frequency: pitch shifts appear as translations in the Mel axis, enabling learned frequency-invariant features. Whisper, wav2vec 2.0, and other speech models use log-Mel spectrograms as input.
evaluation_criteria: States the Fourier transform formula
Explains why STFT is needed (temporal resolution)
Describes the Mel scale and its perceptual motivation
Explains why log compression matches human perception
common_mistakes: Confusing the Mel scale with the Hz scale — Mel is logarithmic and perceptually motivated
