conceptual.question: Explain the CTC (Connectionist Temporal Classification) loss. How does it enable end-to-end speech recognition without forced alignment?
conceptual.model_answer: Traditional ASR required forced alignment — manually aligning each audio frame to a specific phoneme label. Time-consuming, requires expert linguists, error-prone. CTC (Graves et al., 2006): enables end-to-end training by marginalising over all possible alignments. Setup: input is a sequence of T frames, output is a target sequence of U characters (U << T). The model (RNN/Transformer) outputs a distribution over (vocabulary + blank token ε) at each timestep. CTC alignment: a valid alignment maps T frames to U characters by: (1) Collapsing repeated characters and (2) Removing blank tokens. Example: target='cat', T=8. Valid alignment: [c, c, ε, a, ε, t, t, ε] → collapse repeats and remove blanks → 'cat'. Loss: marginalise the probability over all valid alignments: P(y|x) = Σ_{all valid alignments π} Π_t P(πₜ|x). Computed efficiently via dynamic programming (forward-backward algorithm). Gradient: backpropagated through the dynamic programming to update the model. Key property: the model learns to align speech to characters without any labelled alignment data — alignment is a latent variable. Limitation: CTC assumes conditional independence between output tokens given the input — cannot model language model context. Modern ASR: combine CTC with an attention-based decoder (hybrid CTC/attention, used in Whisper's encoder-decoder structure).
evaluation_criteria: Explains the forced alignment problem CTC solves
Describes the blank token and collapsing rules
States that CTC marginalises over all valid alignments
Notes the conditional independence limitation
common_mistakes: Saying CTC 'finds the best alignment' — it marginalises over all alignments, not just the best one
conceptual.follow_up: How does the forward-backward algorithm compute the CTC loss in O(T·U) time instead of enumerating all alignments?

conceptual.question: What is speaker diarisation? What are the main components of a modern diarisation pipeline?
conceptual.model_answer: Speaker diarisation: 'who spoke when?' — segment an audio recording by speaker identity without knowing how many speakers or their identities in advance. Output: a sequence of (speaker_label, start_time, end_time) segments. Main pipeline components: (1) Voice Activity Detection (VAD): distinguish speech from non-speech (silence, music, noise). Binary classifier on audio frames. WebRTC VAD, Silero VAD. (2) Segmentation: divide the audio into short homogeneous segments (typically 1-2s), ensuring each segment contains a single speaker. Change point detection: detect when the speaker changes using PLDA (Probabilistic Linear Discriminant Analysis) distance between consecutive window embeddings. (3) Speaker embedding extraction: extract a speaker representation for each segment. X-vectors: TDNN-based speaker embeddings trained with speaker classification. ECAPA-TDNN: state-of-the-art speaker embeddings. d-vectors: LSTM-based, originally from Google. (4) Clustering: group segments by speaker identity. Agglomerative Hierarchical Clustering (AHC) with cosine distance between speaker embeddings. Spectral clustering: often more robust, especially when the number of speakers is unknown. (5) Resegmentation / overlap detection: refine segment boundaries. Detect overlapping speech regions (two speakers simultaneously). Handle these specially — most basic systems assign overlapping regions to one speaker. (6) Output: RTTM (Rich Transcription Time Mark) format. Evaluation: DER (Diarisation Error Rate) = missed speech + false alarm + speaker error / total speech duration.
evaluation_criteria: Names all pipeline components in order
Identifies VAD as the first stage
Names speaker embedding models (x-vectors, ECAPA-TDNN)
Names DER as the evaluation metric
common_mistakes: Treating diarisation as just speaker recognition — diarisation additionally requires segmentation, VAD, and clustering
conceptual.follow_up: What is the difference between x-vectors and d-vectors, and how does ECAPA-TDNN improve upon x-vectors?

conceptual.question: Compare end-to-end speech recognition models. Contrast CTC-based, attention-based seq2seq, and models like Whisper.
conceptual.model_answer: Three end-to-end ASR paradigms: (1) CTC-based (wav2vec 2.0, HuBERT + CTC head): encoder maps audio frames to representations, CTC head predicts character/subword at each frame. Trains fast, decodes fast. Cannot model output dependencies (conditional independence assumption). Often combined with a separate language model for beam search. (2) Attention-based encoder-decoder (Listen, Attend and Spell — LAS): encoder processes audio, attention-based decoder generates transcript autoregressively. Can model output dependencies (knows what it already generated). Slower to train and decode. Streaming is harder. (3) Whisper (Radford et al., 2022): large-scale weak supervision. Trained on 680,000 hours of internet audio (including YouTube subtitles — weakly labelled). Architecture: Transformer encoder-decoder. Encoder: log-Mel spectrogram → 2D conv layers → Transformer encoder. Decoder: text tokens with cross-attention to encoder output. Multitask: trained simultaneously on ASR, translation (speech-to-English), language identification, VAD, and timestamp prediction. Strengths: exceptional generalisation to diverse accents, languages, domains, and recording conditions — no fine-tuning needed. Weaknesses: not streaming (offline only), larger latency than CTC-based models. State of the art: Whisper large-v3 is the best general-purpose offline ASR. For streaming/low-latency: conformer + CTC (Conformer combines CNN local feature extraction with Transformer global attention — best of both).
evaluation_criteria: Correctly describes CTC, attention-based, and Whisper paradigms
Identifies streaming as a CTC advantage
Explains Whisper's weak supervision training approach
Names the Conformer as the streaming state of the art
common_mistakes: Saying Whisper 'fine-tunes on each language' — Whisper's strength is that it works zero-shot across languages
conceptual.follow_up: How does the Conformer architecture combine CNNs and Transformers, and why does this combination work well for speech?

conceptual.question: What is text-to-speech (TTS)? Explain the pipeline from text to waveform and compare neural TTS architectures.
conceptual.model_answer: TTS pipeline: Text → Phonemes/tokens → Acoustic model (mel spectrogram) → Vocoder (waveform). Text preprocessing: (1) Text normalisation: '12/3/2024' → 'December third, twenty twenty-four'. Numbers, abbreviations, currencies. (2) Grapheme-to-phoneme (G2P): convert written text to phonetic representations (IPA or custom phoneset). Handles heteronyms ('read' present vs past tense). Acoustic model (text → mel spectrogram): Tacotron 2: sequence-to-sequence with attention. Encoder encodes phoneme sequence; attention-based decoder generates mel spectrogram frame by frame. Slow (autoregressive), can have alignment failures (skipping words). FastSpeech 2: non-autoregressive. Predicts duration, pitch, and energy per phoneme, then generates mel spectrogram in parallel. Much faster, more robust alignment. VITS: end-to-end model combining acoustic model and vocoder using variational inference and flow-based models. Generates waveform directly. Vocoder (mel spectrogram → waveform): WaveNet: autoregressive, highest quality, very slow. WaveGlow: normalising flow, fast, high quality. HiFi-GAN: GAN-based, very fast (real-time), high quality. Standard choice for production. Modern approaches: VALL-E (Microsoft): audio codec language model — represents audio as discrete codec tokens, generates tokens autoregressively from text + 3-second speaker prompt. Zero-shot voice cloning. Bark, StyleTTS2: other recent high-quality open-source systems.
evaluation_criteria: Describes the full text → phoneme → spectrogram → waveform pipeline
Contrasts Tacotron (autoregressive) with FastSpeech (non-autoregressive)
Names HiFi-GAN as the standard production vocoder
Mentions VALL-E as a modern approach
common_mistakes: Treating TTS as just 'a model that generates speech' without describing the modular pipeline
conceptual.follow_up: How does VALL-E achieve zero-shot voice cloning from a 3-second speaker reference audio?

conceptual.question: What is self-supervised learning for audio? Explain wav2vec 2.0 and HuBERT's pretraining approaches.
conceptual.model_answer: Self-supervised learning for audio: learn rich speech representations from unlabelled audio by predicting masked or future frames. No human transcriptions needed. wav2vec 2.0 (Baevski et al., 2020): (1) Feature encoder: raw waveform → local features via 1D CNN (stacked CNN with downsampling, ~20ms per frame). (2) Quantisation: discretise continuous features into a finite codebook (product quantisation). (3) Context encoder: Transformer over the sequence (some frames are masked before this step). (4) Objective: contrastive loss — the model must identify the correct quantised representation for each masked frame among distractors. (5) Fine-tuning: add a linear classification head, fine-tune with CTC on labelled data. With only 10 minutes of labelled data, achieves competitive WER on Librispeech. HuBERT (Hidden-Unit BERT, Hsu et al., 2021): (1) Cluster assignment: offline K-means clustering on MFCC features (or previous HuBERT representations) assigns a discrete label to each frame. (2) BERT-style masking: mask ~50% of frames. (3) Prediction loss: predict the cluster labels of masked frames (cross-entropy). The model must learn to predict the cluster assignment from context — forcing it to learn structure. Iterative: repeat with better cluster assignments from the previous HuBERT model. Key difference from wav2vec 2.0: HuBERT uses offline cluster targets (simpler, more stable) vs wav2vec's online quantisation with contrastive loss. Both produce state-of-the-art speech representations for downstream ASR, speaker recognition, and emotion recognition.
evaluation_criteria: Describes wav2vec 2.0's quantisation and contrastive loss
Describes HuBERT's offline clustering and masked prediction
Notes the key difference between them
Quantifies the low-resource ASR performance

applied.question: Design an end-to-end voice assistant pipeline that understands natural speech commands and controls a smart home. Include all components and latency targets.
applied.model_answer: Pipeline stages and latency targets (target: < 500ms end-to-end): (1) Wake word detection (always-on, 5ms): lightweight keyword spotting model (KeywordBERT or a small LSTM) running on-device. Detects 'Hey [Assistant]'. Small model < 1MB, running continuously at low power on a dedicated microcontroller. (2) Voice Activity Detection (10ms): confirm speech is present after wake word. Silero VAD. (3) Speech-to-Text (150ms): Whisper small or a streaming Conformer CTC model. For lowest latency: streaming CTC with beam search, chunk-based processing (process audio in 160ms chunks). On-device or edge server. (4) Natural Language Understanding (50ms): intent classification + entity extraction from the transcript. Model: DistilBERT fine-tuned on home automation commands. Output: {intent: 'turn_on', entity: 'living room lights'}. Or: send transcript directly to an LLM API (GPT-4o-mini) for open-ended understanding — higher latency but more flexible. (5) Smart home action (100ms): execute intent via the home automation API (Matter, Zigbee, HomeKit). Async — don't wait for device confirmation before responding to user. (6) Text-to-Speech response (150ms): FastSpeech 2 + HiFi-GAN for synthesising the response ('Turning on the living room lights'). On-device or edge. Total: ~500ms perceived latency. Optimisations: stream TTS output — start playing audio before full synthesis is complete. Cache common phrases ('Done', 'I didn't understand that'). Fallback: if STT confidence < threshold, ask for clarification.

Proposes wake word detection as always-on low-power step
Addresses streaming for STT to reduce latency
Proposes TTS streaming for perceived latency reduction
common_mistakes: Not addressing wake word detection as a separate always-on component
Ignoring latency targets — specifying a model without estimating its contribution to the pipeline

applied.question: You need to build a call centre quality assurance system that transcribes calls, classifies customer intent, and detects agent compliance failures. Design the system.
applied.model_answer: Scale: assume 10,000 calls/day, average 5 minutes each. Processing: offline (not real-time). Pipeline: (1) Audio ingestion and preprocessing: calls stored as stereo audio (agent + customer channels). Split channels if stereo, or use diarisation if single channel. Normalise audio volume. Resample to 16kHz mono. (2) Speech-to-text: Whisper large-v3 with word-level timestamps. Process each channel separately (agent transcript + customer transcript). Batch processing via Celery workers. At 5 min audio: ~15-20s transcription on GPU. (3) Customer intent classification: classify the customer's call intent from the transcript. Fine-tuned BERT on call centre dataset with 20-30 intent categories (complaint, billing query, cancellation, etc.). Run on customer transcript. (4) Sentiment analysis: track customer sentiment over the call timeline. DistilBERT fine-tuned on call centre utterances. Detect sentiment degradation (escalating frustration). (5) Agent compliance checking: rule-based + ML. Rule-based: check for mandatory disclosures ('This call may be recorded', GDPR consent phrases) using regex. ML-based: fine-tuned classifier detecting: inappropriate language, failure to follow script, promised callbacks not offered. (6) Call scoring: combine compliance score + resolution outcome + customer sentiment into an overall QA score. Flag calls below threshold for human supervisor review. (7) Dashboard: per-agent statistics, trend analysis, flagged calls queue. Storage: transcripts + metadata in PostgreSQL, audio in S3, embeddings in a vector DB for semantic search across calls.
evaluation_criteria: Addresses stereo channel separation
Includes word-level timestamps for alignment
Separates rule-based (mandatory disclosure) from ML-based compliance
Includes a human review queue for flagged calls
common_mistakes: Using a single model for both transcription and compliance — these are very different tasks requiring specialised models
applied.follow_up: How would you handle calls in multiple languages in a single system, given that your compliance classifiers are English-only?

applied.question: Design a system to detect audio deepfakes (synthetic or cloned voice audio). What signals distinguish real from generated speech?
applied.model_answer: Audio deepfake detection: determine whether a speech recording is genuine or synthetically generated/cloned. This is a binary classification problem but with an adversarial component — attackers will try to evade detectors. Feature signals distinguishing real from fake: (1) Codec artifacts: synthetic audio often passes through a vocoder (WaveNet, HiFi-GAN) which introduces characteristic spectral artifacts — non-speech regions, fricatives, and sibilants often sound 'too clean'. (2) Prosody unnatural patterns: TTS systems often have unnaturally uniform prosody. Real speech has micro-variations in pitch and timing that TTS struggles to replicate. (3) Breathing and ambient noise: real recordings contain background noise and breathing at consistent microphone distance. Synthetics often lack realistic microphone and room acoustic fingerprints. (4) Anti-spoofing features: LFCC (Linear Frequency Cepstral Coefficients) with an LCNN (Light CNN) — the ASVspoof challenge benchmark. AASIST (Audio Anti-Spoofing using Integrated Spectro-Temporal Graph Attention Networks): state-of-the-art on ASVspoof 2021. System design: (1) Input: raw audio or log-Mel spectrogram. (2) Model: AASIST or an ensemble of detection models (different feature types reduce evasion). (3) Hardening: regularly update the detector with new synthetic audio as generative models improve. Adversarial training with known deepfake samples. (4) Confidence threshold: flag as 'uncertain' for human review rather than binary classification. (5) Provenance: watermark genuine audio at recording time (AudioSeal, SynthID for audio) — proactive approach. Limitations: detector always lags behind generator — it's an arms race.
evaluation_criteria: Identifies specific acoustic signals distinguishing real from fake
Names AASIST or LCNN as anti-spoofing models
References the ASVspoof benchmark
Addresses the adversarial arms race problem
common_mistakes: Treating deepfake detection as a solved problem — it is an ongoing adversarial contest between generators and detectors
applied.follow_up: How does AudioSeal's watermarking approach differ from passive detection, and what are its limitations in terms of tamper resistance?

applied.question: You are deploying Whisper for multilingual transcription of meeting recordings. What pre- and post-processing steps improve accuracy for domain-specific vocabulary?
applied.model_answer: Challenge: Whisper has excellent general-purpose multilingual ASR but struggles with domain-specific terms (medical, legal, technical jargon), proper nouns, and product names. Pre-processing: (1) Audio quality enhancement: apply a noise suppressor (DeepFilterNet, RNNoise) before Whisper if recordings have background noise. Resample to 16kHz. Normalise volume. (2) Language detection: if language is unknown, run Whisper's language detection on the first 30 seconds. Set the detected language as a prompt to avoid autoregressive language switching. (3) Context prompt: Whisper accepts an initial prompt that biases the decoder. Include domain-specific terms, speaker names, and company names in the prompt: 'This is a meeting at Anthropic discussing Claude, RLHF, and Constitutional AI.' This dramatically reduces proper noun errors. Post-processing: (4) Domain vocabulary correction: after transcription, run a spelling correction pass using a domain-specific vocabulary list. Fuzzy match low-confidence words against known terminology. (5) Punctuation and capitalisation: Whisper produces these but may be inconsistent. Run a punctuation restoration model if needed. (6) Speaker labels: run diarisation (pyannote.audio) and align speaker labels to word timestamps from Whisper. Match diarisation segments to Whisper word-level timestamps. (7) Acronym expansion: expand known acronyms (LLM → Large Language Model) for readability. Fine-tuning for high-volume domains: if processing > 1000 meetings/month on the same domain, fine-tune Whisper on 10-50 domain-specific recordings with corrected transcripts. LoRA fine-tune on the decoder for vocabulary adaptation.
evaluation_criteria: Proposes context prompting as the first-line improvement
Includes audio pre-processing for noise
Addresses speaker label alignment with diarisation
Recommends fine-tuning for high-volume domain use
common_mistakes: Not knowing about Whisper's initial prompt feature — it's the single most impactful improvement for domain-specific vocabulary
applied.follow_up: How would you evaluate the transcription quality improvement from your post-processing steps in a way that scales without requiring human transcription of every recording?

applied.question: Compare spectrogram-based and waveform-based audio models. When would you choose raw waveform input over a spectrogram?
applied.model_answer: Spectrogram-based models: process the log-Mel spectrogram or MFCC as a 2D image-like input. Models: CNNs, ViT (Audio Spectrogram Transformer), Whisper encoder. Advantages: (1) Compact: 80-128 Mel bins × 100 frames/sec — much smaller than raw audio (16,000 samples/sec). (2) Perceptually motivated: Mel scale and log compression match human hearing. (3) Mature: decades of feature engineering in speech community. (4) Enables 2D CNN: exploit image classification architectures (ResNet, ViT). Disadvantages: (1) Lossy: STFT + Mel binning discards phase information. (2) Fixed resolution: the time-frequency resolution tradeoff (Heisenberg) means you can't have both fine time resolution and fine frequency resolution simultaneously. (3) Not end-to-end: two-stage pipeline (preprocessing + model). Waveform-based models: process raw audio samples directly. Models: WaveNet, SampleCNN, wav2vec 2.0 (uses 1D CNN feature encoder), EnCodec. Advantages: (1) Lossless: all audio information preserved including phase. (2) Learns optimal features for the task. (3) Phase-sensitive tasks: music transcription, high-fidelity synthesis, audio watermarking require phase. Disadvantages: (1) Long sequences: 16kHz × 5min = 4.8M samples — attention is infeasible without aggressive downsampling. (2) Harder to train: fewer inductive biases. Choose raw waveform when: phase information matters (high-fidelity synthesis, audio forensics, music processing). Choose spectrogram when: speech recognition, audio classification, speaker recognition — where Mel-scale features are well-established and high-quality pretrained models exist.
evaluation_criteria: Correctly states advantages of each approach
Identifies phase as the key information lost in spectrograms
Notes the sequence length problem for waveform models
Gives concrete guidance for when to choose each
common_mistakes: Saying waveform models 'always learn better features' — spectrogram-based models with Mel features have decades of domain knowledge baked in and are often superior for speech tasks
applied.follow_up: How does EnCodec's neural audio codec represent audio as discrete tokens, and why is this useful for audio language models?

deep_dive.question: Derive the CTC forward algorithm. How does dynamic programming compute the log-likelihood in O(T·U) time?
deep_dive.model_answer: Setup: T input frames, U target characters y = (y₁,...,y_U). Define modified target sequence l' by inserting blank ε between and around all characters: l' = (ε, y₁, ε, y₂, ..., ε, y_U, ε) of length 2U+1. Forward variable: α(t, s) = probability of producing l'₁:s in the first t timesteps, while ending at position s in l'. Initialisation: α(1, 1) = P(ε|x₁), α(1, 2) = P(y₁|x₁), α(1, s) = 0 for s > 2. (The output can only start with ε or y₁.) Recurrence: for t > 1, s > 0: α(t, s) = P(l'_s|xₜ) · [α(t-1, s) + α(t-1, s-1) + (if l'_s ≠ ε and l'_s ≠ l'_{s-2}) α(t-1, s-2)]. The three terms: stay at position s (repeated character), come from position s-1 (advance one step), come from position s-2 (skip a blank — only when the current character ≠ the character two positions back to avoid merging distinct characters). The conditional independence assumption (CTC): P(πₜ|xₜ) for each frame is independent of other frames given the input features xₜ. This is what makes the factorisation tractable. Log-likelihood: P(y|x) = α(T, 2U) + α(T, 2U+1) (can end at last character or trailing blank). Complexity: T × (2U+1) states, each computed in O(1) from at most 3 previous states. Total: O(T·U). Computing the exact loss without DP would require summing over all O(2^T) possible alignments.
evaluation_criteria: Defines α(t,s) correctly
States the initialisation conditions
States the recurrence with all three cases
Derives O(T·U) complexity
common_mistakes: Forgetting the third recurrence term (skip-blank transition) — this handles the case where two identical consecutive characters must be separated by a blank
deep_dive.follow_up: How does the backward algorithm for CTC pair with the forward algorithm to compute the gradient of the CTC loss with respect to the softmax outputs?

deep_dive.question: Explain the Conformer architecture. How does combining convolutional and attention modules address the limitations of each?
deep_dive.model_answer: Conformer (Gulati et al., 2020): designed specifically for speech — combines the global context of Transformers with the local pattern modelling of CNNs in a single block. Motivation: Transformers capture long-range dependencies via attention (global RF from layer 1) but are weak at local feature extraction. CNNs excel at local temporal pattern modelling (onset, offset, articulation) but have limited RF without many layers. Standard Transformer block: MHA → FFN. Conformer block: ½ FFN → MHA → Conv Module → ½ FFN. Feed-forward (first ½ FFN): macaron-style — half the residual weight (0.5 instead of 1.0). Promotes gradient flow. Multi-Head Attention: relative positional encoding (not absolute) — uses sine functions encoding relative distances, robust to sequence length variation. Critical for speech where positional generalisation matters. Convolutional Module: LayerNorm → pointwise conv (expand channels 2×) → gated linear unit (GLU) activation → depthwise conv (kernel size 31, captures ~310ms at 10ms frame rate) → Batch Norm → pointwise conv → dropout. The depthwise conv with kernel 31 captures phoneme-level (~100-200ms) temporal patterns without the computational cost of full convolution. Feed-forward (second ½ FFN): symmetry with the first. Conformer achieves state-of-the-art on Librispeech (1.9% WER test-clean with language model), outperforming both pure Transformer and pure CNN architectures. Used in the Transducer (RNN-T) framework for streaming ASR.
evaluation_criteria: States the Conformer block order correctly (½FFN → MHA → Conv → ½FFN)
Explains why relative positional encoding is used instead of absolute
Describes the depthwise conv kernel size and its temporal coverage
Connects to Librispeech benchmark performance
common_mistakes: Saying the Conformer 'just adds CNNs to a Transformer' — the specific ordering, macaron FFN, and relative positional encoding are all deliberate design choices
deep_dive.follow_up: How does the RNN-Transducer (RNN-T) framework enable streaming ASR, and how is the Conformer used as the encoder in this framework?

deep_dive.question: Explain neural vocoders. Derive why autoregressive WaveNet is extremely slow, and how WaveGlow and HiFi-GAN overcome this.
deep_dive.model_answer: A vocoder converts an acoustic feature sequence (mel spectrogram) to a raw audio waveform. Neural vocoders learn this mapping end-to-end. WaveNet (Oord et al., 2016): autoregressive. P(x) = Π_{t=1}^T P(xₜ | x₁,...,xₜ₋₁, h) where h is the conditioning mel spectrogram. Architecture: dilated causal convolutions with exponentially increasing dilation rates (1, 2, 4, 8, ..., 512, 1, 2, ...) to achieve large RF with few layers. Output: 256-class categorical over quantised audio (μ-law companding). Why slow: must generate one sample at a time autoregressively. At 24kHz, generating 1 second = 24,000 sequential forward passes. Wall-clock time: ~1000s per second of audio on a GPU with a standard WaveNet. Practically unusable for real-time TTS. WaveGlow (Prenger et al., 2019): normalising flow — learns an invertible mapping from Gaussian noise z to audio x. Forward: z → x (generation, single pass through the flow). Inverse: x → z (training). Affine coupling layers: split z into two halves, use one half to predict scale and shift for the other. All samples generated in parallel: O(T) instead of O(T × forward passes). Fast: ~25× faster than WaveNet. HiFi-GAN (Kong et al., 2020): GAN-based. Generator: upsampling network (transposed convolutions progressively upsample mel frames to audio samples at 256× ratio). Multi-receptive field fusion (MRF): parallel residual blocks with different kernel sizes capture different scales of audio structure. Discriminators: Multi-Period Discriminator (MPD) + Multi-Scale Discriminator (MSD) evaluate audio at multiple resolutions. Training: adversarial + feature matching + mel reconstruction loss. Inference: single forward pass through the generator. Speed: real-time (faster than WaveGlow) with higher quality. Gold standard for production TTS.
evaluation_criteria: Derives why WaveNet requires T sequential passes and quantifies the slowness
Explains WaveGlow's parallel generation via normalising flows
Describes HiFi-GAN's upsampling generator and MRF
Identifies HiFi-GAN as the production standard
common_mistakes: Saying WaveGlow 'runs in O(1)' — it's O(T) like all waveform models; the gain is that all T samples are computed in parallel, not sequentially
deep_dive.follow_up: How does the multi-period discriminator in HiFi-GAN evaluate audio quality at different periodicity scales, and why is this important for natural-sounding speech?

deep_dive.question: Explain the signal processing foundation of MFCCs. How are they computed from raw audio, and why were they dominant in pre-deep-learning ASR?
deep_dive.model_answer: MFCC (Mel-Frequency Cepstral Coefficients) computation pipeline: (1) Pre-emphasis: apply a high-pass filter to boost high frequencies: s'[t] = s[t] - α·s[t-1], α ≈ 0.97. Compensates for the natural spectral roll-off of speech (~-6dB/octave). (2) Framing and windowing: divide signal into 25ms frames with 10ms hop. Apply Hamming window: w[n] = 0.54 - 0.46 cos(2πn/(N-1)). Reduces spectral leakage from frame boundaries. (3) DFT: compute the N-point DFT of each frame. Take the magnitude squared |X[k]|² = power spectrum. (4) Mel filterbank: apply M (typically 26-40) triangular filters at Mel-spaced frequencies. Sum the energy in each filter's frequency range. Mel(f) = 2595 log₁₀(1 + f/700). Produces M-dimensional Mel energies. (5) Log: take the log of each Mel energy. Matches human loudness perception (decibel scale) and stabilises variance. (6) DCT (Discrete Cosine Transform): decorrelates the log-Mel energies. The first C coefficients (C=12-13) are the MFCCs. The DCT compresses the information, removing correlated filterbank outputs. (7) Dynamic features: append Δ (velocity) and ΔΔ (acceleration) MFCCs — first and second derivatives. Captures temporal dynamics. Final feature: 39-dimensional vector (13 + 13 + 13) per frame. Why dominant pre-deep learning: (1) Compact: 39 features vs thousands of raw samples. (2) Speaker normalisation: DCT+log partially normalise for speaker differences. (3) Robust to linear channel effects (convolution in time = addition in cepstrum). (4) Pair naturally with Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs) and Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) — the dominant ASR architecture until 2012.
evaluation_criteria: Correctly describes all 6-7 computation steps
Explains why log is applied (perceptual motivation)
Explains why DCT is applied (decorrelation)
Explains the Δ and ΔΔ features
common_mistakes: Skipping the pre-emphasis or DCT steps — these are specific to MFCCs vs raw Mel filterbank features
deep_dive.follow_up: Why did deep neural networks largely replace hand-engineered features like MFCCs for ASR after 2012, and what is the tradeoff in low-resource scenarios?
